# vLLM

> vLLM is a high-throughput, memory-efficient inference and serving engine for large language models.

## Core pages

- [Home](https://vllm.ai): vLLM project homepage and overview.
- [Blog](https://vllm.ai/blog): Technical articles, release announcements, model guides, and community updates.
- [Events](https://vllm.ai/events): Community meetups, office hours, conferences, and release events.
- [Office Hours](https://vllm.ai/office-hours): Bi-weekly vLLM livestream: schedule, recordings, and slides from every session.
- [Releases](https://vllm.ai/releases): Recent vLLM releases and release notes.
- [Contact](https://vllm.ai/contact): Community and partnership contact channels.

## Blog posts

- [Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-20-inkling2-mini): vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
- [Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-18-flydsl-monokernels): How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
- [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-deepseek-v41-flash-vera-rubin): On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 387 tokens/s per user, 58x GB300 NVL72 at the same interactivity.
- [Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-inkling2-small): vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
- [H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-minimax-h3-image-rubin): H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware.
- [Reinforcement Learning: Optimizing 0.6B Dense Models on TPU v7 via vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-rl-small-dense-tpu-v7): Co-designing RL for a Qwen3-0.6B dense policy on Google Cloud TPU v7 across vLLM, Tunix, MaxText, and Pallas, with a 107x end-to-end speedup from ~100 minutes to ~56 seconds per true-8K RL cycle.
- [Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-11-encoder-disaggregation-epd): Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
- [Migrating vLLM to the LibTorch Stable ABI](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-06-stable-abi-cuda): How vLLM migrated its CUDA build and compiled dependencies to the LibTorch Stable ABI, enabling compatible PyTorch upgrades without rebuilding vLLM.
- [VeRL-Omni v0.3.0: Async Training and Broader Multimodal Post-Training](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-06-verl-omni-v0-3-0): VeRL-Omni v0.3.0 expands async RL, makes the V1 trainer the default, and adds reproducible recipes for audio-video generation and multimodal understanding.
- [Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-06-zero-mismatch-async-rl): Asynchronous RL trains on stale weights. Align rollout and training kernels bit for bit, and unclipped importance sampling corrects that lag. Plus zero-mismatch RL for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.
- [Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference): Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.
- [vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-04-kimi-k31-pro): vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode.
- [Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4): Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell.
- [Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at Scale: vLLM Matches DeepInfer and Scales to GB300 NVL72](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep): With P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP on a GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9x our aggregated single-node result.
- [GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse): vLLM serves GLM-5.3 on 16 H200s with PCP and DCP prefill and Hybrid HiSparse decode, reaching 1M-token contexts and 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of data-parallel P/D on the AgentX agentic benchmark.
- [vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-minimax-m31-flash): Day-0 vLLM support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Blackwell, NVIDIA Rubin, and AMD MI350-series GPUs, with NVFP4 MSA kernels, NVFP4 MegaMoE, DSpark speculative decoding, AgentX results, and day-0 RL.
- [Day-0 Support for Flint on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-21-flint): vLLM supports both Flint checkpoints (40B total, 2.5B active) from day 0, decoding a single request at about 500 tokens/s on one GPU.
- [Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-21-humming): Introducing Humming, a quantized inference kernel library from Ant Group and the vLLM community, with broad GPU and quantization support, dense and MoE performance results, and vLLM integration.
- [Introducing vLLM TorchTPU](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-20-vllm-torchtpu): vllm-torchtpu is a new vLLM backend for Google Cloud TPUs built on TorchTPU, with Pallas kernels, multi-host parallelism, KV cache offloading, and disaggregated serving.
- [Achieving near-zero-downtime scaling in Elastic Expert Parallelism](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-19-elastic-ep-near-zero-downtime): How asynchronous preparation and NIXL EP enabled near-zero-downtime Elastic EP scaling in vLLM.
- [Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel): How agent-assisted CuTe DSL optimizations accelerate Kimi K3 decode on NVIDIA GB300, and how scoped changes, correctness tests, and reproducible benchmarks help ship them responsibly.
- [Scaling Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X: Matching NVIDIA HGX B300 Throughput per GPU on AgentX](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-mi355x): Inside the Kimi K3 optimization effort: understanding the bottlenecks and the decisions that made inference faster
- [Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-reflection-beam): vLLM supports Reflection's Beam-1.0 (501B total, 23B active) from day 0, with agent-driven optimization that cut decode latency 2.71× and DFlash2 speculative decoding with adaptive verification.
- [Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-15-muse-spark-open): Day-0 vLLM support for Muse Spark Open: 816B MoE, 1M context, multimodal inputs, DSpark speculative decoding, NVIDIA and AMD serving, initial TPU support, and LoRA RL.
- [Announcing Day 0 Support for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-15-nemotron-3-5-super-vl-vllm): Run NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on vLLM for multimodal agent workflows with image, document, and video understanding, OpenAI-compatible serving, and multi-token prediction.
- [Adaptive Verification Without a Confidence Head](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-adaptive-verification-online-estimator): An online-fitted acceptance estimator that lets every draft-model speculator use Adaptive Verification, by predicting the target's acceptance probability from the drafter's own logits and refitting continuously during serving.
- [Push-Based KV Transfer to Improve TTFT and TPOT for Disaggregated Inference in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector): A push-based NIXL connector for vLLM disaggregated serving: the prefill instance writes KV directly into decode memory over RDMA, taking the router relay, decode-side allocation, and transfer setup off the TTFT critical path.
- [Finish RL Training Faster: Bitwise-Consistent, High-Performance, Agent-Driven](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-train-inference-consistency): We make vLLM rollout and the training forward give bitwise identical logprobs on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (NVFP4), keep 91% of rollout throughput on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and open-source the agent skill.
- [Improve TTFT for Multi-Turn Agentic Workloads with Bi-Directional KV Transfer in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-12-bidirectional-kvxfer-multiturn-agentic-workload): Bi-directional KV transfer lets vLLM prefill nodes reuse previously computed KV from decode nodes on later conversation turns, cutting redundant prefill recompute and reducing TTFT by up to 3.3x on long multi-turn prompts.
- [MAGI-2 Preview on vLLM-Omni: Bringing a 114B Audio-Video MoE DiT to Moore Threads MUSA with torchada](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-12-magi2-preview-musa): vLLM-Omni runs Sand AI's MAGI-2 Preview audio-video generation model on eight Moore Threads MTT S5000 GPUs through torchada's CUDA compatibility layer, then optimizes MoE, mHC, attention, parallelism, and compilation.
- [vLLM Support for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72: 7.8x Throughput over GB200 NVL72](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-09-vera-rubin-preview): vLLM now runs on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 with day-0 model support, Rubin-tuned FlashInfer kernels, and locality-aware MoE, delivering 7.8x the per-GPU throughput of GB200 NVL72 on AgentX.
- [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on vLLM: 5x Agentic Throughput Since Day 0](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-07-deepseek-v41-flash): Within three weeks of release, vLLM made DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1.9x faster at low concurrency and lifted its throughput 5x on SemiAnalysis AgentX, with SWA bounded replay, CUDA graphs, DeepSeek's new kernels, and vLLM kernel fusions.
- [Taking vLLM Apart: A Practical Guide to Disaggregated Serving](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-29-disaggregated-serving-guide): What disaggregated serving actually buys you, how to run it end to end in vLLM today with prefill/decode plus the new GPU-less frontend and the things we're still working on.
- [Watermarking in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-24-watermarking-in-vllm): How vLLM implements distribution-preserving Gumbel-max text watermarking with efficient GPU kernels, statistical detection, speculative decoding, and repeated-context safeguards.
- [Reducing vLLM startup time with one uv flag](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-22-python-bytecode-startup): Shipping Python bytecode saved about 18 seconds per startup in H100 server benchmarks, with images and models already local.
- [Announcing vllm-metal: Concurrent Serving on Apple Silicon](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-22-vllm-metal-v0-28-0): vllm-metal brings vLLM's paged, continuously batched serving stack to Apple Silicon, with flatter TTFT under concurrent agent load, batched MTP, and automatic M5 prefill acceleration.
- [PD Serving of Qwen3.8-2.4T](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-21-qwen38-pd-serving): How vLLM reaches 5K throughput and 180 interactivity on Qwen3.8-2.4T with GB300 NVL72 PD serving and how to reproduce results yourself.
- [Scaling Multi-GPU Video Captioning with PyNvVideoCodec and vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-18-pynvvideocodec): How to leverage NVIDIA Hardware Video Decoders to Achieve Multi-GPU Scaling in Video Captioning and Description tasks.
- [How we trained the fastest DSpark for Kimi-K3 using GB300 NVL72](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-15-kimi-k3-dspark): How Speculators and Mooncake enabled multi-node DSpark training for Kimi K3.
- [vLLM x Novita AI: Chord, Faster INT4 MoE for Kimi K2.x. Up to 1.3x on H200, 2.15x on Untuned B300](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-15-novita-chord-w4a16-moe): Novita AI has open-sourced Chord, a high-performance W4A16 MoE CUDA kernel for Kimi K2.x serving shapes, with a Humming-compatible indexed path and grouped SM90 operators.
- [vime × RL-Kernel × AMD: Bitwise Train–Rollout Consistency on ROCm](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-14-rl-kernel-v0-1-0-train-rollout-bitwise-consistency): vime and RL-Kernel align selected-token logprobs bit for bit across Megatron training and vLLM rollout on AMD Instinct MI300X, with zero mismatches across 200 GRPO steps.
- [Kimi K3 Performance Optimizations in vLLM: The Road to 2.8× Throughput](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-13-kimi-k3-performance-optimization): Kimi K3 serving optimizations across scheduling, KDA prefix caching, ReplaySSM state recovery, PD disaggregation and state offload, parallelism, MoE, and GPU kernels.
- [Following the Bottleneck: Optimizing MiniMax M3 on AMD Instinct MI355X](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-10-minimax-m3-mi355x): A performance model for LLM serving: inspect local shapes, remove repeated work, verify data movement and dispatch, then follow the queue.
- [Tiered KV Cache Offloading in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-10-tiered-kv-offloading): A host-centric framework for scaling KV cache across host memory, filesystems, object stores, and remote peers — reducing recomputation and increasing serving capacity.
- [GLM 5.3 Optimizations, Part 1: Hybrid HiSparse Offloading in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-glm53-part1-hybrid-sparse-offloading): vLLM integrates HiSparse as a pressure-driven memory tier that composes with the Hybrid Memory Allocator and KV offloading, letting GLM 5.3 requests keep decoding when their KV no longer fits in GPU memory, so concurrency stays high.
- [vLLM x AgentX: Optimizing for Real-World Agentic Serving](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx): How vLLM optimizes KV cache management, parallelism, scheduling, and P/D disaggregation for agentic workloads, validated on SemiAnalysis AgentX with up to 130K tokens per GPU-second and a 14.6x-106x serving-cost advantage over Opus 5.
- [Serving LLMs on Tenstorrent Hardware: Inside the vLLM TT Plugin](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-07-vllm-tt-plugin): Tenstorrent accelerators join vLLM as an out-of-tree platform plugin, driven by mesh-architecture choices: phase-based scheduling, single-process data parallelism on Galaxy, on-device sampling with host fallback, and async decode overlap.
- [MiniMax H3 on vLLM-Omni: From System-Wide Optimization to Real-Time Serving with FastVideo’s FastH3](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-01-minimax-h3-production-serving): How vLLM-Omni optimizes and scales the complete MiniMax H3 stack, then integrates FastVideo’s four-step FastH3 for generation faster than playback.
- [Exploring Speculative Decoding in vLLM on AMD GPUs](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-23-speculative-decoding-amd-gpus): A practical guide to speculative decoding in vLLM on AMD GPUs, covering draft-and-verify mechanics, MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark, configuration, tuning, and benchmark results.
- [Large-Scale Sharded Weight Transfer with Ray Direct Transport (RDT) in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-22-rdt-weight-transfer): We implement a native sharded weight transfer engine in vLLM utilizing Ray Direct Transport (RDT), achieving weight transfer for the Kimi K2 model in BF16 on 48 8xH100 nodes in 7.53s
- [IsoExec: Unified Execution to Eliminate Trainer-Inference Mismatch in SkyRL](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-21-isoexec): IsoExec unifies numerical execution across SkyRL's vLLM and Megatron runtimes, reducing the average rollout-versus-training logprob difference below 1e-6 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with 25% overhead.
- [VeRL-Omni v0.2.0: Faster Diffusion RL and Stable Omni Training](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-20-verl-omni-v0-2-0): A release focused on higher-throughput diffusion rollout, reusable omni adapters, and broader recipe coverage.
- [Distributed Layerwise Offload: Scaling Toward 200B+ DiT Models Efficiently in vLLM-Omni](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-17-distributed-layerwise-offload): Distributed Layerwise Offload shards and streams DiT weights across devices, serving a measured 124 GB Cosmos3 model on 64 GB HBM and estimating a path toward 200B+ models.
- [Adaptive Verification in vLLM: DSpark confidence-scheduled verification](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-14-dspark-adaptive-verification): Sizing the DSpark draft-verification budget from per-request confidence instead of verifying every drafted token, so one configuration holds the throughput/latency frontier from batch size 1 to 256.
- [Day 0 Support for Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-12-qwen3.8): Day-0 vLLM support for Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B: a 2.4-trillion-parameter hybrid MoE model served out of the box, with FP8/BF16 checkpoints plus NVFP4 and MXFP4 quantized weights, and co-developed kernels on NVIDIA and AMD hardware.
- [Announcing Day-0 Support for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-10-nemotron-3-5-lightning-vllm): How vLLM serves NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning with OpenAI-compatible APIs, speculative decoding, and BF16/NVFP4 checkpoints across NVIDIA GPUs and edge systems.
- [Efficient Decode Context Parallelism with vLLM for Long Context Workloads](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-07-decode-context-parallelism): Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) in vLLM shards KV cache across GPUs by sequence dimension, enabling 3× higher throughput on long-context agentic workloads compared to standard tensor parallelism.
- [vLLM Reaches 25K Total TPS/GPU on Qwen3.5](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-06-qwen35-25k-tps): How vLLM reaches 25K total TPS/GPU on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4 with GB200 NVL72 disaggregated serving, Blackwell GDN kernels, HMA cache transfer, async scheduling fixes, and srt-slurm recipes.
- [Optimizing vLLM on Arm CPUs](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-29-optimizing-vllm-on-arm-cpus): An overview of Arm CPU enablement and inference performance optimizations in vLLM.
- [Parallel All the Way Down: Beyond Single-Token Generation with Speculative Decoding](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-28-speculators-parallel-drafting): Speculators and vLLM now support P-EAGLE, DFlash, and DSpark — three parallel drafting algorithms that move beyond sequential token generation to deliver faster, simpler, and more scalable speculative decoding for LLM serving.
- [Kimi K3 Is Here: Efficient Day-0 Support on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-27-k3): vLLM delivers day-0 Kimi K3 serving with hybrid KDA prefix caching, DSpark speculative decoding, production-scale disaggregation, and optimized kernels across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.
- [From Day 0 to Production SLAs: Serving GLM-5.2 on 24 NVIDIA B300 GPUs with vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-23-glm-5.2-nvfp4-b300-pd): How we took GLM-5.2-NVFP4 from 40 ms to 17 ms mean TPOT on 24 B300 GPUs with vLLM: P/D disaggregation, MTP speculative decoding, Model Runner V2, and the SLA-first trade-offs behind the final configuration.
- [Announcing vLLM AFD Plugin: Disaggregating Attention and FFN for Flexible MoE Serving](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-23-vllm-afd-plugin): What vLLM AFD Plugin adds to the vLLM ecosystem: Attention–FFN disaggregation for MoE serving, GPU and Ascend NPU backends, connector-based execution, and graph and ubatching support.
- [A Preview of Production-Scale Kimi K3 Support on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-22-kimi-k3-preview): A preview of production-scale Kimi K3 support in vLLM, including KDA-aware prefix caching, fused kernels, optimized MXFP4 MoE, multimodal integration, and initial NVIDIA and AMD paths.
- [Beyond a Single Model: Building Mixture-of-Models Systems with vLLM Semantic Router](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-21-vllm-sr-new-chapter-mom): vLLM Semantic Router is expanding from intelligent routing into a system for building, evaluating, and running Mixture-of-Models.
- [Keeping vLLM Production Quality: A Look Inside CI, Benchmarking, and the Release Process](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-16-keeping-vllm-production-quality): How vLLM maintains production quality with extensive CI across diverse accelerators, nightly performance benchmark and accuracy evaluation, and a two-week release process.
- [TML Inkling on vLLM: Day-0 Support with Optimized Performance](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-15-inkling): vLLM brings day-0 support to TML Inkling, a 1T-parameter multimodal model, with MTP, long-context serving, parallelism, and up to 380 tokens per second per user on NVIDIA GB200 GPUs.
- [vLLM x TileRT: Specialized Decode for Latency-Critical Serving](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-14-vllm-tilert-pd): vLLM prefill paired with TileRT decode through vLLM V1's connector interface: a specialized, latency-optimized decode engine that coexists with native vLLM decode behind one shared serving layer, with zero changes to vLLM.
- [EAGLE3 Speculative Decoding on AMD Instinct GPUs: Training and Serving with vLLM and AMD Quark](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-13-eagle-3-amd-instinct): How AMD Quark trains, quantizes, and serves EAGLE3 speculative-decoding drafts with vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, delivering up to 2.00x throughput gains for Kimi-K2.5 and 1.79x for MiniMax-M2.5.
- [vime + ROCm: End-to-End RL Post-Training on AMD Instinct™ GPUs](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-10-vime-rocm): Announcing ROCm support for vime, now running end-to-end on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs with prebuilt container.
- [vLLM × HPC-Ops: High-Performance Attention and MoE Backends from Tencent Hunyuan](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-06-vllm-hpc-ops): How HPC-Ops integrates Hopper-optimized attention and FP8 MoE backends into vLLM for Tencent Hunyuan Hy3, improving mixed-length decode, MoE latency, TTFT, and TPOT on NVIDIA H20.
- [Experience and Lessons Learned from Serving Multi-Stage Qwen3-Omni in vLLM-Omni](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-07-01-qwen3-omni-optimization): How vLLM-Omni serves and optimizes Qwen3-Omni with staged Thinker-Talker-Code2Wav execution, batching, CUDA Graphs, async chunk, async output, replicas, hot-path cleanup, and perf validation.
- [Micro-Agent: Beat Frontier Models with Collaboration inside Model API](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-29-micro-agent-frontier-models): How vLLM Semantic Router turns vllm-sr/auto into a bounded micro-agent runtime for Confidence, Ratings, ReMoM, Fusion, Workflows, and benchmark-shaped collaboration.
- [Engineering TTS Inference in vLLM-Omni](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-23-vllm-omni-tts): How vLLM-Omni supports and optimizes Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2, Higgs Audio V3, and Fish Speech S2 Pro with staged serving, batching, CUDA Graphs, and model-specific kernels.
- [Beyond One Model: Fusion in vLLM Semantic Router](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-16-vllm-sr-fusion-api): How vLLM Semantic Router Fusion runs a panel of models, uses a judge to analyze agreement and gaps, and synthesizes one answer while preserving routing policy, traces, and OpenAI-compatible serving.
- [MiniMax M3 in vLLM: Day-0 Serving for 1M-Token Multimodal Reasoning](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-12-minimax-m3-vllm): How vLLM serves MiniMax M3 with MiniMax Sparse Attention, multimodal and reasoning parsers, MXFP8 weights, and long-context deployment recipes.
- [DiffusionGemma: The First Diffusion LLM (dLLM) Natively Supported in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-10-diffusion-gemma): How vLLM supports DiffusionGemma, the first native diffusion language model in vLLM, using Model Runner V2 state hooks, iterative denoising, bidirectional attention, and reused speculative decoding paths.
- [Announcing vime: A Simple, Stable, and Efficient RL Framework for LLMs](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-09-announcing-vime): vime connects slime's training stack with vLLM rollouts to provide a simple, stable, and efficient RL post-training pipeline.
- [vLLM Semantic Router v0.3 Themis: From Signals to Stateful Production Routing](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-05-v0.3-vllm-sr-themis-release): What vLLM Semantic Router v0.3 Themis adds for production routing: canonical config, inspectable signal-decision-policy flows, safer operations, CLI/dashboard/Kubernetes alignment, and replayable routing behavior.
- [Announcing Day-0 Support for NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra on vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-06-04-nemotron-3-ultra-vllm): How to serve NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra with vLLM for long-running agentic reasoning, including BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints, supported GPU configurations, OpenAI-compatible deployment, and NeMo RL integration.

- [vLLM V1: A Major Upgrade to vLLM's Core Architecture](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-27-v1-alpha-release): What changed in vLLM V1: a re-architected engine with a simpler scheduler, near-zero-overhead prefix caching, cleaner tensor parallelism, multiprocessing API server, and default optimizations for higher-throughput serving.
- [High Performance and Easy Deployment of vLLM in K8S with vLLM production-stack](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-21-stack-release): What vLLM production-stack adds for Kubernetes serving: prefix-aware routing, LMCache-backed KV cache sharing, autoscaling, observability, fault tolerance, and cluster deployment with higher throughput and lower latency.
- [Structured Decoding in vLLM: a gentle introduction](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-14-struct-decode-intro): How structured decoding works in vLLM, covering JSON outputs, grammar-guided generation, outlines, XGrammar, TPOT improvements, constrained decoding, and agentic workflow use cases.
- [Installing and Developing vLLM with Ease](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-10-dev-experience): How to install and develop vLLM using stable releases, nightly wheels, uv, source builds, Python and C++/CUDA workflows, and version tracking for production deployments.
- [vLLM 2024 Retrospective and 2025 Vision](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-10-vllm-2024-wrapped-2025-vision): A vLLM 2024 retrospective and 2025 roadmap covering community growth, model and hardware support, production adoption, office hours, ecosystem partnerships, and the path toward universal open-source serving.
- [Serving LLMs on AMD MI300X: Best Practices](https://vllm.ai/blog/2024-10-23-vllm-serving-amd): Best practices for serving LLMs with vLLM on AMD MI300X, covering ROCm setup, Llama 3.1 70B and 405B benchmarks, chunked prefill, multi-step scheduling, prefix caching, graph capture, and AMD tuning.
- [How Speculative Decoding Boosts vLLM Performance by up to 2.8x](https://vllm.ai/blog/2024-10-17-spec-decode): How speculative decoding works in vLLM, covering EAGLE, Medusa, n-gram proposals, draft and target runners, scheduler and memory-manager changes, and continuous batching for lower token latency.
- [vLLM v0.6.0: 2.7x Throughput Improvement and 5x Latency Reduction](https://vllm.ai/blog/2024-09-05-perf-update): What changed in vLLM v0.6.0 to improve throughput and latency, including API server isolation, reduced CPU overhead, multi-step scheduling, async execution, and benchmarks against earlier vLLM versions.
- [vLLM’s Open Governance and Performance Roadmap](https://vllm.ai/blog/2024-07-25-lfai-perf): vLLM's open governance and performance roadmap, covering LF AI and Data incubation, public benchmarks, optimized kernels, async scheduling, API frontend overhead, torch.compile, disaggregated prefill, and community research.
- [Announcing Llama 3.1 Support in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2024-07-23-llama31): How vLLM supports Meta Llama 3.1 models, including 128K context, Llama 3.1 405B serving, chunked prefill, FP8 quantization, tensor and pipeline parallelism, CPU offloading, and early performance results.
- [Notes on vLLM v.s. DeepSpeed-FastGen](https://vllm.ai/blog/2023-11-14-notes-vllm-vs-deepspeed): A performance comparison of vLLM and DeepSpeed-FastGen, explaining when Dynamic SplitFuse helps, where vLLM is faster, and how memory allocation, output length, and workload shape affect throughput.
- [vLLM: Easy, Fast, and Cheap LLM Serving with PagedAttention](https://vllm.ai/blog/2023-06-20-vllm): What the original vLLM launch announced: PagedAttention for KV cache management, up to 24x throughput over Hugging Face Transformers, and lower-cost high-throughput LLM serving.

# vLLM full site content for AI assistants --- --- This file concatenates core vLLM site descriptions and vLLM blog markdown content for AI assistant retrieval. --- --- # vLLM Source: https://vllm.ai/ vLLM is a high-throughput, memory-efficient inference and serving engine for large language models. The project focuses on production-grade serving performance, broad model support, and an open ecosystem for LLM inference. --- # vLLM Blog Source: https://vllm.ai/blog The vLLM blog publishes technical deep dives, release announcements, model support guides, benchmarks, and community updates from the vLLM project. --- # vLLM Events Source: https://vllm.ai/events The events page tracks vLLM office hours, community meetups, conferences, release events, and other project gatherings. --- # vLLM Releases Source: https://vllm.ai/releases The releases page lists recent vLLM releases and links to release notes for users tracking new versions. --- # Contact vLLM Source: https://vllm.ai/contact The contact page provides channels for community questions, website feedback, partnerships, collaborations, and other vLLM project communications. --- # Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-20-inkling2-mini Published: 2026-11-20 Authors: Inferact, Thinking Machines and NVIDIA Tags: model-support, performance, multimodal, speculative-decoding Summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-20-inkling2-mini/hero.png) Thinking Machines [announced](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) [Inkling 2 Mini](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini) today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, [TML-d24-varloop-research](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research), on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a **looped** model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. ## TL;DR - **Looped layers.** Layers 6–17 run three passes with shared weights. Each pass keeps its own KV cache and reads gated messages from the one before. - **26B total, 3.5B active, 1M context, Native DSpark.** A multimodal MoE built from Inkling 2 Small's components, with NVFP4 experts (MXFP8 in the last 4 layers) and a native DSpark speculator. - **Optimized day-0 support on Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark.** vLLM manages each pass's caches like any other cache layer, fuses the message reads and controllers, and reuses Inkling 2 Small's fused kernels. - **RL support.** vLLM serves Inkling 2 Mini for reinforcement learning with [SkyRL](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL). - **Variable-loop research checkpoint.** vLLM also serves TML-d24-varloop-research, where you choose the number of passes, and whether the passes share one KV cache, at startup. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, `vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini`. You can serve the model with: ```bash docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini \ --reasoning-parser inkling --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' ``` And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: ```bash docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research \ --reasoning-parser inkling --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --hf-overrides '{"text_config": {"loop_num_passes": 2, "loop_share_cache": true}}' ``` ## The Loop *Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before.* **Prelude, core, coda.** The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the [block attention residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031) used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. **Every pass starts from the prelude's output.** A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. **Messages are read at every sublayer.** From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: ``` h = W_down · [rms(input), rms(message)] out = (1 − tanh(W_forget · h)) · input + tanh(W_gain · h) · message ``` With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. **Each pass keeps its own memory.** Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. **DSpark draft from inside the loop.** The 3-layer DSpark draft reads the target's hidden states at four layer visits: one in the prelude, one each in the second and third passes, and the final output. **The layers themselves follow Inkling 2 Small.** Each layer uses Inkling 2 Small's components at hidden size 2,304: block attention residuals, relative-bias attention with a gate and sink (20 sliding-window and 4 full-attention layers, 24 query and 8 KV heads), short convolutions, and 128 routed experts (top-8) in NVFP4 (layers 0–19) and MXFP8 (layers 20–23). Images go through a 23-layer ViT encoder configured like Inkling 2 Small's. ## Serving the Loop in vLLM **Per-pass caches as regular cache layers.** vLLM registers each extra pass of a core layer as its own attention layer with its own KV and conv-state cache. The KV cache manager and prefix caching treat these caches like any others, so serving the loop needed no new cache-management logic. **Fused message reads and controllers.** A direct implementation launches 4 message reads and 4 controllers, several kernels each, for every core layer in a later pass. vLLM reads all four messages of a layer in one attention-residual kernel and stacks the four controllers' weights, so their down and gain/forget projections run as batched GEMMs. One Triton kernel computes the controllers' RMS normalizations, and another fuses the gated merge with the RMSNorm of the sublayer the message feeds. The merge runs in FP32 without FMA contraction, matching the reference. **Fused kernels around every sublayer.** For Inkling 2 Small, vLLM fuses each sublayer's all-reduce, short convolution, residual update, attention-residual mix and RMSNorm into one kernel. vLLM generalizes these kernels from hidden size 4,608 to 2,304 and adds a mode that returns the FP32 mix before the RMSNorm, so the later passes can merge their messages into it. Inkling 2 Mini uses them at every tensor-parallel size, including TP1; at TP > 1, small batches also fuse the all-reduce over NVLink multicast. ## Variable-Loop Research Checkpoint Thinking Machines also releases [TML-d24-varloop-research](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research), a research checkpoint trained to run with a variable number of passes. vLLM exposes its two options through `--hf-overrides`: ```bash docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research \ --reasoning-parser inkling --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --hf-overrides '{"text_config": {"loop_num_passes": 2, "loop_share_cache": true}}' ``` - `loop_num_passes` sets the number of passes (at least 1; the default is the checkpoint's 3). Fewer passes are faster; more passes give higher quality. DSpark requires the default, since the draft reads fixed layer visits. - `loop_share_cache` makes all passes of a core layer share one KV cache: each pass overwrites the keys and values of its tokens, so later tokens read the last pass's. Conv states stay per pass. Both options are rejected on fixed-loop checkpoints such as Inkling 2 Mini. On one GB200 (TP1, 4K context, forward pass only): | Passes | Decode step, batch 1 | Decode step, batch 32 | KV cache capacity | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 1.51 ms | 3.81 ms | 352K tokens | | 2 | 2.67 ms | 5.92 ms | 233K tokens | | 3 | 3.85 ms | 8.11 ms | 175K tokens | | 3, shared KV cache | 3.86 ms | 8.10 ms | 194K tokens | Sharing the KV cache frees less memory than dropping a pass, because the per-pass conv-state caches remain. ## Accuracy Evals vLLM keeps the reference implementation's numerics: the same data types at every step, the same NVFP4 and MXFP8 activation quantization, and FP32 message merges, with only the reduction order differing. On a fixed prompt, vLLM's hidden state at each of the 48 layer visits differs from the reference by about as much as the reference's own FlashAttention-4 and PyTorch attention paths differ from each other, and the MoE outputs match bitwise given the same inputs. End to end, we tested accuracy on needle-in-a-haystack up to 1M tokens, MMMU-Pro and HLE with [inkling-verify](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/inkling-verify), and on GSM8K, with DSpark enabled. ## Acknowledgements We thank the Thinking Machines and NVIDIA teams for their close collaboration in integrating and optimizing Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM. --- # Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-18-flydsl-monokernels Published: 2026-11-18 Authors: Felix Li, Lingpeng Jin, Hattie Wu, Carlus Huang, Fangzhou Ai, Zaidy Ali, Amanzhol Salykov, Hyukjoon Lee, Ziming Huang, Jun Chen, Yifeng Huang, Bin Ding, Xiaobing Zhang, Yi Gan, Vinayak Gokhale, Hongxia Yang, Doug Lehr, Richard Li, Andy Luo, Peng Sun, and Emad Barsoum Tags: performance, hardware Summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration. ## Introduction Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how **MonoKernels** written in [FlyDSL](https://github.com/ROCm/FlyDSL) reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. ## How MonoKernels Reduce Decode Latency A **MonoKernel** combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, *mono* means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by [TileRT](https://github.com/tile-ai/TileRT), the implementations discussed here use a **persistent launch**: a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. - **Reuse thread blocks across stages.** After completing its current work, a block can take on ready work from the next stage without a separate kernel launch. This reduces repeated GPU kernel startup and drain. - **Read later weights while earlier work computes.** For example, output-projection or expert up/gate weights can be prefetched during earlier computation. Where the schedule and resources allow it, that overlaps part of the HBM traffic with useful work rather than exposing all of it on the critical path. It does not eliminate weight reads or guarantee that all memory latency is hidden. - **Hand off data at the granularity the consumer needs.** A *tile* is a portion of a tensor. A **tagged mailbox** holds an intermediate result and a tag indicating readiness. A downstream stage, or a reduction on a peer GPU, can proceed once the required data is ready rather than waiting for unrelated work in the producing stage. Consumers still wait for all inputs required by their own computation. ### Choosing Model-Specific Kernel Boundaries A key design challenge is deciding **where a MonoKernel begins and ends**: which operations share one launch, and which remain in separate kernels. Fusing more stages is not automatically better. The boundary must fit the model’s data dependencies, communication pattern, and GPU resource limits. MonoKernel boundaries are therefore model-specific, rather than a universal one-layer, one-kernel template. For example, the initial DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash implementation ([#60397](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60397)) divides the standard decoder-layer path into K1 and K2. Figure 3 shows the operations within each boundary, not their execution timing. K1 prepares attention inputs and updates the KV cache. K2 completes attention and continues through the feed-forward work, with both TP all-reduces using symmetric peer memory inside the kernel. These reductions sum in fp32 in rank order, then convert to bf16, and overlap with surrounding work. Their placement inside K2 does not mean that communication or cross-rank synchronization disappears.
Operator-level mapping for this example
LaunchStages
K1mHC (hyper-connection) mixing before attention → attention front: wqkv, q/kv norms, KV-cache insert, wq_b
K2attention back (split attention, combine, wo_a, wo_b) → TP all-reduce → mHC mixing before the FFN → MoE (router, top-6, shared expert, MXFP4 experts) → TP all-reduce
**A narrower boundary: MiniMax-M3.** The initial implementation ([#62712](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62712)) fuses the FFN portion, including its surrounding communication, while attention stays on the stock path. Compared with the DeepSeek example, it chooses only part of the layer for mono execution. These examples illustrate different boundary choices, not a fixed recipe that transfers unchanged to every model. ## Why FlyDSL Fits This Execution Model The boundary and schedule are designed by the kernel author, not automatically created by choosing a language. [FlyDSL](https://github.com/ROCm/FlyDSL), AMD’s Python DSL and MLIR compiler for high-performance ROCm kernels, provides the controls needed to express and compile that design. **The author designs, FlyDSL compiles, and vLLM selects and integrates the execution path.** Figure 4 shows the hand-off from Figure 2 between two thread blocks, with the FlyDSL primitive behind each step. Block i stores its result, waits until the stores have landed (`s_waitcnt` and a barrier), then raises one flag per token with a mailbox write. Block j issued its stage-B weight loads earlier, so the weights arrive while it polls the flags it needs; it starts stage B as soon as they are up, with no kernel boundary in between. FlyDSL compiles this order as written; it does not fuse or reorder stages on its own. The [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash attention front](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/7691ff6e5b70930b80d09ec14fed84d1a2ea612f/vllm/models/deepseek_v41/amd/mono/attention/front.py) in vLLM follows this pattern. The model, GPU architecture, and supported step widths still determine which variants can run. The following section explains how vLLM integrates them without replacing the rest of the serving engine.
Implementation details: layouts, compilation and supported configurations

Control data movement and synchronization. To overlap stages, the implementation must decide how work is divided across blocks, waves, and threads, when loads are issued, and when results become available. FlyDSL lets the author express these choices down to specific buffer and matrix instructions where needed. The benefit comes from the resulting schedule, not from Python syntax itself.

Match layouts and low-precision computation to each stage. Projections, attention, and experts do not all use the same data layout. FlyDSL lets the author choose how each stage partitions and accesses its tensors, and map low-precision computation to the GPU's matrix instructions. On MI355X, the mono implementation can read vLLM's loaded weights in place, including AITER's shuffled MXFP4 expert layout, rather than keeping a second copy. These controls also support porting, but do not make it automatic: CDNA3 needs tile sizes suited to its smaller shared memory (LDS) and different matrix-instruction paths from CDNA4.

Specialize and compile for the supported configuration. Kernels written with @flyc.kernel and @flyc.jit are compiled on first use and cached. The implementation is specialized for its model, TP size, and supported step widths—the number of token rows processed in a forward step, including speculative positions and graph padding. vLLM builds the required width variants during warm-up and replays them under HIP graphs. This is targeted specialization, not a guarantee that one schedule serves arbitrary models or batch sizes.

The kernel source remains in the model's vLLM directory, with the flydsl wheel as its new runtime dependency. Deterministic compilation also supports ISA and resource-usage comparisons during review.

## Specialized Decode in vLLM To vLLM, a MonoKernel path is a *specialized decode*: a model- and hardware-specific decode forward pass behind vLLM's normal interfaces. The scheduler, KV-cache manager, sampling, speculative decoding, and HIP graphs stay unchanged; only the decoder layers run differently, and only on steps the kernels can serve. Every merged mono PR follows the rules agreed in RFC [#60904](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60904): - **Opt-in, refused when unsupported.** The path is off by default; `--monokernel` turns it on (equivalent to `--additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}'`, which Kimi-K3 reads). A deployment the kernels can't serve fails at startup with every reason listed. - **The model owns the code.** Kernels, runtime, and tests live under `vllm/models//amd/`. Kimi-K3 added 26 lines to its existing model files and nothing to vLLM's core. - **Mono or stock, per layer, per step.** One `plan()` per step decides. Prefill, mixed batches, and steps too wide for the kernels run on the stock layers. Mono layers use vLLM's weights and KV cache and return the same tensors, so the two can mix within a step. - **Works with HIP graphs and speculative decoding.** Capture sizes don't change, and speculative verify steps can run on the mono path too. ## Results The merged-PR evaluations summarized in Figure 5 were measured by their authors on MI355X or MI325X. The separate GLM-5.2 subsection reports the RFC measurements on MI350X; those results are not included in Figure 5. AgentX is InferenceX's benchmark built from multi-turn, long-context agent sessions. Each AgentX point is one 3,600-second run. **Interactivity** is 1 / inter-token latency (P90 unless noted), in tokens/s/user (higher is better). Figure 5a shows the concurrency-1 speedup from each merged PR with a same-node stock baseline; DeepSeek-V4-Pro is excluded because its comparison uses a historical InferenceX run. Figure 5b follows the three PRs that sweep concurrency against a same-node stock baseline; their bars in 5a have the same colours as their lines. Each value is a ratio of the metric its PR reports, oriented so that higher is better: interactivity as mono / stock, TPOT and decode step time as stock / mono. The per-model subsections below give the absolute numbers and link the PRs. ### DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [#60397](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60397) runs the 30 standard layers as K1 + K2; on the same TP2 MI355X node, turning mono on raises concurrency-1 P90 interactivity from 318.1 to 429.1 tok/s/user. The same PR's FFN launch for the other 10 layers adds another 1.02–1.19×; at TP4, P90 interactivity at concurrency 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 is **1.66× / 1.56× / 1.64× / 1.38×** that of InferenceX's published run of the same recipe. On one TP8 server with only `--monokernel` toggled, a decode step with DSpark speculative decoding drops from 8.59 to 5.36 ms (392 → 580 tok/s). Full results for each configuration are in the linked PRs. Ports for GLM-5.x, Qwen3.8, and MiniMax-M3.1 are in review. Mono decode is opt-in, so add `--monokernel` to a supported recipe. For example, the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash setup used in the PRs on MI355X: ```bash VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 \ vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 --trust-remote-code --language-model-only \ --max-num-seqs 8 --block-size 128 \ --attention_config.indexer_kv_dtype=mxfp4 \ --moe-backend aiter \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5}' \ --monokernel ``` If the deployment isn't supported, vLLM refuses to start and lists every reason. The supported configurations for each model are documented in its package under `vllm/models//amd/`. ## Scope and Limitations Mono decode is a latency optimization with three limits: - **Best at low concurrency.** Gains are largest at concurrency 1 and smaller at higher concurrency (Figure 5b). For DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, TP8 mono decode is a concurrency-1 configuration: at concurrency 4, one TP8 server delivers 26% less throughput than two TP4 replicas ([#64101](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64101)). - **Steps are limited in width.** Speculative tokens and graph padding count toward the limit: up to 48 rows for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on MI355X (42 on MI325X, which has less LDS) and 16 for MiniMax-M3 and Kimi-K3. Wider steps run on the stock path. - **Weight copies on MI300X/MI325X.** Without scaled FP4/FP8 MFMA, the kernels keep their own copy of the weights: 170 GiB per rank instead of 99 GiB for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at TP4. That still leaves a large KV cache on MI325X, but little room on MI300X. ## Summary Small-batch decode spends much of its time between kernels: launching them, waiting for whole stages to finish, and streaming weights while the GPU idles. FlyDSL MonoKernels remove much of that time by running each decoder layer, or part of it, as a few persistent launches that reuse thread blocks across stages, prefetch weights, pass ready data forward through tagged mailboxes, and reduce across GPUs inside the kernel. FlyDSL makes this practical: the author controls each stage's layout, data movement, and synchronization down to individual instructions, and each kernel is specialized and compiled just in time for its model, TP size, and step widths. In vLLM, mono decode is now merged for five models and follows a common, opt-in standard. It improves concurrency-1 interactivity or time per output token by 1.20× to 2.26×, and every PR reports accuracy with mono on and off. We invite the vLLM community to try `--monokernel` on AMD Instinct GPUs, review the in-flight ports, and use the [authoring guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62256) (in review) to bring mono decode to new models. ## References 1.
