All rights reserved. --- # DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-deepseek-v41-flash-vera-rubin Published: 2026-11-12 Authors: Inferact and the vLLM Team Tags: deepseek, performance, large-scale-serving, disaggregation Summary: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 387 tokens/s per user, 58x GB300 NVL72 at the same interactivity. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-12-deepseek-v41-flash-vera-rubin/hero.png?v=20261112) **TL;DR:** On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at **1.7M** tokens/s per GPU while each user gets **387** tokens/s, **58×** GB300 NVL72, and reaches **2.52M** at peak throughput and **1,810** tokens/s for a single user. The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The [first post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-07-deepseek-v41-flash) covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The [second](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep) scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we [introduced last month](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-09-vera-rubin-preview). Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: - **Rubin-optimized kernels for DEP prefill and decode.**[^terms] We reworked the MoE, attention, GEMM, mHC and indexer kernels for Rubin: bandwidth-bound data stays in each SM's own memory domain, SM107's wider MMA instructions do more work per issue, and kernels start their loads, and their dependents, before they wait. DEP2 prefill steps are about 28% faster, and DEP decode steps about 25% faster. - **A specialized TP decode path for the lowest latency.** We perform cross-operator fusions, overlapping computation with communication, and tuning, then spread the model over two trays with TP8, to achieve 1,810 tokens/s (P90) at batch size 1. - **Dynamo workload-aware routing over rack-scale memory pools.** Rubin's speed brings much higher concurrency, so we pool the rack's memory: the Mooncake KV pool extends from DRAM to spare HBM, and the Engram tables are sharded across GPU HBM. Even at very high concurrency the prefix hit rate stays at 96.5–97%, and routing alone balances the ranks. ## Performance overview *Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ([GB300 source](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/inference/deepseek-v41-flash?i_seq=agentic-traces&g_model=DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash&i_metric=y_tpPerMw&i_best=0&i_active=gb300_dynamo-vllm)).* We measure performance with the [SemiAnalysis AgentX](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx) benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. #### How we measured We use the same methodology as in our [previous GB300 post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep#how-we-measured). For kernels and model forward profiling, `vllm bench forward` times exact prefill and decode batches through the real `execute_model` path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. ## Rubin through the lens of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. Where an optimization is specific to Rubin, we say which of them it relies on. - **Each GPU has two memory domains.** SMs read their own domain much faster than interleaved memory, and slower still from the other domain. As the [Rubin preview](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-09-vera-rubin-preview#locality-domain-support) showed, this matters for bandwidth-bound data: MoE weights, the LM head, MegaMoE's combine buffer and the mHC residual stream. - **SM107 adds wider block-scaled MMA instructions.** We use the new K64 mixed-precision (FP8×FP4) MMA, which does twice the work per instruction, in MegaMoE and the low-latency routed GEMMs: MegaMoE gets 8–11% more throughput at 8K+ tokens per rank, and the low batch size routed GEMM runs 12% faster. In the indexer, the new K128 FP4 MMA, together with six-token query tiles, makes the decode MQA-logits kernel 15–22% faster. - **72 GPUs share one NVLink domain.** TP8 can span two compute trays at almost no extra all-reduce cost. Prefill instances can read each other's HBM efficiently, so a large table no longer has to be copied to every instance. *Figure 2: Weight stages of the routed-expert GEMM in one SM's shared memory, with the SM100 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA and with SM107's K64 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA on packed FP4.* ## Diving into optimizations ### Kernels We kept GB300's three engine shapes: DEP2 prefill, Wide-EP decode (DEP16 or DEP32), and a TP decode path for the lowest latency (next section). We also kept DeepSeek's kernel set (MegaMoE, MegaAttn, Mega-mHC, MegaGate, DeepSelect) and rebuilt much of it for SM107. #### DEP prefill: about 28% less time per step At 32K tokens per rank, a prefill step is dominated by the expert GEMMs; most of the rest goes into streaming the residual and attention's working set through HBM. So this round went into the kernels around the GEMMs and into Rubin's two memory domains: Mega-mHC keeps the residual die-local, MegaAttn keeps its tensor cores issuing instead of waiting on loads, and MegaGate scores only the experts that can still make the top 6. Together they cut a 32K-token DEP2 prefill step by 28%. *Figure 3: Three of the prefill kernel changes: Mega-mHC's die-local residual, MegaAttn's pipeline and MegaGate's contender filter, and the step they add up to.*
Prefill optimization details - **MegaMoE: size tiles for the busiest rank.** vLLM does not pad DP batches in eager prefill, so in 86% of real DEP2 prefill steps an idle rank sized MegaMoE tiles for its own tiny token count while its experts served the busy rank's tokens. Tiles now follow the larger of the local and DP-average token counts. MegaMoE time drops 55% over a 40-step replay, and single-request TTFT next to an idle rank 13–39% from 8K to 32K tokens. - **Mega-mHC: the residual stream in die-local memory.** At prefill sizes, Mega-mHC is HBM-bound, streaming about 100 KB of four-route residual per token. The residual now lives in a pool striped across both memory domains, and Mega-mHC keeps one task counter per domain, so each SM drains its own domain before helping the other. That left large grids instruction-cache bound, so they now loop over one copy of the Post body instead of four. Mega-mHC drops from 354 to 317 µs per call at 32K tokens; DEP2 steps of 5K+ tokens get 0.6–1.3% faster. - **Query up-projection on SM107's K64 block-scaled MMA.** MegaAttn's [tokens × 1,280] × [1,280 × 32,768] query GEMM moved from cuDNN's SM100 kernel to FlashInfer's CuTe DSL GEMM on SM107's K64 MMA: 13–18% faster from 4K to 32K rows, and 1.1–1.7% off DEP2 steps at 16K–32K. - **MegaAttn: keep the tensor cores fed.** At 16K–32K tokens per rank, sparse attention was bound by issue and load latency. An idle warp now issues the SVs so QKs no longer wait behind them, the KV producer loads the next block's top-k indices before waiting for a slot, the cluster-launch-control warp prefetches the next job's index row into L2, and the next job's queries load before the current job's last QK. Each TMEM lane group now scores its own keys completely, so the softmax no longer swaps partial sums through shared memory. The kernel is 15% faster at 16K–32K tokens and 23% at 4K, and DEP2 steps 0.9–2.1%. - **Mega-mHC: a ticketed task ring.** At long prompts, fixed task strides left the RMSNorm workers so far behind Post that their rereads of Post's output missed L2. Large grids now take tasks from an atomic ticket counter (−18% at 32K). Norm tasks also issue all loads up front, the next task's coefficients arrive early, and both Post warpgroups share one code copy to spare the instruction cache: another 13–22% per call from 4K to 32K tokens. - **MegaGate: read each token once, score only the contenders.** For long prompts, one CTA pair computes all 384 experts of a token block from one shared-memory stage (M=256 and M=128 UMMAs) instead of rereading tokens per 128-expert group. The router evaluates the exact sqrt-softplus only for experts that can still make the top 6: a bound on the sixth-largest score and the function's slope give each expert a threshold, and about 7 of 384 pass. The kernel gets 3–13% faster from 4K tokens (77 → 68 µs at 32K).
#### DEP decode: about 25% less time per step Decode is MoE-bound, as on GB300. Against our first Rubin build, which already had die-local weights, the Wide-EP dispatch changes and the MQA logits change, these optimizations cut the target forward of a DEP32 decode step (20 requests × 6 tokens per rank, DSpark k=5, simulated on one 4-GPU node) by about 25%. *Figure 4: Four of the Wide-EP decode changes: die-local expert weights, one NVLink round trip per dispatched token, a combine that waits for data, and split-K projections across an SM107 cluster.*
Decode optimization details - **Die-local MegaMoE weights.** Decode MoE is bound by weight reads, and an SM streams its own memory domain much faster than interleaved memory. vLLM splits expert weights by output columns across the domains, and MegaMoE gives each domain's SMs only local tiles. The DEP2 decode forward gets 10.1% faster at batch size 32 and 5.5% at 168. - **Wide-EP dispatch: one NVLink round trip per token.** At DEP8 decode, NVLink ran at only 39% of peak. Each pulled token now issues all remote loads before any local store, paying one round trip instead of two or three. Warps publish pulls with one fence and one elected release, and expert counts go out as non-returning `red` atomics, so the first SM's 392 remote updates no longer serialize. MegaMoE gets 17% faster at DEP8 (192 → 160 µs). - **MegaMoE: a combine that waits for data, not a barrier.** The combine buffer starts each launch filled with a sentinel no output can take, so a CTA combines as soon as its own GEMM tasks finish, re-reading only 16-byte groups still holding the sentinel and then restoring it. The cross-rank tail barrier is signalled at one launch's end and awaited at the next one's start. With few local experts, all first-GEMM tasks are claimed before any second-GEMM task, keeping weights streaming. MegaMoE gets 3.5–10.8% faster at decode sizes. - **Split-K GEMMs on SM107 clusters.** With a few dozen rows per rank, the attention input and output projections launch too few CTAs to stream weights at full bandwidth. A split-K GEMM spreads K over an SM107 cluster and reduces partial sums through distributed shared memory, or from registers through L2 when a CTA's peer slices exceed 28 KB. The GEMMs get 10–38% faster, and the decode forward 3.1% at ≤16 requests per rank, 1.9% at 17–24. - **MQA logits: six-token tiles and SM107's K=128 MMA.** DSpark verification sends 5–6 query rows per request to the indexer. The kernel now packs them into one 192-wide tile on two warpgroups instead of two 4-token tiles on three, issues each 128-dim head as one SM107 K=128 MMA rather than two K=64 ones, and stores at immediate offsets without per-split 64-bit address math: 15–22% faster at 5–6 tokens per request. - **Split Mega-mHC: only what the next layer needs on the critical path.** The next layer needs Mega-mHC's Post, route collapse and RMSNorm, but not its next mixes. A small kernel now does just those three, and the mixes run on a side stream joining at the next boundary. It moves each route in coalesced 16-byte chunks, with up to three tokens per CTA, so 636 tokens fit in one wave on 212 SMs. The decode forward gets 2.0–4.8% faster at 20–30 requests per rank; the coalesced rewrite makes the kernel another 30–58% faster at 18–192 tokens. - **MegaAttn decode: deeper pipelines.** Decode attention runs one or two tokens per CTA, a latency chain of index loads, KV gathers and unpacking, then per-block QK, softmax and SV. Three blocks of index loads and four gather batches now stay in flight, the idle query warpgroup unpacks the KV when each SM has one job, and the kernel triggers dependents right after its own dependency wait, overlapping the output projection's prologue with attention. The kernel gets 7–10% faster at 6–424 rows.
### Low latency: a specialized decode path with TP For the lowest latency, we run a specialized decode path. We ported it from our GB300 post, largely rebuilt it for Rubin, and spread it across two compute trays with TP8. On real AgentX sessions at concurrency 1, with a fixed DSpark acceptance of 3.51 tokens per step, it went from 1,117 to 1,844 tokens/s per user at P50. Apart from the first expert GEMM, a step is a chain of small kernels near their latency floor. *Figure 5: One step of the specialized TP8 decode path: the engine spread over two compute trays, and the per-layer kernel chain with its boundaries fused.*
Low-latency optimization details - **TP8 across two trays over NVL72.** Each rank holds a 288-column slice of every expert and 8 attention heads. A cross-tray all-reduce costs only 0.3 µs more than an in-tray one, so TP8 halves per-GPU weight reads almost for free. With native TP8 shapes for the routed GEMMs and sparse MLA, a step got 35% faster. - **Packed-FP4 weight stages on SM107.** The first expert GEMM is limited by the weight bytes each SM keeps in flight. UMMA descriptors address only 256 KB of shared memory, which fit 7 stages in SM100's one-byte FP4 layout. SM107's K64 MMA reads packed FP4, so the same space holds 11 stages (Figure 2), saving 57 µs per step. - **A die-local LM head.** The LM head reads a copy of its weights split across the two memory domains. Each SM streams only its own half, at close to the domain-local ceiling. - **All-reduce and mHC in one pass.** Both all-reduces publish from their GEMM epilogues straight into a Lamport mailbox with NVLink multicast stores. The receiving kernel sums the ranks, applies mHC Post, collapses the four routes and computes RMSNorm; at the MoE boundary it also runs the router GEMM before its grid wait (about −30 µs per step). The next layer's mHC pre-norm runs on a side stream, split 64 ways (5.8 → 3.7 µs), and the routed GEMMs leave 16 of Rubin's 212 SMs free for it (−4 to −10 µs). - **Sparse MLA.** At TP8, each rank runs an 8-head sparse MLA kernel. While the previous kernel still runs, it gathers every KV row except the step's new ones, and each PV block sends its partial to the owner as soon as its MMAs finish (−16 to −21 µs). Query RoPE and the KV-cache insert are fused into the kernels around attention, which also starts its prologue early (another −36 µs). - **Shared expert inside the routed GEMMs.** The shared expert was the MoE sublayer's tail in 80% of layers. Below 16 rows it now runs inside the routed GEMMs, saving 220 µs per step. - **Launch the next kernel early.** The all-reduce finalizer launches its dependents right after its own grid wait (−16 µs), and the indexer's MQA logits load KV before their grid sync (−24 µs). - **Engram all-gathers on the layer's stream.** At TP8, NCCL all-gathers put 22 µs on Engram's critical path. A fused entry kernel and Lamport all-gathers on the layer's own stream save about 40 µs per step.
### Dynamo workload-aware routing + rack-scale shared memory pools Rubin computes fast, so a rack sustains far higher concurrency than GB300, and the live prefixes of all those agentic sessions outgrow any per-rank cache. On GB300, we kept prefixes in a per-rank CPU tier and pinned each session to a rank; at Rubin's concurrency that tier was too small, and pinning left some ranks idle while others queued. We pushed memory to the limit by pooling it across the rack: KV in DRAM and spare HBM, loaded over RDMA, and the Engram tables in HBM, read over NVL72's NVLink. Even at very high concurrency, the prefix hit rate stays at 96.5–97%, close to the theoretical hit rate. With no session tied to a rank, workload-aware routing alone keeps the ranks balanced. *Figure 6: Every prefill rank loads KV from one Mooncake pool over the rack's DRAM and spare HBM (RDMA) and reads Engram tables from peers' HBM (NVLink), so the Dynamo router can send each request to the least-loaded rank.* **Mooncake pool.** One [Mooncake store](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-06-mooncake-store) across the DRAM of every prefill and decode tray replaces the per-rank CPU tier, so any rank can load any prefix over RDMA and a moved request costs a KV load, not a recompute. We optimized how the prefill scheduler waits on the pool: lookups run asynchronously out of process, a request already hit in local HBM skips the lookup but still refreshes its lease, and KV loads start as soon as a lookup returns instead of at the next step. Prefill steps left underfilled by pending lookups fell from 6–14% of step time to under 0.5%, and those waiting on KV loads from 13.5% to 1%. **HBM pool.** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is small and its KV cache per token is small, so serving a request uses only a fraction of a prefill and decode GPU's HBM. Once Mooncake holds the prefixes, the rest would sit idle. Each prefill rank now keeps just enough KV cache for one maximum-length request and gives the rest of its KV budget to Mooncake as an HBM segment, sized automatically, extending the pool from DRAM to the spare HBM of every prefill GPU; those segments are read over the same RDMA path. The HBM pool is still experimental. **Engram pool.** Both roles now keep Engram's two 94.4 GiB hashed n-gram tables in HBM. Decode already split them across its DP ranks ([vllm#54371](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54371)), but every DEP2 prefill instance kept its own copy in host memory, about 378 GiB per tray. Over NVL72, the prefill engines now form one peer group that splits the tables, 10.5 GiB on each of 18 GPUs, and reads the rest from peers' HBM over NVL72's NVLink, not RDMA ([vllm#66552](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/66552), Figure 7). Lookups get faster than they were from host memory, and the freed host memory holds the live prefixes of about 1,500 more sessions. *Figure 7: Engram tables per instance in host DRAM (before) vs. split across the HBM of a peer group (after).* **Workload-aware routing.** With every prefix in a shared pool, sessions no longer need to stay on one rank, which removes the DP imbalance that session affinity caused. Dynamo places each request on the (worker, DP rank) with the least uncached work, a configuration-only change. On three DEP2 instances at concurrency 4,800, the pools plus routing serve 68% more requests, cut TTFT P50 from 29.8 s to 4.2 s and lift the hit rate from 91.8% to 96.1% (Figure 8). In a 12 × DEP2 simulation, the time ranks sit idle while another rank queues drops from 10.3% to 1.3%, and TTFT P90 from 0.98 s to 0.38 s. *Figure 8: Requests/s, TTFT P50 and hit rate on three DEP2 prefill instances at concurrency 4,800.* ## Acknowledgements We thank **DeepSeek** for open-sourcing DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and its kernels, and **NVIDIA** for providing early access to Vera Rubin NVL72. We are especially grateful to Hanjie Qiu, Lisa Wang, Jie Hao, Yaoyao Ding, Pei Li, Xin Li, and Pen Chung Li from NVIDIA for their close collaboration on performance optimizations and continued support for **vLLM** and **Dynamo**. We also thank the **Mooncake** team for their KV cache store and **SemiAnalysis** for developing the AgentX benchmark. This work was led by **Inferact**. [^terms]: DEP2, DEP16 and DEP32 mean data-parallel attention plus expert parallelism over 2, 16 and 32 GPUs. --- # Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-inkling2-small Published: 2026-11-12 Authors: Inferact and Thinking Machines Tags: model-support, performance, multimodal, speculative-decoding Summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-12-inkling2-small/hero.png) vLLM supports Thinking Machines' [Inkling 2 Small](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. ## TL;DR - **594B total, 17B active, 1M context.** A 48-layer MoE with 384 experts (top-8) that takes images and text and outputs text. - **Architecture upgrade from Inkling.** Block attention residuals, attention sink, gated attention, and ViT image encoder. - **Mixed-precision MoE.** The MoE uses NVFP4 (layers 0–39) and MXFP8 (layers 40–47), so the model can be served with a single node. - **Native DSpark speculator.** DSpark with an RNN head drafts 7 tokens per step. - **Extensive optimizations.** Kernel fusion, PDL, highly tuned Gluon attention kernel, and sequence parallelism, achieving up to 630 TPS/user on GB200 at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5. - **RL and LoRA support.** vLLM supports RL (via SkyRL) and LoRA for the model. You can serve the model with: ```bash vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Small \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --reasoning-parser inkling --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' ``` ## Model Architecture *Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling.* | | Inkling | Inkling 2 Small | |---|---|---| | Layers | 66 (55 sliding-window + 11 full) | 48 (40 sliding-window + 8 full) | | Residual path | residual stream | block attention residuals (8 blocks of 6 layers) | | Attention | GQA with relative bias, no RoPE | same | | Heads (query / KV) | 64 / 8 full, 64 / 16 sliding | 48 / 8 in all layers | | Sliding window | 512 | 1,024 | | Attention output | plain | sigmoid gate and per-token sink | | Short convolutions | 4 per layer (K, V, attention out, MLP out), kernel size 4 | same | | MoE | 256 routed (top-6) + 2 shared expert sinks, first 2 layers dense | 384 routed (top-8), no shared experts, all layers MoE | | Expert precision | NVFP4 | NVFP4 (layers 0–39), MXFP8 (layers 40–47) | | Modality | text, image, audio in; text out | text, image in; text out | | Image encoder | 4-layer hMLP on 40×40 patches | 23-layer ViT (1,024 wide) on 20×20 patches | | Speculative decoding | 8 chained MTP heads | DSpark draft, 7 tokens per step | **Inkling backbone + recent advances.** Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. [Block attention residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031) replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. [Gated attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708) puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token [attention sink](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453). It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. **Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4.** Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ([Four Over Six](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02010)): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). **DSpark speculator with an RNN head.** The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that [DeepSeek's DSpark paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05147) described. ## vLLM Integration & Optimization *Figure 2. Kernels in one decoder layer, for decode and large prefills.* **Kernel fusion and PDL.** vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, `allreduce_conv_mix` (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. **MoE with fused activation quantization.** vLLM quantizes the expert activations (NVFP4 or MXFP8, matching each layer) inside the kernels that produce them, so no separate quantization pass touches the hidden states: the routing kernel quantizes the tokens before the gate/up projection, and the softcapped SwiGLU quantizes its output before the down projection. The expert GEMMs run on TensorRT-LLM's batched-GEMM kernels, shipped with FlashInfer. **Sequence parallelism for prefill.** Under plain tensor parallelism, every GPU runs the short convolution, attention-residual mix and RMSNorm on all tokens after each all-reduce: the same work, repeated on every rank. That is cheap in decode but costly in prefill. vLLM removes the redundancy with sequence parallelism (purple and gold in Figure 2). Each GPU reduce-scatters, runs the short convolution, residual update, attention-residual mix and RMSNorm in one fused `conv_mix` kernel on only its slice of tokens, and all-gathers the result for the next GEMM. This cuts an 8K-token prefill step by 22% at TP4 and 26% at TP8, and frees 1.3–1.9 GiB per GPU for KV cache. **Optimized Gluon relative attention kernel for decode.** Inkling's FlashAttention-4 decode path is slow for Inkling 2 Small: the 6:1 GQA ratio silently disables GQA packing. To fix this, we wrote a warp-specialized Gluon kernel for decode and verify that packs the 6 heads into one 64-row tile and reads KV once: a TMA warp streams KV, a tcgen05 warp runs the MMAs and four softmax warps apply the relative bias. A batch-1 decode step at 100K context drops from 15.1 ms to 4.8 ms. Prefill keeps Inkling's sheared-bias FlashAttention-4 path. ### Performance We benchmarked Inkling 2 Small on an agentic workload at TP8 (two 4-GPU nodes) with DSpark (probabilistic drafting) and prefix caching. Each session keeps a long context and, on every turn, appends the previous answer and a ~2K-token tool output, so only about 3K tokens per turn are new; each turn then generates 1,024 tokens with reasoning on at temperature 1.0. The table gives output throughput per GPU at the concurrency where each user gets 100 tokens/s. | Session context | Output tok/s per GPU at 100 tok/s/user | Concurrent sessions | Prefix-cache hit rate | Acceptance length | |---|---|---|---|---| | 32K | ~1,070 | ~84 | 91% | 3.3 | | 64K | ~915 | ~72 | 95% | 3.4 | | 128K | ~700 | ~55 | 98% | 3.5 | | 256K | ~450 | ~37 | 99% | 3.5 | For a single user at TP4, the model decodes at about 630 tok/s with an acceptance length of 3.5. ## Accuracy Evals vLLM keeps the reference implementation's numerics: the same data types at every step, FP32 attention output and router, and the same NVFP4/MXFP8 activation quantization, with only the reduction order and the all-reduce's BF16 partials differing. End to end, we verified accuracy on NIAH up to 1M tokens, MMMU-Pro and HLE with [inkling-verify](https://github.com/thinking-machines-lab/inkling-verify), with DSpark enabled; the scores match our runs without speculative decoding. ## Acknowledgements We thank the Thinking Machines team for their close collaboration in integrating and optimizing Inkling 2 Small in vLLM. The work was led by Aurick Qiao (Thinking Machines) and Woosuk Kwon (Inferact). --- # H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-minimax-h3-image-rubin Published: 2026-11-12 Authors: vLLM-Omni team Tags: vllm-omni, image-generation, hardware, performance Summary: H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware. ![vLLM-Omni and MiniMax H3-Image.](/blog-assets/figures/minimax-h3-image-rubin/social-preview-compact.png) We brought [MiniMax H3-Image](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image) to **NVIDIA Vera Rubin** with vLLM-Omni. On four GPUs, native 4096×4096 generation reaches **0.87 seconds median** in our short-prompt serving benchmark. A separate throughput configuration delivers **6,115 images/hour**, projecting to **146,755 images/day**. At **USD 0.06879 per image**, using [MiniMax's official Standard 4K API pricing example](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/pricing/overview) before launch discounts as an assumed sale price, peak throughput projects to **USD 105.16/GPU/hour in gross revenue** at full billable utilization, or **USD 78.87/GPU/hour** at 75%. These estimates are before operating costs; the daily capacity is an extrapolation of the measured rate. H3-Image is an open-weight model for text-to-image generation and image editing. One checkpoint handles both tasks in six sampling steps, generates native high-resolution images without an upscaler, and supports up to 16 reference images. We bring H3-Image to **consumer and data-center GPUs**, spanning **NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Moore Threads (MUSA)**, as well as **Huawei Ascend NPUs**. - **Single- and multi-GPU serving.** Run on a single RTX GPU or distribute generation across multiple data-center GPUs, with configurations for different memory capacities. - **Measured across 10 NVIDIA hardware types.** Compare latency for text-to-image generation and editing across output resolutions and reference-image counts. ## Quality Oil-paint strokes, a multi-view camera drawing, Japanese poster lettering and tiny words on a rice grain reveal what a smaller image can lose. A game environment adds weathered stone and reflected light. Each uses one H3-Image-generated **4K** image, resized to **1K** and **2K** with its aspect ratio preserved, so composition stays fixed. ## Performance The two API modes are straightforward: **Text-to-Image** takes a prompt; **Image Edit** takes a prompt and one or more reference images. Our main comparisons use **2K (2048×2048)** and **4K (4096×4096)** output, with one image returned per request. The prompts and reference files stay fixed across machines. See MiniMax's [API guide](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/guides/image-generation) for the request parameters. Choose **Text-to-image** or **Image Edit** below. For editing, select **1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 reference images**; output sizes reflect the measured cases. For **4K text-to-image**, four GB300 GPUs average **1.48 seconds**. A **4K image edit with one reference** averages **1.77 seconds**. A single RTX 5090 with CPU layerwise offload takes **52.29 seconds** and **61.45 seconds** for those same requests. Each timing includes the complete PNG response. For **2K text-to-image**, a **single H200** averages **1.49 seconds** with BF16 and resident weights. For the detailed coffee-product prompt used here, Rubin averages **1.09 seconds** at 4K. The **0.87-second** headline comes from a separate short-prompt serving benchmark in **Rubin Bringup**, not this request. Both use four GPUs, SP4 and MXFP8; the request corpus, HTTP client and summary statistic differ. Every result shows its GPU count. **Test setup** lists the exact GPU model, CUDA-visible VRAM per GPU, interconnect, power limit and serving configuration. GPU count, precision and memory placement vary, so these figures compare deployed systems rather than isolate GPU architecture. The 1K checks return 1024×1024 images; with the local model's default minimum canvas, they are generated at 2048×2048 and resized. They therefore do not represent native 1K diffusion compute. Some 1K and 2K runs also use different allocator settings, shown in Test setup. [Benchmark data](/assets/figures/minimax-h3-image-rubin/api-workload-results.csv). Bars show three-seed means after warmup, with min–max ranges. Configurations, timing scope and the 10-minute request limit are documented in **Test setup**. ## Inference Optimizations H3-Image pairs a **Qwen3-VL encoder** with a **33.1B dense DiT** and an image VAE. A native 4096×4096 output contributes **16,384 target-image tokens** across six denoising steps, before VAE decoding. References add encoding work and conditioning tokens. This gives us three practical targets: DiT compute, decoding overhead and model memory. See the [model architecture](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image#model-architecture). ### Faster DiT On Blackwell and Rubin, **MXFP8 GEMMs** accelerate eligible DiT linears while reducing their weight footprint. **Ulysses SP4** distributes sequence work across four GPUs; DiT TP1 keeps the weights replicated. **AdaLN caching** reuses exact conditioning projections when their inputs and weights match. All six denoising steps still run. The encoder and VAE keep their configured precision; Hopper and Ampere use BF16. ### Faster Decoding The VAE decodes independent image tiles. We distribute those tiles across GPUs, then combine **CUDA Graph replay with multiple CUDA streams** on each GPU: replay reduces repeated launch overhead, while streams allow tiles to overlap. A separate BF16 control on four GB300 GPUs shows why this matters. VAE decoding fell from **2.635 s to 0.213 s**, bringing end-to-end latency from approximately **4.0 s to 1.6 s**, or **2.5× faster**. Both paths already distribute tiles across four GPUs; this is the combined graph-and-stream gain. [Control measurements](/assets/figures/minimax-h3-image-rubin/vae-decoding-control.json). ### Fitting Smaller GPUs **Layerwise CPU offload** trades weight-transfer time for GPU memory. RTX 5090 and RTX 5080 offload the DiT and text encoder and decode the VAE eagerly. RTX 6000D and RTX PRO 6000 keep the DiT resident, offload the encoder and use VAE CUDA Graph. This enables single-GPU deployment while explaining part of the latency gap with resident data-center configurations. ## Rubin Bringup Our starting point was vLLM-Omni's H3-Image implementation and [vLLM's Rubin support](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-09-vera-rubin-preview), using a CUDA 13.4 runtime. H3-Image adds a dense diffusion workload to that foundation: a native 4096×4096 image contributes 16,384 target-image tokens across six denoising steps, followed by VAE decoding. We tested how this path translates Rubin's capabilities into interactive latency and serving throughput. We made two changes for these runs: - **MXFP8 integration.** We connected Omni's diffusion linears to vLLM's online MXFP8 loading and kernel selection. On Rubin, eligible DiT linears use **FlashInfer CuTe-DSL MXFP8 GEMM**; attention uses **`TRTLLM_ATTN`**. These are existing library kernels. The text encoder and VAE retain native precision. - **Reliable 4K output.** Repeated 4K requests exposed a stall in the output transfer path. We moved the final image-layout conversion to the CPU, after transferring the decoded uint8 tensor. Regression checks confirmed repeated requests completed and decoded pixels were unchanged. We then compared SP4, SP2×DP2 and SP1×DP4, using the existing VAE CUDA Graph and AdaLN caching paths. Four GPUs reached **0.87-second responses** with SP4, or **6,115 images/hour** with four replicas. The following sweep fixes native 4K text-to-image, no references, six steps and MXFP8 DiT linears, with a separate 160-request prompt–seed corpus at each concurrency point: 20 short prompts, each 122–160 characters, across eight seeds. The cross-hardware coffee-product request above uses a 1,292-character prompt and reports a three-seed mean. ### Latency With SP4 at concurrency 1, median latency is **0.866 seconds** (p95 **0.944 seconds**): **2.21× faster than GB200** and **1.64× faster than GB300**. All three latency configurations use four GPUs, SP4 and MXFP8. ### Throughput Four single-GPU replicas (**SP1×DP4**) reach **6,115 images/hour** at concurrency 8, with **4.411-second median latency**. SP4 reaches **4,407 images/hour** at concurrency 2 with a **1.421-second median**. Replicas add **38.7% throughput**; the subsecond and peak-throughput headlines are separate operating points. With SP4 fixed across platforms, Rubin delivers **2.20× GB200** and **1.60× GB300** peak throughput. Each plotted point contains 160 warm requests; replicas serve independent images without combining them into a DiT batch. ### Economics **6,115 images/hour** projects to **146,755 4K images/day** per four-GPU Rubin system. We use **USD 0.06879 per image**, the [MiniMax official API pricing example](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/pricing/overview) for **Standard 4K text-to-image with no references, before launch discounts**. At that assumed sale price, projected gross revenue is **USD 105.16/GPU/hour** at 100% billable utilization, or **USD 78.87/GPU/hour** at 75%. Revenue = images/hour × price/image × billable utilization ÷ 4 GPUs. Actual hosted-API charges vary with text-token usage. Revenue figures are before operating costs; daily capacity extrapolates the measured rate, rather than a 24-hour load test. ## Other Hardware H3-Image is also supported on **AMD Instinct, Intel Arc Pro, Huawei Ascend and Moore Threads** hardware through the implementations and recipes below. These community validations use their own workloads and configurations; the matched performance figures above cover our NVIDIA runs. **AMD Instinct.** The [AMD recipe](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/blob/main/recipes/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image-AMD.md) includes text-to-image and editing measurements on **MI325X and MI350X**, from one to eight GPUs, using BF16 and `FLASH_ATTN`. We also thank the OpenDirector contributors for their work on H3-Image integration in creative workflows. --- # Reinforcement Learning: Optimizing 0.6B Dense Models on TPU v7 via vLLM Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-12-rl-small-dense-tpu-v7 Published: 2026-11-12 Authors: Loki Chen, Yang Song, Hongye Xie, Ming Lei, Greg Rehm, Chongyang Bai, Dre Olgiati, Bob Kamma, Tej Choudhary, Hang Cui, Imed Zitouni, Hamed Firooz (Meta ASA); Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Yufei Li, Frank Shyu, Parish Aggarwal, Senthil Manickavelu, Xi Liu, Luke Simon (Meta Ranking AI Research) Tags: reinforcement-learning, performance, hardware Summary: Co-designing RL for a Qwen3-0.6B dense policy on Google Cloud TPU v7 across vLLM, Tunix, MaxText, and Pallas, with a 107x end-to-end speedup from ~100 minutes to ~56 seconds per true-8K RL cycle. *Authors —*
***ASA:** Loki Chen, Yang Song, Hongye Xie, Ming Lei, Greg Rehm, Chongyang Bai, Dre Olgiati, Bob Kamma, Tej Choudhary, Hang Cui, Imed Zitouni, Hamed Firooz.*
***Ranking AI Research:** Mingfu Liang, Kavosh Asadi, Yufei Li, Frank Shyu, Parish Aggarwal, Senthil Manickavelu, Xi Liu, Luke Simon.* **Takeaways** - In small dense-model RL, decode scheduling, synchronization, attention geometry, and KV-cache lifecycle become first-order bottlenecks. - We co-designed across the open-source TPU stack (vLLM, Tunix, MaxText, and Pallas) and upstreamed the changes, so developers on Google Cloud TPU v7 can reach the 56-second (~183K tokens/s) path with the merged [tpu-recipes recipe](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-recipes/pull/387) and the flags listed in [Appendix B](#appendix-b--how-to-reproduce), without repeating our bring-up work. - The complete rollout-to-update cycle is 107x faster on Google Cloud TPU v7, falling from roughly 100 minutes to about 56 seconds while keeping the full 8,192-token response budget. ## Why a small model matters for research Generative reasoning is reshaping how ranking and decision systems work. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [[arXiv:2606.31984](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31984)] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: *for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability?* A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time. Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination. ## The research challenge ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-09-rl-small-dense-tpu-v7/why-small-dense-needs-co-design.webp) We ran RL for a 0.6-billion-parameter model on a 64-chip Google Cloud TPU v7 (Ironwood) slice. The model has far fewer weights than the large dense and mixture-of-experts systems that usually motivate distributed training work, and its small size made the workload hard to run efficiently. For a large dense or MoE model, each layer performs enough matrix computation that device utilization is often dominated by the familiar questions: how to shard parameters, move activations, route experts, and keep large matrix units busy. Those problems are hard, but their costs scale visibly with the model. A small dense model changes the balance. The useful matrix work per device shrinks, but many fixed costs do not: - the host still schedules decode iterations; - every token still traverses the attention stack; - every layer still launches or enters compiled kernels; - every rollout step still updates and synchronizes weights; - the runtime still tracks thousands of sequences and their stopping conditions; - the RL cycle still includes reward computation, training, cache invalidation, and distributed orchestration. As the model gets smaller, these fixed costs take a larger share of each step. A few milliseconds of dispatch overhead, an overly large attention compute block, or a cache allocation repeated on every update could dominate the work we wanted TPU v7 to perform. Small dense-model RL is therefore a coordination-sensitive workload with its own bottlenecks, and it benefits from hardware-software-model co-design. ## Why co-design mattered ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-09-rl-small-dense-tpu-v7/co-design-rl-0p6b-dense.webp) As with any distributed accelerator stack, the first step was aligning basic configuration parameters (parallelism, batch concurrency, mesh shape, and HBM limits) with our workload geometry to establish a clean baseline. The remaining bottlenecks sat deeper in the open-source stack and were specific to long-context, high-concurrency small-model RL with frequent on-policy weight synchronization. We then profiled the full RL cycle, identified the mechanism behind each new bottleneck, and worked downward through MaxText, Tunix, vLLM/tpu-inference, Pathways/XLA, and Pallas in three stages: configuration tuning; cross-stack decode co-design across the XLA device loop, Pallas VMEM pipeline, and host-device scheduler; and full-cycle optimization of host-side overheads, KV-cache lifecycle, training attention geometry, and rollout shape. Configuration tuning plateaued at roughly 30K tokens/s, the decode co-design raised the full-batch decode rate to approximately 130.5K tokens/s, and the final configuration sustained ~183K tokens/s averaged over the whole rollout. Throughout, we kept the model, GRPO recipe, completions per step, and 8,192-token response cap fixed (the prompt cap changed once; see Benchmark methodology), and upstreamed the fast paths. Most are opt-in settings; Appendix B lists the ones the final configuration uses. ## Benchmark methodology and dataset Because proprietary Ads ranking and generative recommendation (GR) models and user-interaction logs at Meta cannot be shared publicly, we built an open, reproducible benchmark proxy using Qwen3-0.6B on public math reasoning prompts. It mirrors the systems geometry of production generative ranking: a compact sub-billion-parameter dense policy generating long multi-step reasoning traces (up to 8,192 tokens) across thousands of concurrent candidates. Our headline workload is Qwen3-0.6B Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) true-8K: 256 prompts × 8 generations (2,048 completions per rollout), up to 8,192 generated tokens, BF16, and synchronous on-policy execution. The bring-up and Phase I–II milestones (up to 299 s) ran with a 16,384-token prompt cap (24K maximum context) on NuminaMath and OpenMath prompts. From the 88-second milestone on, runs use [OpenMathInstruct-2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/OpenMathInstruct-2) (`train_1M`) with a 4,096-token prompt cap (12,288-token context). Model, GRPO recipe, completions per step, and the 8,192-token response cap are identical, and real prompts are short in both (~170 tokens for NuminaMath, 149 tokens on average for OpenMathInstruct-2), so the generated work per step is comparable; the larger prompt cap mainly reserves more KV capacity per sequence. We report steady-state complete-cycle wall-clock time, excluding compilation, warmup, and checkpoint writes. We tracked rollout throughput and full-cycle latency across the campaign, then used controlled ablations to isolate individual mechanisms. **Metric definitions.** *Step time* is the steady-state wall-clock time of one complete rollout-to-update cycle (TensorBoard `perf/train/global_step_time`, median over steps 3 and later of a 20-step run); for the final configuration the headline 56 s is its fastest steady-state steps (p10 55.7 s), next to the 57.9 s median. *Decode throughput (tokens/s)* counts generated (completion) tokens only, excludes prefill, and is aggregated over the whole 64-chip slice. For the milestones up to 299 seconds it is the full-batch decode rate measured in controlled runs. For the 88-second milestone and the final configuration it is the generated tokens of one rollout divided by the whole rollout phase (~9.2M tokens in 68 s; ~9.0M tokens in 49.1 s), which includes the low-occupancy tail and is therefore a conservative lower bound on the full-batch rate. **Milestones at a glance.** Rollout dominated every step. Up to the 299-second milestone it took 80–90% of the step, so those rows give approximate (~) phase times; the 88-second and final splits are measured from per-phase step timers. Rows up to 299 s used the 16K-prompt-cap contract; the 88-second and final rows use the 4K-prompt-cap contract (see Benchmark methodology). | Milestone | Step time | Decode throughput | Rollout | Everything else | |---|---|---|---|---| | Un-tuned bring-up | ~6,000 s | ~4K tok/s | ~5,100 s | ~900 s | | Configuration and mesh tuning | 1,260 s | ~30K tok/s | ~1,070 s | ~190 s | | Controlled baseline (colocated, TP/DP rebalanced) | 616 s | ~30K tok/s | ~525 s | ~90 s | | + Continue Decode | 369 s | ~64.9K tok/s | ~315 s | ~55 s | | + RPA block split + EOS-check interval | 299 s | ~130.5K tok/s | ~255 s | ~45 s | | + Continuous-batching decode, sharded sampling, reward pool, packing, GC control | 88 s | ~135K tok/s | 68 s | 20 s (training 8 s, weight sync 7 s) | | Final configuration (TP1×DP128) | **56 s** fastest steady-state steps (p10 55.7 s); 57.9 s 20-step median | **~183K tok/s** | 49.1 s | 8.4 s | In the final configuration a rollout generates about 9.0M tokens (2,048 completions × ~4.4K mean completion length; 27.8% of completions reach the 8,192-token cap), and the median phase times are 49.1 s of rollout and 8.4 s for training, weight sync, reward, and cache lifecycle combined (85% rollout). ## Optimizing on Google Cloud TPU v7 We ran the true-8K reference workload on a 64-chip Google Cloud TPU v7 (4×4×4) slice using TP1×DP128 rollout parallelism: 128 independent vLLM engines, one per TPU device (two per chip), each holding the full 0.6B model (1.2 GB in BF16) and all eight KV heads, with requests spread across engines by round-robin data-parallel routing. Earlier in the campaign we used 4-way tensor parallelism to pool HBM for the KV caches; the move to TP1×DP128 is quantified in Phase III. The complete step included: - rollout generation; - reward computation and advantage construction; - MaxText training; - policy-weight synchronization; - KV-cache and request-state lifecycle; - preparation for the next rollout. We intentionally began with a serial full-batch design. It made policy ownership, weight versions, cache invalidation, and timing boundaries explicit. Pathways managed the multi-host mesh and in-memory transitions, while the learner and sampler shared the 64-chip resource over the cycle. We later brought up an asynchronous RL prototype, but kept the main performance ladder on the serial path so the timing boundaries remained explicit and optimizations could be compared without adding hardware. All milestones below reflect steady-state steps. To isolate sub-second kernel and runtime deltas from cluster topology variance, we used dedicated slices and same-window controls. ### Phase I: align basic workload configuration to establish a proper baseline Our initial un-tuned bring-up (2,048 synchronous 24K-context rollouts, before mesh sizing or continuous device-side decode) generated roughly 4K rollout tokens/s, or about 100 minutes per full RL cycle. Before modifying any runtime or kernel code, we tuned the configuration space of the existing stack. The work included: - tensor- and data-parallel mesh sweeps; - rollout batch size and concurrency; - maximum active sequences and token budgets; - HBM allocation and host-memory limits; - prompt and response geometry; - sampler and trainer resource balance; - Pathways JobSet placement, compilation, checkpoint, and staging behavior. This first phase increased decode throughput from roughly 4K to approximately 30K tokens/s (7.5x) and reduced the full cycle from ~100 minutes (6,000 s) to 21 minutes (1,260 s, 4.8x). Colocation and TP/DP host-mesh rebalancing then established our 616-second controlled baseline, and we moved into stack co-design. These steps aligned basic configuration parameters (mesh topology, batch concurrency, and HBM limits) with a 24K-context, 2,048-rollout workload shape. The slow starting point came from a configuration not yet tuned for this workload shape; fixing it gave us a properly configured baseline and exposed the real runtime bottlenecks. Decode throughput improved much more than full-cycle latency: the full-batch decode rate is only part of rollout time, and prefill, host returns, and the low-occupancy tail of long completions did not speed up with it. ### Phase II: cross-stack decode co-design, from MaxText and vLLM down to XLA and Pallas At approximately 30K tokens/s, configuration sweeps stopped paying off. Profiling showed that device execution on TPU v7 took only milliseconds per decode step, while end-to-end rollout time was dominated by host-device dispatch round trips, XLA compilation and runner overheads on the Flax NNX path, and Pallas kernel pipeline stalls over 24K-token contexts. The Phase II changes landed in tpu-inference and MaxText (PRs in the table at the end of this phase) and act along this execution path: MaxText → Tunix → vLLM/tpu-inference (Runner & Scheduler) → Ragged Paged Attention (RPA v3)/Pallas → Pathways/XLA This phase raised steady-state decode throughput (attending over up to 24K context tokens per sequence across 2,048 synchronous rollouts) to approximately 130.5K tokens/s (4.35x the 30K operating point), cutting full-step latency in the controlled ladder from 616 seconds to 299 seconds. #### Compiling multi-step device decode loops across Flax NNX, vLLM, and XLA Autoregressive decoding is sequential across tokens, but re-entering the Python host scheduler on every token is too expensive for a 0.6B model: the fixed cost of host-device dispatch, request-state bookkeeping, and trace serialization exceeds the matrix compute of the forward pass itself. Continue Decode in vLLM moved many decode iterations into a single compiled XLA device loop, which required changes to how MaxText, Flax NNX, and tpu-inference compile and run the loop. We repaired `continue_decode` on the `flax_nnx` serving path and prevented the runtime from dropping XLA compile options ([tpu-inference #3374](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3374)), eliminated mutable metadata state leaks across compiled linear layers ([tpu-inference #3101](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3101)), stopped the vLLM runner from over-padding steps past `max_num_batched_tokens` ([tpu-inference #3466](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3466)), and capped per-step request-ID trace serialization overhead at 2,048 concurrent rollouts ([tpu-inference #3510](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3510)). In the controlled MaxText production ladder, this cross-stack path reduced a 616-second clean step to 369 seconds, a 40.1% reduction. This result showed where the time went: the small model was waiting on the runtime and compiler stack to deliver uninterrupted device work to the TPU v7 MXUs. #### Splitting RPA v3 KV fetch and compute blocks for 24K-context caches Once host dispatch was amortized, on-device attention memory movement became the primary bottleneck. Ragged Paged Attention v3 (RPA v3), written in Pallas, overlaps HBM-to-VMEM DMA transfers with TensorCore compute using a double-buffered VMEM pipeline. However, its default heuristic coupled the KV fetch block size and the compute block size to a single monolithic value (~16K tokens). On our 24K-context RL workload, a 16K compute block starved the Pallas double-buffered pipeline: each compute stage had to wait for a large KV tile transfer to complete, reducing pipeline depth between DMA and MXU execution. We refactored the kernel interface to decouple HBM fetch geometry from VMEM compute tiling across decode, prefill, and mixed paths ([tpu-inference #3102](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3102)) and plumbed those kernel controls up through the tpu-inference MaxText serving bridge ([tpu-inference #3395](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3395)) and MaxText RL trainer configs ([MaxText #5100](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5100)). Keeping a 16,384-token HBM fetch block to maximize burst DMA bandwidth while slicing execution into 4,096-token VMEM compute blocks restored deep DMA/MXU overlap and lifted decode throughput from 64,929 to 96,273 tokens/s (+48%). The kernel's default heuristic could not know this workload's block geometry; exposing the block sizes as settings let us match it. The split above was measured with 4-way tensor parallelism. In the final TP1×DP128 configuration every chip holds all eight KV heads, so the tiles were re-tuned to 2,048-token decode blocks (`RPA_V3_DECODE_BLOCK_SIZES=1,2048,1,2048`, with matching prefill and mixed overrides; see Appendix B): at TP1, a 4,096-token decode tile is slower and an 8,192-token tile exceeds VMEM. #### Checking EOS less often inside the fused decode loop Even inside a fused device loop, Continue Decode still executed an on-device reduction (any-sequence-hit-EOS) and evaluated the early-exit condition on every token step. Across 2,048 concurrent rollouts, that per-token reduction created an unnecessary synchronization barrier inside the compiled loop. We modified the compiled loop to skip the per-step on-device EOS reduction when the check is off ([tpu-inference #3509](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3509)) and exposed cadence control to balance device execution against host scheduling ([tpu-inference #3174](https://github.com/vllm-project/tpu-inference/pull/3174)), while per-sequence masking preserved the true EOS boundary. The interval is a trade-off: checking every step incurred on-device sync overhead, whereas checking every 32 steps delayed returning to the vLLM host scheduler to evict finished sequences and free batch slots. An interval of 8 steps balanced uninterrupted XLA loop execution against timely scheduler retirement. Together with the RPA block split, this change took the step from 369 seconds to the 299-second true-8K milestone; we did not retain a separate step-time measurement for each of the two. In the final configuration we turn the in-loop EOS check off entirely (`CONTINUE_DECODE_EOS_CHECK_INTERVAL=0`) and instead lengthen the fused loop to 512 decode steps per return to the host scheduler (`max_decode_steps=512`); per-sequence masking still preserves each EOS boundary (see the continuous-batching decode window in Phase III). Phase III had two stages. The first took the step from 299 seconds to 88 seconds by late August (rollout 68 s, training 8 s, weight sync 7 s). On the rollout side, a continuous-batching decode window kept the fused loop full by retiring finished sequences as inert masked slots instead of exiting on EOS, and vocab-sharded sampling removed a full-vocabulary logits all-gather (~78 MB per data-parallel rank) and the top-k/top-p sweeps from every decode iteration. Off the rollout path, serial reward scoring, measured at ~30 s per step, moved to a process pool, and sequence packing and configurable garbage collection shortened training and host time. Per-change contributions within this stage were not isolated. The move to the 4K prompt cap also happened here (see Benchmark methodology). KV persistence, faster weight synchronization and detokenization, the Splash Attention retune, and the final rollout configuration then took it from 88 seconds to 56 seconds. #### Separating logical cache invalidation from physical allocation Every RL step changes the policy weights. KV values computed under the old policy must never be visible to the new policy. The conservative lifecycle reset the prefix cache, deleted the physical KV allocation, synchronized weights, and reallocated the cache. We observed that resetting prefix mappings already made every old block logically unreachable. When HBM headroom allowed it, the physical allocation could persist safely across the weight update even though its contents were invalid. The next rollout re-prefilled and overwrote the blocks before reading them. On the earlier TP4 stack, an opt-in KV-persistence path reduced the measured setup phase from ~37 seconds to 3 seconds. On the final configuration, turning it on (`free_kv_cache_during_weight_sync=false`) still moves the 20-step median from 60.3 s to 57.9 s. The weight-sync unroll ([Tunix #2232](https://github.com/google/tunix/pull/2232)) and the overlap of detokenization and log-prob extraction with decode ([Tunix #2233](https://github.com/google/tunix/pull/2233)) landed with KV persistence in the 88 → 56 s stage. The reward process pool ([Tunix #1904](https://github.com/google/tunix/pull/1904), [MaxText #5255](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5255)) and configurable garbage collection ([Tunix #2086](https://github.com/google/tunix/pull/2086), [MaxText #5236](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5236)) landed earlier, in the 299 → 88 s stage. The [public implementation](https://github.com/google/tunix/pull/2231) is default-off and requires two safety conditions: prefix mappings must be reset on every policy update, and the weight reshard must not depend on freeing the cache allocation for HBM headroom. #### Retuning Splash Attention for the training shape Training took 8 s of the 88-second step. After enabling RL sequence packing ([MaxText #5100](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5100)) in the 299 → 88 s stage, we switched training to flash attention and retuned the Splash Attention block sizes for the production sequence geometry, passed as MaxText config overrides on the RL trainer command line: ```bash attention='flash' \ sa_block_q=1024 sa_block_q_dkv=1024 sa_block_q_dq=1024 \ sa_block_kv=2048 sa_block_kv_compute=2048 \ sa_block_kv_dkv=2048 sa_block_kv_dkv_compute=2048 sa_block_kv_dq=2048 \ sa_use_base2_exp=false ``` In a same-window control, the retune saved about 2 s per step. #### Final rollout configuration The table below lists the remaining changes in the 88 → 56 s stage. Part of the gain came with the software itself: running the 88-second launcher unchanged on an image built at upstream head (which includes Tunix #2232, #2233, and #2309 and MaxText #5235) measured 74 s on a second cluster, and launcher tuning on that image took it the rest of the way; cluster-to-cluster differences were not separated. Unless a row says otherwise, each change was measured against a same-window control run on an earlier image and was not re-measured on the final image. We include them because they kept plausible but incorrect explanations from becoming roadmap commitments. ### Weight and KV byte reduction gave little decode speedup We verified a weight-only INT8 path and observed no meaningful decode improvement. For a 0.6B model with long contexts, model weights were a small fraction of the data movement and fixed execution cost. We also verified an FP8 KV-cache path by checking that cache capacity doubled. The latency result was far smaller than a bandwidth-proportional speedup. That ruled out one hypothesis: at this operating point, decode time depended on more than HBM bytes. Dispatch, fusion, per-iteration fixed cost, and other kernels set a floor that byte reduction alone could not remove. Quantization helps most when weights or KV traffic dominate, and it helps little when a different roofline controls the workload. ### Shared-prefix cascade attention gave no net gain at production scale Eight generations from the same prompt appear to be an ideal case for explicit shared-prefix attention. Early prototypes looked promising against a naive JAX baseline. When compared with the real pipelined RPA kernel at production scale, the advantage fell sharply. A composed prefix/suffix cascade measured no net gain because the stock paged-attention path already benefited substantially from shared physical pages and the extra calls and merge overhead consumed the remaining opportunity. The negative result saved a larger kernel project. It also reinforced a benchmarking rule: compare against the production kernel on the production image at the production batch size, because a mathematically equivalent reference implementation (here, the naive JAX baseline) overstated the gain. ### A larger training microbatch did not shorten training A larger training microbatch fit after memory tuning, but halving the number of gradient-accumulation loops did not reduce the total training FLOPs. The step remained flat. Similarly, lighter rematerialization freed HBM but did not shorten the compute-bound training path. ### Shorter response caps had diminishing returns Reducing the response cap from 8,192 to 6,144 removed a large low-occupancy tail and reached approximately 56 seconds, but it changed the RL recipe and therefore remained a separate candidate. Reducing the cap further to 5,120 produced no reliable additional gain. By then, training and setup time set the floor. This was a separate experiment on the stack before the final Splash and rollout changes. The later Splash, KV-persistence, weight-sync, and final rollout changes reached approximately the same latency while preserving the true 8,192-token cap; every headline number in this post uses the full 8,192-token cap. ## Our optimization loop The performance curve came from repeating the same engineering loop: - Measure the full cycle. Isolated tokens/s was useful, but the decision metric was rollout-to-update time. - Profile the current winner. Every successful optimization changed the phase breakdown. - Form a mechanism hypothesis. We asked what specific synchronization, allocation, block shape, or data movement created the wall time. - Change one mechanism at a time where possible; risky paths were environment-gated and default-off. In the 299 → 88 s stage several changes landed together and were not isolated. - Use dedicated-slice or same-window controls. Cluster placement and contention can overwhelm small deltas. - Validate semantics. EOS boundaries, policy versions, token/log-prob alignment, finite loss, cache invalidation, and reward behavior were part of performance testing. - Bank negative results. A null result that closed a large engineering branch was considered a successful experiment. - Profile again. The next bottleneck was rarely the one that had mattered one round earlier. What we kept and what we dropped: | Change | Outcome | |---|---| | Continue Decode (compiled XLA decode loop) | Adopted: 616 s → 369 s | | RPA v3 block-size override | Adopted: +48% decode tok/s at TP4; 2K decode blocks at TP1 | | EOS-check interval of 8 steps | Superseded: 369 s → 299 s with the RPA split in Phase II; the final configuration turns the check off (`CONTINUE_DECODE_EOS_CHECK_INTERVAL=0`) and runs 512 decode steps per host return | | KV persistence across the weight update | Adopted: setup ~37 s → 3 s on the earlier TP4 stack; 60.3 s → 57.9 s on the final configuration | | Reward scoring in a process pool | Adopted (299 → 88 s stage): serial scoring had measured ~30 s per step; saving not isolated | | Continuous-batching decode window; vocab-sharded sampling | Used in the 299 → 88 s stage (contributions not isolated); the final configuration runs on upstream code, with the decode window covered by `CONTINUE_DECODE_EOS_CHECK_INTERVAL=0` and sharded sampling still to be upstreamed | | Sequence packing; flash/Splash retune | Adopted: ~2 s per step from the Splash retune | | 512-step decode loop; TP1×DP128 with round-robin routing | Adopted: ~4 s and ~1 s per step | | Weight-only INT8 | Not adopted: no meaningful decode gain | | FP8 KV cache | Not adopted: 2× capacity, small latency gain | | Composed prefix/suffix cascade attention | Not adopted: no net gain at production scale | | Larger training microbatch | Not adopted: step time flat | | Shorter response cap (8,192 → 6,144, then 5,120) | Not adopted: 6,144 reached ~56 s on an earlier stack but changes the RL recipe; 5,120 gave no reliable further gain | ## When systems optimization exposes a learning bottleneck The 56-second result runs RL from the raw 0.6B checkpoint without an SFT warm-start, which stresses the systems side: 27.8% of the 2,048 completions hit the 8,192-token cap, and the mean completion length was ~4.4K tokens. Policies warm-started with SFT converge to more concise reasoning traces, so their training cycles run faster than the steps measured here (56 s fastest, 57.9 s median). Combining a lightweight format-and-task SFT warm-start and reward shaping with on-policy RL post-training (GRPO / Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization, DAPO) teaches the compact policy to solve reasoning and ranking tasks with shorter average completion lengths, which adds to the systems speedups. Shorter completions also shorten rollout, which is 85% of the step in the final configuration, so in RL post-training the policy's behavior is part of the workload the hardware sees. ## What comes next Next, we plan to work on the following in vLLM, Tunix, and MaxText on Google Cloud TPU v7: - Scaling multi-stage SFT + RL (GRPO/DAPO) recipes across broader generative ranking and reasoning model families; - Auto-tuning the Pallas RPA v3 and Splash Attention heuristics so DMA/compute block sizes and layouts are chosen automatically from model and context shape; - Upstreaming replay-exact sharded sampling for deterministic, reproducible multi-host RL evaluation at scale; - Scaling to 128-chip (4×4×8) and larger TPU v7 slices for higher rollout concurrency and decode throughput; - Asynchronous and agentic RL (AgenticAsync) with strict policy-version and behavior-log-prob guarantees; - Multiple Program, Multiple Data (MPMD) disaggregated rollout and training to overlap generation and learner updates across dedicated TPU sub-meshes. We plan to upstream these as well, so they also run without custom patches. ## Conclusion The project started with a small dense model that appeared easy to run and a full RL cycle that took roughly 100 minutes. Configuration and mesh tuning gave the first 7.5x in decode throughput. Decode-path changes in tpu-inference (including the Pallas RPA v3 kernel) and MaxText took the step from 616 s to 299 s. A continuous-batching decode window and vocab-sharded sampling on the rollout side, plus a reward process pool, sequence packing, and GC control, took it to 88 s. KV persistence, the weight-sync and detokenization changes, the Splash retune, and TP1×DP128 rollout took it to 56 s. Across the program on Google Cloud TPU v7, decode throughput increased from approximately 4K to ~183K tokens/s (the final value is a whole-rollout average, so this is a conservative comparison), while end-to-end cycle time fell from roughly 100 minutes to approximately 56 seconds. That is about 46x higher throughput and 107x faster full-cycle execution. All runtime, trainer, and kernel PRs in Appendix A are merged into tpu-inference, Tunix, and MaxText, and the [tpu-recipes recipe](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-recipes/pull/387) with the Appendix B flags reproduces the 56-second (~183K tokens/s) configuration. ## Acknowledgments We thank Tianyu Gu (@gutianyu-google), Alisa Chen, Pysith Vanuptikul, Summer Yang, Hossein Sarshar, Jianting Cao, Weiren Yu and the Google Cloud TPU, vLLM, Tunix, and MaxText engineering teams for their close collaboration in co-designing and upstreaming these optimizations. ## Appendix A — Merged upstream PRs All 23 PRs below are merged upstream (the last on September 21, 2026), across **vllm-project/tpu-inference**, **google/tunix**, and **AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext** during this optimization campaign: **vLLM / tpu-inference — 10 merged PRs** -
