with EPD Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-11-encoder-disaggregation-epd Published: 2026-11-11 Authors: Inferact, InferMatrix, IBM, and Mooncake Tags: multimodal, disaggregation, performance Summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing. Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's [inference deployment Q&A](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/doc/inference_deployment_qa.md) describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since [our December 2025 architecture post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-12-15-vllm-epd), and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: - **Metadata-only requests** that let downstream instances consume remote embeddings without repeating media preprocessing. - **Dedicated encoder execution** with a separate Model Runner V2 path, encoder-only CUDA Graph support, and reduced checkpoint-loading I/O. - **Remote embedding transfer** through NIXL and Mooncake integrations. - **Cross-encoder output reuse** through Mooncake Store. - **Lower orchestration overhead** in the Python EPD proxy and EPD orchestration with vLLM Router, SMG, and llm-d. The [EPD tracker](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52409) links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through [#62802](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62802). The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. ## Why Separate the Encoder? A multimodal request typically passes through three stages: 1. **Encoder (E):** preprocess media and produce multimodal embeddings. 2. **Prefill (P):** process the prompt and multimodal embeddings, building the state needed for generation. 3. **Decode (D):** generate output tokens using that state. EPD supports two deployment patterns: **E+PD**, with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and **E/P/D**, with all three stages deployed separately. ![Encoder, prefill, and decode deployment patterns](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-18-encoder-disaggregation-epd/01-epd-architecture.png) *Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode.* An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. ## Metadata-Only Requests: Avoiding Duplicate Preprocessing Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. A straightforward EPD implementation sends the original media to the encoder, transfers the resulting embeddings through an EC connector, and forwards the original request to P/PD. This can work correctly, but the consumer may still fetch, decode, resize, normalize, or patchify the media to recover its input layout. The encoder has already performed that work. **A metadata-only request replaces the downstream media item with a reference containing the structural information already produced on the encoder side.** The consumer reconstructs placeholders from that metadata and receives the actual embeddings through the EC connector. Only the multimodal item changes: the text prompt and generation settings remain, and the embeddings still travel through the EC data path. ![The router forwards raw-media or metadata-only requests while EC connectors deliver embeddings separately](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-18-encoder-disaggregation-epd/02-control-and-data.png) *Figure 2. The router/proxy dispatches media to E and forwards requests to P/PD. In the metadata-only path, E returns layout metadata to the router, which replaces the downstream media item. Embeddings travel separately through the EC connector in both paths. Arrows show logical data flow, not an execution timeline.* For example, Qwen-family image inputs require grid information such as `image_grid_thw` to construct the appropriate multimodal layout. The encoder can publish the grid it already computed, allowing P to use it directly. | Comparison | Raw media forwarded to P | Metadata-only | | --- | --- | --- | | Downstream media item | Image URL, base64 data, or another raw-media input | Input identity and model-required structural metadata | | Input-layout reconstruction | Media processing, or reuse of cached preprocessing results | Placeholder construction from encoder-published metadata | | Embedding source | EC connector; an available remote embedding avoids another encoder forward | EC connector | | Main overhead or requirement | Potentially duplicated fetching, decoding, and preprocessing | A metadata contract consistent with the transferred embedding and input layout | Without metadata-only forwarding, the encoder does not necessarily run twice, since the remote embedding already covers it. The duplication is in media processing, and forwarding a URL can also make the consumer fetch the media again. ### Metadata Across Images, Video, and Audio The Python EPD path supports metadata-only forwarding for images, video, and audio in supported models. All three use the same handoff: the consumer reconstructs the input layout from encoder-published metadata while receiving the embeddings through an EC connector. The required fields depend on the model and modality: - **Images:** image grids such as `image_grid_thw` let the consumer construct the visual placeholder range without processing the pixels again. - **Video:** the frontend accepts `video_embeds` references with the metadata needed to reconstruct the video layout. For Qwen3-VL, this includes `video_grid_thw` and the encoder-published timestamps, which affect the prompt's token layout. - **Audio:** audio token counts and required feature lengths let the consumer rebuild placeholders without repeating audio preprocessing. Metadata serialization is a separate optimization. Model-declared metadata fields can now be represented as numeric JSON arrays, avoiding PyTorch tensor serialization and base64 conversion for small structural fields. This also gives the router and other frontends a language-neutral representation. The audio evaluation below illustrates the benefit of this handoff. The audio change covers the relevant Qwen2-Audio, AudioFlamingo3, Ultravox, Qwen2.5-Omni, and Qwen3-Omni paths for pure-audio Chat Completions requests; realtime and combined audiovisual inputs are outside its scope. ![Audio metadata-only throughput and latency results](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-18-encoder-disaggregation-epd/03-audio-results.png) *Figure 3. Audio metadata-only evaluation on MMAU test-mini: 1,000 samples over two passes, Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct, BF16, TP=1, Model Runner V2, Mooncake TCP, 1E+1PD, concurrency 64, and CUDA Graphs enabled.* In this [audio evaluation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57887), metadata-only forwarding increased throughput from **62.21 to 73.13 requests/s** and reduced mean latency from **980 to 853 ms**. Accuracy changed from 75.90% to 75.65%; that difference remains to be investigated. The comparison measures two audio input paths within EPD, rather than EPD against colocated serving. ## A Dedicated Execution Path for Encoder Instances An encoder-only instance runs no language model, maintains no language-model KV cache, and produces no sampled tokens. Its execution lifecycle should reflect those differences. Model Runner V2 isolates encoder-only execution in a dedicated `MMEncoderModelRunner`. It manages GPU completion without relying on token sampling, preventing premature buffer reuse while encoder work is still in flight. Related changes make encoder execution more consistent: - **Configuration normalization:** producer-only EC instances automatically enter encoder-only mode. - **Correct asynchronous execution:** encoder-only steps skip token sampling, including standalone `--mm-encoder-only` instances without an EC connector. - **Reduced startup I/O:** encoder-only loading skips pure language-model checkpoint shards when the weight layout can be classified safely. On a pruned Kimi-K3 checkpoint, the encoder read 2 of 96 shards and weight loading dropped from 683 s to 0.31 s. - **Encoder CUDA Graph capture:** the encoder-only V2 runner supports opt-in ViT graph capture using the existing budget selection, replay, and eager fallback mechanisms. ### GPU Video Processing GPU preprocessing and NVDEC hardware decoding accelerate media processing on E. In a [30-frame MMVU evaluation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53675), end-to-end throughput improved by approximately 94–115% over three runs, each on a separate 4-GPU GB200 node. Each run used Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, a 1E+3PD topology with a shared-storage EC connector, eager execution, and concurrency 64. The gains include both GPU preprocessing and hardware video decoding; as the encoder became faster, the PD tier became the bottleneck. ## Remote Embedding Transfer and Failure Isolation `ECExampleConnector` provides a shared-filesystem path for validating EPD. Cross-node deployments need network transport, destination-buffer management, and clear ownership of in-flight outputs. Two remote-transfer paths have landed: | Backend | Capability | Documentation | | --- | --- | --- | | NIXL + CPU EC | Shares CPU-offloaded encoder outputs between instances using NIXL transfers between registered CPU mmap regions | [CPU EC guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/ec_cpu_connector/) | | Mooncake EC | Delivers encoder outputs through Mooncake TransferEngine, with TCP and RDMA configuration paths | [Mooncake EC guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/mooncake_ec_connector_usage/) | ### Transfer Shapes Must Match Encoder Outputs Transfer buffers may need to be allocated before an item is encoded. Their size cannot be inferred reliably from a single language-model hidden-size field: different modalities and model architectures can produce different encoder output widths. For example, the tested Qwen3-Omni checkpoint produces visual outputs of width 8192, including DeepStack information, and audio outputs of width 2048. EC producers now measure output widths per modality during initialization and carry the actual shape through the transfer protocol. The NIXL EC protocol version was also updated, requiring producers and consumers to be upgraded together. ### A Failed Transfer Should Fail the Affected Request Metadata-only requests make failure handling especially important. A consumer with the original media may be able to fall back to local encoding. A consumer holding only metadata lacks that input. The consumer now handles this distinction explicitly: when remote encoding cannot arrive and local recovery is unavailable, it reports the affected request as unavailable instead of taking an unsafe fallback path that can terminate EngineCore. Resource-lifecycle fixes, including releasing shared memory after NIXL setup failures, further improve failure handling. ## Reusing Outputs Across Encoder Instances Instance-local caching leaves a reuse gap. An image encoded by E0 may later be routed to E1 after load balancing, scaling, or recovery. If E1 has no cached output, it can repeat an encoder forward that another instance has already completed. Mooncake Store enables cross-encoder output reuse. On a local miss, the encoder checks the shared Store. A hit supplies the embedding without another forward; a miss follows normal encoding and asynchronously publishes the output. Delivery to the selected P instance continues through Mooncake P2P. ![Cross-encoder embedding reuse with Mooncake Store](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-18-encoder-disaggregation-epd/04-cross-encoder-cache.png) *Figure 4. Mooncake Store provides shared output reuse across encoders. ECMooncakeConnector retains the P2P delivery path to the selected consumer.* Shared reuse validates input identity, model identity, and the output tensor contract. Initial support includes images, Model Runner V2, encoder TP=1, and no dynamic LoRA. Publication is asynchronous, so concurrent cold requests can still duplicate computation. See the [cross-encoder reuse guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/cross_encoder_cache/) for configuration and supported combinations. A [controlled reassignment experiment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56242) used six H20 GPUs, InternVL3_5-38B-HF, a 2E+4PD topology, and same-node Mooncake TCP. After cache population, images were reassigned between encoders to create local misses. Across 128 measured requests containing 512 images, shared reuse reduced repeated image encodings from **512 to zero**. TTFT p50 decreased from **1.209 to 0.819 seconds**, and p90 from **1.656 to 0.891 seconds**, with essentially unchanged TPOT. This was a single run of a workload in which every image was reassigned, so it shows the best case for shared reuse. Production savings depend on how often outputs are reused, against the Store's memory and I/O costs. ## EPD Orchestration and Routing **Independent scaling of the compute stages requires an orchestration path that can keep pace.** Distributing media, collecting encoder metadata, and forwarding requests can become a bottleneck as encoding gets faster or cache hits eliminate it. Metadata-only requests reduce downstream media traffic, while JSON metadata avoids tensor serialization for structural fields. The [Python EPD proxy](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56657) further reduces CPU overhead with faster JSON encoding and decoding and direct forwarding of final response bytes, including streaming responses, without decoding and re-encoding them. ### EPD Orchestration in [vLLM Router](https://github.com/vllm-project/router) vLLM Router supports HTTP [E+PD and E/P/D deployments](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/266), metadata-only forwarding, multi-image distribution across encoders, and [data-parallel P/PD consumers](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/507). Encoder and consumer counts can be configured independently. Supported EC backends include Mooncake, NIXL, and the shared-filesystem example connector. See the [router EPD guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/blob/main/docs/epd.md) for native CLI configuration with static workers. ### EPD Orchestration in [SMG](https://github.com/smg-project/smg) [SMG supports vLLM E/P/D deployments](https://github.com/smg-project/smg/pull/5230) over gRPC, including metadata-only forwarding, encoder-side media preprocessing, and Mooncake and NIXL EC backends. It supports [both Python and Rust servicers](https://github.com/smg-project/smg/pull/5387) and can [distribute images within a single image-only request across multiple E workers](https://github.com/smg-project/smg/pull/5447), batching images assigned to the same encoder. ### EPD Orchestration in [llm-d](https://llm-d.ai) llm-d runs vLLM EPD on Kubernetes, with E+PD and E/P/D layouts in its [multimodal serving guide](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/multimodal-serving). Each role runs as a separate pod tier, so encoders can scale independently of prefill and decode and use different hardware. The llm-d Router (an Endpoint Picker, or EPP) selects encoder pods, while the routing sidecar or [Coordinator](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/tree/main/guides/coord-disaggregation) distributes encode requests across them to process multiple images in parallel. Embeddings reach consumers through the NIXL-based EC connector, and text-only requests skip encoding. The llm-d team has collaborated with the vLLM community to provide a validated, Kubernetes-native deployment path for EPD. See [llm-d's multimodal serving blog](https://llm-d.ai/blog/serving-multimodal-at-scale-in-llm-d#when-the-encode-stage-needs-its-own-hardware) for more on the architecture and when to separate encoding. ## DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: EPD in Practice We compared PD serving with EPD on GB200 using DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and 512 MP-DocVQA validation questions, each containing four to six original document pages. Requests averaged 4,905 input tokens and 5.2 output tokens. Each concurrency level ran three times, with caches and CUDA Graphs enabled. The PD baseline used four GPUs for P and four for D. EPD added four single-GPU encoder instances while keeping the same P/D configuration: TP=1, DP=4, expert parallelism, and GPU-resident Engram tables sharded across DP ranks (DEP4). EPD used Mooncake GPU RDMA for embeddings; both deployments used NIXL for KV transfer. Both ran main at `5314c58281` plus the [DeepSeek metadata-only extension](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62802). ![DeepSeek V4.1 Flash throughput per GPU versus P90 time to first token, comparing PD and EPD](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-18-encoder-disaggregation-epd/05-deepseek-v41-epd.png) *Figure 5. Higher throughput and lower P90 TTFT are better. C denotes client concurrency. Throughput counts input plus output tokens, divided by elapsed time and all deployed GPUs: eight for PD, twelve for EPD, including all four encoder GPUs. Points pool three rounds; P90 pools all 1,536 requests per concurrency level. [Plot data](/assets/figures/2026-10-18-encoder-disaggregation-epd/05-deepseek-v41-epd.csv).* At concurrency **64–128**, EPD delivered **6.6–9.5% higher input-plus-output throughput per GPU** than the eight-GPU PD baseline, counting all **12 EPD GPUs**, including the encoders. P90 TTFT was **44–47% lower**. At concurrency 16, however, EPD had lower per-GPU throughput; at 32 it was approximately break-even. The benefit depends on load and resource allocation, rather than separation alone. ## Getting Started Start with E+PD to validate the encoder-to-consumer handoff before adding a separate decode tier. The [Disaggregated Encoder guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/disagg_encoder/) links the example deployments and integration tests. With a compatible vLLM checkout, Mooncake installed, and two available GPUs, the following integration script runs a baseline and compares outputs with a disaggregated deployment: ```bash GPU_E=0 GPU_PD=1 MOONCAKE_EC_PROTOCOL=tcp \ bash tests/v1/ec_connector/integration/run_epd_mooncake_ec_full_pipeline.sh ``` Use the [Mooncake EC guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/mooncake_ec_connector_usage/) for transport dependencies and consumer control-address configuration, or the [CPU EC guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/ec_cpu_connector/) for CPU-offloading and NIXL-based sharing. Choose the E/PD resource split using the target media mix, cache behavior, and latency requirements. ## What's Next Recent work has expanded EPD beyond its core execution and transport paths. MiMo-V2-Omni now declares the embedding fields needed for image EPD, while XPU support includes EC integration and an encoder-only producer runner. Further work includes observability, additional transport and cache backends, frontend integration, and clearer upstream error propagation. Operators need to distinguish time spent computing embeddings, loading cached outputs, and transferring them remotely. Another opportunity is coordinating encoder work with prefill-side reuse. In an E-first pipeline, encoding can begin before P discovers that its KV cache already covers a multimodal occurrence, or that a reusable embedding is available locally. An ongoing [design discussion](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55639) explores how P's demand could suppress unnecessary upstream work. The design must balance saved computation and delivery against additional lookup, coordination, and cold-request latency. Have questions about EPD or interested in getting involved? Join the [EPD / EC-connector channel on vLLM Slack](https://vllm-dev.slack.com/archives/C0CAPN6GGBV) to discuss use cases, share feedback, and collaborate. ## Acknowledgements We thank the following contributors for their work and feedback: - **[Inferact](https://inferact.ai):** [Tianyu Guo](https://github.com/gty111), [Zifeng Mo](https://github.com/Isotr0py), [Siyu Liu](https://github.com/liusy58), [Roger Wang](https://github.com/ywang96) - **[InferMatrix team](https://infermatrix.si):** Ziheng Zhou, Chenzhou Jiang, Ruixin Li, Hang Wu, Chenguang Zheng, Tai Ho Chiu Hero, Hongsheng Liu - **[IBM](https://www.ibm.com):** [Omer Paz](https://github.com/omerpaz95), Or Ozeri, Danny Harnik - **[Mooncake](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake):** [Teng Ma](https://github.com/stmatengss) ## Related Resources - [Encoder Disaggregation for Scalable Multimodal Model Serving](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-12-15-vllm-epd): the original architecture and motivation. - [Disaggregated Encoder documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/disagg_encoder/): deployment examples and configuration. - [EPD tracker](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52409): ongoing implementation work.

--- # Migrating vLLM to the LibTorch Stable ABI Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-06-stable-abi-cuda Published: 2026-11-06 Authors: vLLM Team, Red Hat PyTorch Team, and Meta PyTorch Team Summary: How vLLM migrated its CUDA build and compiled dependencies to the LibTorch Stable ABI, enabling compatible PyTorch upgrades without rebuilding vLLM. ### Introduction vLLM relies heavily on PyTorch, with frequent calls to LibTorch in its C++ backend. As a result, changes to LibTorch’s binary interface may require vLLM to be rebuilt and relinked, even when the APIs remain unchanged. What if we could update LibTorch without rebuilding vLLM? That’s where the LibTorch Stable ABI comes in. With a LibTorch Stable ABI, updating LibTorch does not require rebuilding or updating vLLM in order to keep using it. Instead, we could swap out the torch wheel and import it directly into our vLLM package. As of v0.33.0, vLLM publishes LibTorch ABI Stable CUDA wheels. ![Unstable import](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-06-stable-abi-cuda/unstable_import-v4.png) ![Stable import](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-06-stable-abi-cuda/stable_import-v4.png)

Left: Unstable ABI—new torch requires vLLM to rebuild. Right: Stable ABI—vLLM can import new torch directly.

_Note: Compatibility between vLLM and PyTorch still depends on other factors, including Python APIs, GPU-related requirements (such as the minimum supported CUDA version), and third-party dependencies. The LibTorch Stable ABI addresses binary compatibility but does not eliminate these other constraints._ ### What Is the LibTorch Stable ABI? An application binary interface (ABI) defines how compiled code interacts with a library: how functions are called, data is laid out, and symbols are named. Even if an API looks the same in source code, an ABI change can force extensions to rebuild. A stable ABI preserves a supported set of binary interfaces across compatible versions, so extensions that use them can keep working without a rebuild. PyTorch's LibTorch Stable ABI has three layers: a stable C shim exposing selected LibTorch APIs, C++ wrappers that make the shim easier to use, and headeronly utilities in `torch::headeronly` that do not link against `libtorch.so`. ![LibTorch Stable](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-06-stable-abi-cuda/libtorch_stable.png) ### Why Stable ABI Matters Before the Stable ABI, a new PyTorch release could require a vLLM rebuild, delaying support for the new version and its features. With the Stable ABI, the same vLLM wheel can work across compatible PyTorch releases, letting users upgrade sooner and reducing rebuilds for package distributors. For developers, this means you can update and rebuild PyTorch, then test those changes in vLLM without rebuilding vLLM.

Left: vLLM needs to change as LibTorch changes. Right: vLLM can change independent of LibTorch.

### Tradeoffs The LibTorch Stable ABI is a limited subset of all of LibTorch. While many common ops are already supported through the C shim and through the higher level C++ convenience wrappers, not all are. For example, `is_pinned()` lacked a stable equivalent during the migration. Thankfully, there is a general-purpose `torch_call_dispatcher` C shim that allows us to call ATen ops through the dispatcher in an ABI stable manner! This let us maintain behavior and achieve ABI stability at the same time. This migration also helped inform PyTorch which APIs were commonly used, and in version 2.14 they added a stable C++ `is_pinned()` method. **Before: direct LibTorch method call** ```cpp if (cpu_tensor.is_pinned()) ``` **After: ABI stable dispatcher call** ```cpp std::array is_pinned_stack{ torch::stable::detail::from(cpu_tensor), torch::stable::detail::from(std::nullopt)}; TORCH_ERROR_CODE_CHECK(torch_call_dispatcher( "aten::is_pinned", "", is_pinned_stack.data(), TORCH_ABI_VERSION)); if (torch::stable::detail::to(is_pinned_stack[0])) ``` The second tradeoff is a small amount of additional host-side overhead. The stable C shim adds type-conversion overhead and, for some wrappers that rely on `torch_call_dispatcher`, operator lookup and boxing. This overhead is usually negligible and disappears after warmup under CUDA Graphs, but it can matter in eager mode when repeatedly launching very fast kernels. We saw no noticeable runtime regression during the migration.
### Migrating vLLM to the Stable ABI We have broken down the migration to the Stable ABI into a series of steps: 1. **Assess the situation** First, we assessed whether vLLM could migrate using the stable APIs available at the time. We inventoried its PyTorch API calls, identified gaps, and planned the stable APIs needed to fill them. This work is outlined in the original [RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/26946) for updating vLLM's CUDA build to use the LibTorch Stable ABI. 2. **Migrate AutogradFunctions and meta functions to Python** As of today, the LibTorch Stable ABI does not support stable SymInt, so meta functions need to be written in Python instead of C++. Luckily, vLLM already had most of its meta functions in Python, so migrating the few that were not was relatively simple and made the project more consistent. Similarly, the Stable ABI does not expose PyTorch's autograd machinery, so AutogradFunctions also need to be written in Python. This matters less for an inference engine like vLLM, but if a backward function is implemented, it would need to be in Python. 3. **Set up necessary scaffolding** Since vLLM is such a big project, with over 175 .cpp/.cu source files plus another 120+ headers in its CUDA build alone, migrating everything in one go would have been unwieldy and difficult to review. Instead, we created a separate stable library (see CMakeLists.txt updates in the first migration [PR #31509](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31509/changes#diff-1e7de1ae2d059d21e1dd75d5812d5a34b0222cef273b7c3a2af62eb747f9d20a)), and we migrated the kernels to this library in manageable chunks. The `TORCH_TARGET_VERSION` build flag helps keep the new library LibTorch ABI stable by causing the build to fail if it includes any unstable LibTorch headers. ![vLLM migration from the unstable library to the stable library](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-06-stable-abi-cuda/unstable_to_stable_library.png)

As the stable library grows, the unstable library shrinks then disappears.

4. **Make sure you register ops through the dispatcher** As of today, registering your LibTorch Stable ops requires registration through `STABLE_TORCH_LIBRARY`. This is very familiar if you already register your ops through `TORCH_LIBRARY`, which vLLM does. The biggest difference with the new stable registration is that the implementation needs to be wrapped with `TORCH_BOX`. This generates an adapter that boxes and unboxes the C++ data types into the generic StableIValue types that can cross PyTorch’s Stable ABI. If your kernels are registered through another mechanism, such as pybind11, we recommend first converting the registration to `TORCH_LIBRARY` before registering through `STABLE_TORCH_LIBRARY` (more on this below in the **Challenges Along the Way** section). 5. **Migrate each source file to use stable APIs** Once steps 1–4 are in place, we can migrate each source file to stable APIs. Any PyTorch headers we include should come from the C++ stable wrappers, the headeronly utilities, or the C shim itself: - `torch/csrc/stable` - `torch/headeronly` - `torch/csrc/stable/c/shim.h` (or `torch/csrc/inductor/aoti_torch/c/shim.h`) The source file changes are mostly mechanical. For example: - `torch::Tensor` → `torch::stable::Tensor` - `at::kInt` → `torch::headeronly::ScalarType::Int` - `t.view({...})` → `torch::stable::view(t, {...})` To help migrate the source files, we created skills for AI agents that map existing APIs to their stable equivalents and flag common mistakes, such as changes unrelated to the migration. These skills also support the earlier steps (1–4). They have been useful in our work, but we have not yet developed evaluations to measure their effectiveness (see [abi-stable-skills](https://github.com/janeyx99/abi-stable-skills)). 6. **Verify!** vLLM is used by millions of users across multiple industries, and we do not want to interrupt any of their processes with the migration. Therefore, the most important step in this list is to **verify** that the migration did not make any significant changes. This means running appropriate unit and performance tests and manually reviewing each migration diff line by line to make sure there were no unintended updates. Along with verifying correctness, we also need to verify that the new library is actually LibTorch ABI Stable. For this, we use [torch-abi-audit](https://pypi.org/project/torch-abi-audit/) (thanks Ralf Gommers!). This tool inspects .so files and categorizes stable and unstable PyTorch symbols. If there are no unstable symbols, the library is LibTorch ABI Stable. It also reports the minimum LibTorch version that provides all the required stable symbols (for example, `min-torch=2.11.0`). We used it to track migration progress and check for regressions, and now use it in vLLM CI to ensure the wheel remains LibTorch ABI Stable.

### Challenges Along the Way The biggest challenge was keeping pace with a large, rapidly changing project. Upstream files often changed while our migration patches were in progress, so we had to update those patches before they could merge. vLLM’s external dependencies also meant coordinating across projects and building support for the migration. #### DeepGEMM: A Migration Case Study DeepGEMM brought several of these challenges together. While our migration was in progress, DeepGEMM moved from version 1 to version 2 and added DeepJIT, another LibTorch-dependent project that also needed to be migrated. vLLM then switched from the upstream `deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM` repository to its own `vllm-project/DeepGEMM` fork, requiring us to redo the migration on the new fork. Those upstream changes were only part of the challenge. Because DeepGEMM registered its operators through pybind11, we also needed to move its registration to `TORCH_LIBRARY` before adopting the Stable ABI. For example, the original binding of `fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits` was: ```cpp m.def("fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits", &fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits, py::arg("q"), ..., py::arg("max_context_len"), ...); ``` where `q` is a `std::tuple>&` and `max_context_len` is a `const int&`. To make these arguments compatible with `TORCH_LIBRARY`, we added a wrapper that accepts the tuple elements separately and uses `int64_t` in its C++ signature: ```cpp static torch::Tensor fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits( const torch::Tensor& q, const c10::optional& q_sf, ... const int64_t& max_context_len, ...) { return attention::fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits( std::make_tuple(q, q_sf), ..., static_cast(max_context_len), ...); } ``` This can now be registered with `TORCH_LIBRARY` as: ```cpp TORCH_LIBRARY_FRAGMENT(deep_gemm, m) { m.def("fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits(Tensor q, Tensor? q_sf, ..., int max_context_len, ...) -> Tensor"); } TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(deep_gemm, CUDA, m) { m.impl("fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits", TORCH_FN(fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits)); } ``` The Python interface unpacks the tuple before calling the registered operator: ```python def fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits(q, ..., max_context_len, ...): q_fp, q_sf = q[0], q[1] return _torch_ops.fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits( q_fp, q_sf, ..., max_context_len, ...) ``` This lets the registration use `TORCH_LIBRARY` without changing the user-facing API. After DeepGEMM was migrated to TORCH_LIBRARY, the Stable ABI migration followed a similar process as the other migrations. We replaced its unstable APIs and updated the operator registrations: ```cpp STABLE_TORCH_LIBRARY_FRAGMENT(deep_gemm, m) { m.def("fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits(Tensor q, Tensor? q_sf, ..., int max_context_len, ...) -> Tensor"); } STABLE_TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(deep_gemm, CUDA, m) { m.impl("fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits", TORCH_BOX(fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits)); } ``` Because DeepGEMM was vLLM’s final build dependency to be migrated, completing this work made the entire vLLM wheel LibTorch ABI Stable! ### Example Run on Newer PyTorch ```python # stable_abi_demo.py import os os.environ.setdefault("VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER", "0") import torch import vllm from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams print(f"PyTorch runtime: {torch.__version__}") print(f"vLLM: {vllm.__version__}") llm = LLM( model="HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct", max_model_len=128, gpu_memory_utilization=0.1, enforce_eager=True, ) outputs = llm.generate( ["The capital of France is"], SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=8), ) print(outputs[0].outputs[0].text) ``` Build vLLM and run the demo with PyTorch 2.14.1: ```text > python stable_abi_demo.py PyTorch runtime: 2.14.1+cu132 vLLM: 0.1.dev24716+gcb95d994f.d20261105 Paris. Paris is a city known for ``` Update the PyTorch wheel to `torch==2.15.0`: ```shell uv pip install torch==2.15.0 \ --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu132 ``` Rerun demo without rebuilding vLLM: ```text > python stable_abi_demo.py PyTorch runtime: 2.15.0+cu132 vLLM: 0.1.dev24716+gcb95d994f.d20261105 Paris. Paris is a city known for ``` _Note: Routine vLLM initialization logs, progress bars, and unrelated deprecation warnings have been omitted from the outputs above for clarity._ ### Future Work Now that vLLM’s CUDA build uses the LibTorch Stable ABI, our next steps are to make all of vLLM’s builds ABI stable, including the CPU and ROCm builds. These migrations are smaller than the CUDA migration but remain important to the vLLM ecosystem. The ROCm build shares many source files with the CUDA build: hipify converts `.cu` files to `.hip` files, so these files already use the LibTorch Stable ABI. Only a few ROCm-specific files remain to be migrated. We are also expanding the stable API surface so that vLLM and its dependencies no longer need wrappers. Following our [August v0.2.0 release](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-20-verl-omni-v0-2-0), [VeRL-Omni](https://github.com/verl-project/verl-omni) **v0.3.0** widens what you can train with reinforcement learning in a single, unified stack. This release brings asynchronous execution to more multimodal RL workloads, makes the V1 trainer the default for everyone, and expands post-training coverage across image, video, audio, and multimodal understanding. Building on v0.2.0's rollout batching and reusable model adapters, the focus this time is on making the whole pipeline work *together*: generation, reward evaluation, policy updates, and weight synchronization. Two end-to-end recipes show what that means in practice: **MiniMax H3 audio-video post-training with DiffusionNFT**, and **MiniCPM-o 4.5 GSPO with colocated-sync or separate-async execution**. Together they demonstrate an important design principle: the right execution mode depends on your workload. Overlapping rollout and training helps only when that overlap pays for the resources assigned to each role — and now you have the tools to measure exactly that. **Release:** [v0.3.0 release notes](https://github.com/verl-project/verl-omni/releases/tag/v0.3.0) · **Code:** [verl-omni](https://github.com/verl-project/verl-omni) · **Previous release:** [v0.2.0 blog](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-20-verl-omni-v0-2-0) ## 1. Async and Decoupled RL Execution Multimodal RL has several expensive stages, each with different resource needs. An autoregressive model can spend a long time generating responses; a diffusion model runs repeated denoising steps; audio-video rewards add decoding and scorer inference on top. A strictly alternating loop leaves one role idle while another works. v0.3.0 breaks that bottleneck open with a richer set of execution paths: - **Fully asynchronous rollout** now extends Qwen3-Omni training to text and audio-input workloads, using the supported FSDP recipes identified in the release notes. - **Separate-async Omni training** places the actor and rollout engine on separate GPU pools. A replay buffer connects generation and training, while configurable synchronization intervals control how often rollout workers receive policy updates. - **Separate-async diffusion training** gains from weight synchronization and dynamic hybrid rollout switching. When the replay buffer runs low, colocated actor replicas can be lent to rollout and reclaimed for training on demand. - **Diffusion on-policy distillation (OPD)** gains asynchronous teacher scheduling and standalone teacher routing, so teacher execution can be managed independently of the actor. The point of these changes is *choice*, not a one-size-fits-all prescription. The MiniCPM-o case study below shows why GPU partitioning, generation length, and the trainer's critical path should always be measured together. ## 2. A Shared V1 Training Foundation The V1 trainer, built around **TransferQueue and ReplayBuffer**, is now the default. v0.3.0 extends V1 synchronous recipes across diffusion models while strengthening the handoff between rollout and training: grouped trajectories are written together, unnecessary data reads are reduced, and scheduling and batch ordering receive additional validation. The rollout stack moves to **vLLM 0.30.0 and vLLM-Omni 0.30.0 (`12e9280`)**. Lifecycle changes make request cancellation and policy updates more explicit: requests are aborted before pausing, sleep/wake transitions require acknowledgements, and weight-update failures propagate to callers. That matters when generation, memory reclamation, and weight synchronization repeatedly cross execution boundaries. For diffusion workloads, prompt embedding caching avoids repeated encoding, and rollout sequence parallelism and VAE parallelism expose additional scaling controls. Named media artifacts make image, video, audio, and latent outputs explicit, so rewards and exporters consume declared outputs instead of inferring modalities from tensor shapes. ## 3. Recipes and Training Results ### 3.1 MiniMax H3: Joint Audio-Video Post-Training MiniMax H3 generates video and audio jointly, and its post-training pipeline has to preserve both modalities through generation, reward evaluation, actor updates, and export. v0.3.0 adds H3 training coverage with FlowGRPO and DiffusionNFT — here we focus on the DiffusionNFT **T2VA** and **FL2VA** case study. **T2VA** generates audio-video from text. **FL2VA** is first-frame image-to-audio-video by default. Align rollout and training kernels bit for bit, and unclipped importance sampling corrects that lag. Plus zero-mismatch RL for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X. **TL;DR** - Asynchronous RL is faster, but it trains on samples generated by older weights. - The rollout-to-learner gap has two parts. Weight lag changes smoothly and unclipped importance sampling (IS) controls it. Kernel mismatch, where rollout and training compute different numbers for the same weights, fluctuates and persists despite IS. - Align the kernels, and unclipped IS corrects the remaining weight lag without sample-rejection gates. [REINFORCE Zero](https://github.com/hijkzzz/REINFORCE-Zero) (NVIDIA Research and Inferact) trains stably for **20,000 updates**, learns at **policy lag 64**, and reaches **2.40×** the training-step throughput of synchronous training with aligned kernels. - Zero mismatch now covers **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** (DAPO rollout step within 10% of the fast baseline), **Kimi K3.1** on day 0, and both DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3.1 on **AMD MI355X**. - Everything is in [Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl](https://github.com/Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl). ## 1. From synchronous to asynchronous Last month, [we showed](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-train-inference-consistency) that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): [REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling](https://github.com/hijkzzz/REINFORCE-Zero). All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. ## 2. Asynchronous RL: faster, but off-policy In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is **weight lag**. A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. ## 3. Two gaps that behave differently The logprob gap between learner and rollout splits into two terms: ``` log π_θk − log μ_v = (log π_θk − log π_θv) + (log π_θv − log μ_v) weight lag kernel mismatch ``` π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. **Weight lag changes smoothly.** It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. **Kernel mismatch fluctuates.** It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. *Figure 1: Peak-to-median ratio of the importance-weight deviation D3, log scale, for two asynchronous runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: REINFORCE Zero with aligned kernels and IS with standard kernels. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2.* The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. Each token's term is 0 when w = 1 and grows as w moves away from 1. With aligned kernels, D3 peaks at 1.50× its median: unclipped IS keeps the remaining weight-lag mismatch smooth and controlled. With standard kernels, it peaks at 442.54×: large importance-weight fluctuations persist despite IS. **So remove the kernel term first.** Then what remains is weight lag, and plain unclipped IS corrects it, with no truncation and no rejection gates. ## 4. REINFORCE Zero REINFORCE Zero is the recipe that follows from section 3. It has three parts. ### The recipe 1. **Align the kernels.** The rollout and the learner compute the same logprob for the same weights and tokens, as in our last post. The kernel term is exactly 0, so whatever gap remains is weight lag. 2. **Correct weight lag with token-level IS, unclipped.** The rollout already records the logprob of every token it samples. The learner divides its own probability by that recorded one and uses the ratio as is: no truncation, no filtering. 3. **Optimize plain REINFORCE.** Each response's advantage is its reward minus the mean reward of its group. Tokens are averaged within a response. No value model, no rejection gates. For a batch of B responses, with A_i the advantage of response i: ``` L(θ) = − (1/B) Σ_i (1/T_i) Σ_t A_i · π_θ(a_it | h_it) / μ_i(a_it | h_it) ``` That is the whole algorithm. ### Why unclipped IS At a fixed history, weighting each sampled token by the exact ratio w = π / μ makes the expected update equal the update under the current policy. Clipping the weights generally introduces bias. A correct mean gradient is not enough for stable training. In a Gaussian model, the paper derives the exact update error and shows that mismatch amplifies update variance and narrows the stable step-size range, even under unbiased IS: the same step size learns with no mismatch and loses reward with it. The experiments point to kernel mismatch as the source of large excursions (Figure 1), so removing it is what lets unclipped IS stay stable. ### What happens without alignment The paper runs the same asynchronous IS with standard kernels: - The median rollout-to-learner KL rises **83.33×** between the first and last 1,000 updates, and online AIME24 pass@1 falls from 34.27% to 13.96%. With aligned kernels it stays flat. - The largest gradient norm before clipping reaches **38.27**, against **0.0555** with aligned kernels. - Adding a sequence gate stabilizes training, but by the last 1,000 updates it rejects **24.48%** of sequences. REINFORCE Zero rejects none. ### Learning at lag 64 The paper pushes the lag to 64. With Qwen3-4B, Python tools and a 16K context, REINFORCE Zero trains at policy lag 64: a sample can come from weights up to 64 versions older than the learner's. It keeps learning through 5,000 updates: mean reward rises from 0.287 in the first 100 updates to about 0.78, and AIME24/25/26 pass@1 improves over the same run. ![REINFORCE Zero at lag 64: training reward and AIME pass@1](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-06-zero-mismatch-async-rl/lag64.png) *Figure 2 (REINFORCE Zero, Figure 6): Learning at lag 64 with Qwen3-4B and Python tools, through 5,000 updates. Left: training reward, 100-update means. Right: equal-weight AIME24/25/26 pass@1 at 200-update checkpoints (points) and a smoothed trend (curve).* ### Results | Setting | Result | |---|---| | Throughput, 16 GPUs, 12K updates | **2.40×** the training-step throughput of synchronous training with aligned kernels (68.55 vs 164.77 hours), comparable quality | | 20K-update reasoning, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B | Stable at lag 2 and 8; rollout-to-learner KL stays flat | | High lag, Qwen3-4B + Python tools | Learns at **lag 64** through 5,000 updates; mean reward 0.287 → about 0.78 | | MoE with tools, Qwen3-30B-A3B | Macro pass@1 31.29% → 71.55% in 3,000 updates | | Computer use, Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B on OSWorld | Pass@1 50.97% → 56.16% after 428 updates | On the 1.5B reasoning task at 6,000 updates, the variants line up as the analysis predicts: | Recipe | Aligned kernels | Async | Macro pass@1 | |---|:---:|:---:|---:| | Base model | — | — | 40.29% | | Synchronous | ✓ | | 48.91% | | IS | | ✓ | 45.32% | | IS + sequence gate | | ✓ | 46.79% | | IS + token gate | | ✓ | 44.59% | | Score Centering, no IS | ✓ | ✓ | 47.50% | | **REINFORCE Zero, lag 2** | ✓ | ✓ | **48.80%** | | **REINFORCE Zero, lag 8** | ✓ | ✓ | **48.53%** | Asynchronous REINFORCE Zero matches synchronous training. The paper's models were aligned with the agent skill from our last post; the training code is in [NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt). ## 5. Flagship models: DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1 REINFORCE Zero starts from aligned kernels, and every new model brings new operators to align. Since the last post, two flagship releases reached zero mismatch: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Kimi K3.1 on its release day. The runs below validate alignment on these models; long asynchronous runs on them are next. Throughout, diff 0 means the rollout and the trainer compute the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit. ### DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, at release precision The consistent path keeps release precision end to end: FP8 and MXFP4 weights, MegaMoE, sparse attention with sliding window, and DSpark speculative decoding, with CUDA graphs. The Megatron-LM trainer (mLite, by Yan Bai of NVIDIA DevTech) calls the rollout's own kernels in the same order. The key operator is the sliding window under prefix caching: agentic RL needs the prefix cache on, and a cache hit must give the same logprobs as a miss. On 16 nodes × 4 GB200, SWE-bench Pro agentic RL at 128K context stayed at diff 0 at every step. For DAPO math rollout, with 128 trajectories per node and responses up to 8K tokens, the consistent rollout step stays within **10%** of the fast baseline. ### Kimi K3.1, on day 0 Kimi K3.1 launched with [day-0 vLLM support](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-04-kimi-k31-pro), zero-mismatch RL included. The hard part was KDA linear attention: prefill computes it chunk by chunk and decode token by token, and the two round differently. Decode now repeats prefill's arithmetic for the same chunk row, so prefill, decode and the trainer agree, for the base model and for a LoRA adapter on every module. On 4 nodes × 4 GB300, 100 DAPO steps with LoRA stayed at diff 0 and AIME 24/25/26 mean@8 rose from 0.451 to 0.664. Performance optimization is ongoing. ## 6. Beyond NVIDIA: AMD MI355X Zero mismatch is a property of the kernels, not of one vendor. On MI355X, as on NVIDIA, the trainer's forward calls vLLM's own modules and kernels, and `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` switches between the consistent and the fast version. **DeepSeek-V4-Flash** held diff 0 for 36 GRPO steps on 4 nodes × 8 MI355X, including across a resume. Batch-invariant mode alone changed nothing at first: bisection found ten sources of batch variance. Half were libraries choosing kernels by shape (hipBLASLt, AITER/CK, Triton, TileLang); the rest included the indexer's top-k, decode using a different kernel from prefill, and an expert-parallel combine that summed ranks in arrival order. Bit-preserving optimizations then cut the serving-throughput loss from 62–66% to 7.4–10.1%. Recipe and image: [verl#8505](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/pull/8505). **Kimi K3.1** runs the GB300 setup (LoRA r32 on every layer including experts, frozen MXFP4 base) on 2 nodes × 8 MI355X, at diff 0 every step, checked token by token. It needed two fixes: route the trainer's bmm and indexer linear away from hipBLASLt, which picks a different tile at 4,096 rows than at 4,097; and deduplicate KDA state-slot writes after wake-up, where an eviction and a reuse could write the same slot in one step. A bit-preserving MoE path cut the RL step from about 2,300 s to 1,350 s; the cost against the fast baseline is still being measured. Recipe and patches: draft [verl#8574](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/pull/8574). ## 7. Open source REINFORCE Zero: the paper and code are at [hijkzzz/REINFORCE-Zero](https://github.com/hijkzzz/REINFORCE-Zero), and the training code is in [NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/labs-molt). Zero mismatch: [Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl](https://github.com/Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl) holds the agent skill and, for every model in this post, its recipe, what broke, how it was fixed, and the code. **Next**: long asynchronous runs on these large models, and performance optimization on Kimi K3.1. ## Acknowledgments Thanks to (alphabetical by organization): - Verda, for the sandboxes behind the SWE-bench Pro agentic RL runs - The [verl](https://github.com/verl-project/verl) team --- # Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference Published: 2026-11-04 Authors: the Kinference Team Tags: kinference, inference-control-plane, inference, scalable-platforms Summary: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. We’re excited to announce [Kinference \[kay-inference\]](https://kinference.ai/), a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. ![Kinference by Buoyant](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference/by-buoyant-black.svg) We created Kinference at [Buoyant](https://buoyant.io/) after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. ![Kinference Architecture](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference/image2.webp) Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. ## **Inference load balancing and performance** In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our [public Kinference benchmarks](https://buoyant.io/blog/distributed-inference-benchmarks-kinference-vs-plain-kubernetes), we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), **Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45%** of requests on one workload type. ![Time to First Token at light load](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference/image3.webp) By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our *unloaded latency* benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our *capacity* benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. ![Goodput by concurrency](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference/image4.webp) In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served **7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn**. It was able to attain our chosen SLO at concurrency 32 (the highest measured) on our shared-prefix workload, and concurrency 8 on the multiturn workload, whereas the kube-proxy approach was not able to attain the SLO at any concurrency level. Read more details on our benchmarking setup, process, and findings [here](https://buoyant.io/blog/distributed-inference-benchmarks-kinference-vs-plain-kubernetes). ## **A policy-driven approach** Central to Kinference is the idea of *inference policies*. Inference policies allow platform owners to balance tradeoffs across usage, performance, and priorities. We observed our customers tackle questions like: * How do we allow users to request not just specific model checkpoints (“Qwen 3.8 with 27B params and the FP8 quantization, please”) but broader classes of models, such as “any Qwen 3.8 model” or “whatever is good for coding”? * How do we redirect “easy” inference requests to cheaper models, even if the user requested an expensive model? And how do we do that without sending the whole prompt history to a cold GPU and incurring a huge latency hit? Rather than build a set of one-off features, we built a policy layer in Kinference that can express them all—and many others as well. For example, here’s how you can define a YAML policy for Kinference to semantically classify prompts by complexity level, and route simpler prompts to cheaper models—unless, taking cache usage into account, it will be faster to send it to an expensive model. ```yaml apiVersion: kinference.buoyant.io/v1alpha1 kind: InferencePolicy metadata: name: smart-semantic-routing namespace: inference spec: rules: - name: low-complexity-consider-qwen matches: - model: glm-5.3 tag: complexity-low route: consider: - models: { names: [ qwen-3.6-27b, glm-5.3 ] } select: [ { minimize: PredictedTTFT } ] ``` Here’s another example of using Kinference to burst the excess requests to cloud provider endpoints (like OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks etc) when queue depth or cache pressure indicate GPUs are saturated. ```yaml apiVersion: kinference.buoyant.io/v1alpha1 kind: InferencePolicy metadata: name: burst-policy namespace: inference spec: rules: - name: burst-to-cloud route: exclude: - name: drop-overloaded-workers drop: backend: { type: Local } queuedPrompts: { greaterThan: 2 } select: - { type: Local, minimize: PredictedTTFT } - { type: Provider, order: [bedrock, databricks] } ``` Finally, here's an example of a policy that semantically classifies prompts according to whether they contain PII, and bursts requests to the third-party provider if the GPU pool is saturated. ```yaml apiVersion: kinference.buoyant.io/v1alpha1 kind: InferencePolicy metadata: name: pii-stays-local namespace: inference spec: rules: - name: serve route: exclude: - name: pii-never-leaves-cluster if: { tag: pii-detected } drop: { backend: { type: Provider } } select: - { type: Provider, order: [ databricks ] } - { type: Local, minimize: PredictedTTFT } onEmpty: Reject # fail closed ``` With inference policies, platform owners can create explicit rules for how inference requests should be routed (or rejected) based on tenant, model requested, state of the underlying GPU pool, semantic classification of the prompts, and many other factors. These policies can go through human or agentic review; they can be committed to git; they can be linted and vetted; and they can be applied or rolled back independently. We think this policy engine is critical for providing a true inference platform. See our [Kinference policy docs](http://kinference.ai/docs/) for more. ## **Inference metrics and SLOs** Finally, there is a comprehensive suite of inference-related metrics for platform owners to monitor, alert on, and build SLOs around. Kinference reports about what’s happening on the system, including not just its own health but: * Tokens rates in and out, and histograms of input and output token sizes * TTFT, ITL, and E2E latency histograms * Uncached vs cached prompt tokens, for cost estimation * Model usage, GPU saturation, etc ![Kinference per-tenant metrics dashboard](/blog-assets/figures/2026-11-04-introducing-kinference/image5.webp) Almost every metric is also available per tenant, so you can track tenant usage, build specific SLOs around performance for specific tenants, and everything else you might need to ensure the platform you’re building is living up to its requirements. ## **Try it today** Getting started is easy: ### 01 Install the Gateway API CRDs **Note:** This guide installs Kinference into the `default` namespace. To install into a different namespace, override the namespaces in the following helm commands. The first step is to install the [Gateway API](https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/docs/introduction/) CRDs, which provide standard mechanisms for handling traffic. ```bash GWAPI_VERSION=1.5.1 kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v$GWAPI_VERSION/standard-install.yaml ``` ### 02 Install the Kinference gateway Kinference has two basic components: a traffic gateway and an inference handler. Each is released independently and ships its CRDs as a separate chart, installed before the component itself. Install the gateway CRDs and components: ```bash helm upgrade -i gateway-crds \ oci://ghcr.io/buoyantio/charts/gateway-crds \ --devel helm upgrade -i gateway \ oci://ghcr.io/buoyantio/charts/gateway \ --devel --wait ``` ### 03 Install Kinference Now, install Kinference and the Kinference CRDs: ```bash helm upgrade -i kinference-crds \ oci://cr.kinference.ai/kinference-ai/charts/kinference-crds \ --devel helm upgrade -i kinference \ oci://cr.kinference.ai/kinference-ai/charts/kinference \ --set extension.enabled=true \ --devel --wait ``` ### 04 Make sure it’s working ```bash kubectl get pods ``` Verify the processes are running: ``` NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE gateway-cp-566cddc46d-jsqlq 1/1 Running 0 8s kinference-7bb854cfc5-pp4t7 1/1 Running 0 8s ``` Please always refer to the latest documentation at [http\://kinference.ai/docs/](http://kinference.ai/docs/) as these steps will evolve over time. Kinference is fully open source under Apache v2. It’s available on [GitHub](https://github.com/Kinference-AI/kinference) today. Feedback, issues and benchmark reports from other deployments are very welcome. --- # vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-04-kimi-k31-pro Published: 2026-11-04 Authors: Inferact and the vLLM Team Tags: models, day-0-support, sparse-attention, performance Summary: vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode. Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. ## TL;DR - **Sparse attention on a hybrid model:** K3.1 Pro keeps K3's KDA + MLA hybrid and adds a DSA indexer to all 24 MLA layers. At long context, a decode step reads about a quarter of the bytes per layer that dense MLA reads. - **One KV cache for three kinds of state:** vLLM packs each block's MLA latent, indexer keys and KDA state together. The packed cache runs with FlashInfer and FlashMLA sparse kernels with FP8 or NVFP4 KV and optional MXFP4 index keys, and P/D disaggregation transfers it unchanged. - **Token-sharded prefill attention:** up to 1.69× faster time to first token (TTFT) than head-sharded prefill at 340K tokens on 8× GB300. - **Decode context parallelism (DCP) with a sparse indexer:** an exact top-k merge with **~10× less traffic** makes the attention module **1.3–1.5× faster** at DCP8. DCP prefill attention runs 4.1–4.3× faster per layer, and DCP8 holds 7.2× the KV tokens of TP8. - **Fused low-latency decode:** the specialized CuTe DSL decode path from Kimi K3 now covers DSA layers, making decode 1.2–1.6× faster on 8× GB300, and 1.9× faster under DCP8. - **Agentic serving:** on NVIDIA GB300, up to 375.9 tok/s per user at the latency-sensitive end and 37.8K total tok/s per GPU at the throughput end; on NVIDIA Rubin, up to 815.6 tok/s per user and 68.7K total tok/s per GPU on the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark. - **Zero-mismatch RL on day 0:** for the first time, day-0 support comes with zero-mismatch RL: vLLM and Megatron produce bit-identical log-probs for both the base model and the LoRA adapter, so the PPO KL is exactly 0 at every step of a 100-step full-model run. ## Quick start On NVIDIA GPUs: ```bash # See the Kimi K3.1 recipe for the Docker image and multi-node commands. vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --load-format fastsafetensors \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser kimi_k3 \ --reasoning-parser kimi_k3 \ --speculative-config '{"model":"Inferact/Kimi-K3.1-Pro-DSpark-preview","num_speculative_tokens":5,"method":"dspark","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' ``` On AMD GPUs: ```bash VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1 \ vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro \ --served-model-name kimi-k31-pro \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --load-format fastsafetensors \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --speculative-config '{"model":"Inferact/Kimi-K3.1-Pro-DSpark-preview","num_speculative_tokens":5,"method":"dspark","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' ``` ## What's new in Kimi K3.1 Pro | | Kimi K3 | Kimi K3.1 Pro | |---|---|---| | Layers | 93: 69 KDA + 24 full attention | 93: 69 KDA + 24 full attention | | Full-attention layers | dense MLA | MLA + DSA indexer (top-2048), NoPE | | Indexer | none | 32 heads × 128 dims, FP8 keys | | MoE | 896 experts, 16 active, MXFP4 | unchanged | | Context window | 1M | 1M | | Total parameters | 2.8T | 2.8T | ### Sparse Attention in K3.1 Pro Each sparse attention layer has a small *indexer* next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our [DeepSeek-V3.2 post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-29-deepseek-v3-2) covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. *Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it.* ### KV cache footprint The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. | KV cache per token, per GPU (24 full-attention layers) | Bytes | |---|---| | Kimi K3, FP8 MLA latent | 13,824 | | Kimi K3.1 Pro, FP8 latent + FP8 index keys | 16,992 | | Kimi K3.1 Pro, NVFP4 latent + MXFP4 index keys | 10,080 | The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. *Figure 2: Measured KV cache capacity on 8× GB300. Change the latent and index-key formats, the parallelism, or the context length to see how many full contexts fit.* ## A KV cache for three kinds of state Each DSA layer stores two per-token caches of different widths: the MLA latent (576 bytes in FP8, 352 in NVFP4) and the index keys (132 bytes in FP8, 68 in MXFP4). Neither width is a multiple of the other. The 69 KDA layers each add a recurrent state per request that is much larger than one layer's page of tokens. A cache that gives every layer pages of the same size would have to pad the small pages up to the largest one. vLLM packs the cache by block instead of by layer. One block of the cache is a single contiguous row that holds that block's MLA pages and index-key pages for all 24 DSA layers, together with the KDA states that share the block. Pages inside a row can have different sizes; the only constraint is that the row holds the KDA states. The block size is a power of two, so blocks of prefill and decode instances that run at different TP sizes divide evenly and can be paired for KV transfer. The attention kernels still see the small fixed-size pages they expect. vLLM translates block tables and cache slots into kernel-page addresses before each step, so FlashInfer's and FlashMLA's sparse MLA kernels and DeepGEMM's indexer kernels read the packed cache without changes. This layout makes the rest of the stack work: - **Any sparse MLA kernel and KV format.** On Blackwell the default is FlashInfer's sparse MLA with an FP8 latent. FlashInfer's new PrimsTS kernels also serve an NVFP4 latent. - **Disaggregated serving.** Each block is one contiguous range of memory, so a P/D transfer moves it with one large RDMA read instead of dozens of small per-layer reads. - **Shared infrastructure.** The same packed planner serves GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4, whose caches have the same problem of mixed page sizes (see the [DeepSeek V4 post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-04-24-deepseek-v4)). *Figure 3: How the packed cache is laid out at TP8. The attention group and the three KDA groups share one pool of block rows; pick a token, a DSA layer and a KDA layer to see which block and page each one lands in.* ## Prefill: shard the attention by token, not by head Under TP8, each GPU owns 12 of K3.1 Pro's 96 attention heads. That is a poor fit for sparse MLA prefill, for the same reasons described in our [GLM-5.3 post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse): - MLA's latent KV is shared by all heads, so every GPU reads the full cache to serve only 12 heads, and the sparse kernels pad those 12 heads to their minimum tile. - The indexer is not split by head at all: every GPU scores every token, so its quadratic cost is repeated eight times. For large prefill steps, vLLM shards the attention by token instead. An all-to-all moves each GPU's query from "all tokens, 12 heads" to "1/8 of the tokens, all 96 heads". Each GPU runs the indexer and sparse MLA for its own tokens, and a second all-to-all returns the output to the head layout. The KV cache is already replicated under TP, so nothing else changes. MoE, sequence parallelism and the cache layout stay as they are. To balance causal attention, each request is cut into 16 pieces and GPU *r* takes pieces *r* and 15 − *r*, the same balanced split as prefill context parallelism. Both all-to-alls write directly into peers' symmetric memory. *Figure 4: Token-sharded prefill, before and after, on four GPUs. Split by head, every GPU repeats the indexer and pads its head tile; after an all-to-all, each GPU scores only a balanced slice of the tokens with every head. Step through it.* The result on 8× GB300 with TP8, real weights and one request at a time: | Prompt tokens | TTFT, head-sharded | TTFT, token-sharded | Speedup | |---|---|---|---| | 27K | 0.82 s | 0.71 s | 1.16× | | 108K | 3.72 s | 2.89 s | 1.29× | | 340K | 15.89 s | 9.42 s | 1.69× | Short appends on a long cached prefix, common in agentic turns, benefit too. For a 2K-token append on a 150K-token cached prefix, the indexer and sparse MLA kernels take about 15 ms per GPU instead of 56 ms (8× GB300, FlashInfer sparse MLA). The cost is the exchange buffers, about 0.8 GiB of KV cache per GPU. ## Long context: decode context parallelism with a sparse indexer TP replicates the MLA latent on every GPU, so adding GPUs does not add KV capacity. [Decode context parallelism](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-07-decode-context-parallelism) (DCP) shards the cache by token instead: GPU *r* of *W* stores every *W*-th token. For dense MLA, each GPU attends over its shard and the partial outputs are combined by their log-sum-exp (LSE). DSA adds one step: each GPU can rank only its own 1/*W* of the tokens, so the global top-2048 has to be merged across GPUs in every layer before attention starts. ### An exact top-k merge with 10× less traffic The generic merge sends every GPU's full local top-2048, as FP32 score and token id pairs, to every other GPU. At DCP8 on 8× GB300, with 64 AgentX-like requests of 5 query tokens each, it takes 258 µs of a 671 µs attention module. vLLM sends far less. Each GPU picks only its best 1.5 × 2048 / *W* candidates straight from the BF16 scores and packs each with its score into 32 bits, about 10× fewer bytes. Every GPU then radix-selects the same global top-2048 from the gathered candidates. The merge stays exact: if a GPU holds more of the top-2048 than it sent, the select detects it and that GPU resends its full local top-k for that row. *Figure 5: One DSA attention module at DCP8 on 8× GB300 with 5 query tokens per request. The exact one-round merge is 1.27–1.51× faster than the generic merge. Hover a bar for its value.* From batch 32 up, and at 128K context, K3.1 Pro's sparse attention under DCP8 is now faster than K3's dense MLA. The partial attention outputs are then exchanged and combined by LSE with two CuTe DSL kernels on symmetric memory: up to 3.7× faster than the existing CUDA implementation (320 BF16 shapes on 8× GB300), with bit-identical output. This helps every MLA model under DCP. ### DCP prefill without a merge A plain DCP prefill would pay the merge and the LSE combine for every prompt token, and repeat the attention work on every GPU. When the DCP group is the TP group, vLLM instead gathers the step's context, both MLA latent and index keys, from all GPUs into a symmetric-memory workspace (about 0.7 GB per 1M tokens per GPU with FP8). It then runs the token-sharded prefill from the previous section over it. No merge or combine remains, and the output matches token-sharded prefill without DCP bit for bit. | One DSA layer, DCP8 on 8× GB300, AgentX mixed 16K-token step | DCP prefill | Gathered-context prefill | |---|---|---| | FP8, FlashInfer trtllm-gen | 24.8 ms | 5.8 ms (4.3×) | | FP8, FlashInfer PrimsTS | 24.8 ms | 5.7 ms (4.3×) | | NVFP4, FlashInfer PrimsTS | 25.7 ms | 6.2 ms (4.1×) | End to end, a single request prefills as fast under DCP8 as under TP8: 1.10, 4.40 and 14.61 s at 27K, 108K and 340K tokens, vs 1.10, 4.39 and 14.50 s (8× GB300, FP8 KV). ### When to use DCP DCP trades per-step latency for KV capacity: DCP8 cuts the per-GPU MLA and index-key caches by eight, and KDA state is already split by head. When the context fits, plain TP decodes faster at low concurrency; DCP pays off when KV is the limit, as with very long contexts or many long-lived agentic sessions. On 8× GB300, DCP8 holds 21.8M tokens of FP8 KV vs 3.04M for TP8 (32.1M vs 4.49M with an NVFP4 latent). At concurrency 1, TPOT is 9.35 ms with TP8 and 11.48 ms with DCP8 at 32K context (9.45 vs 11.58 ms at 128K); the fused decode path brings DCP8 to 5.96 and 6.04 ms. Eight GPUs at TP8 also serve full 1M-token requests: on 8× GB300 with FP8 KV the cache holds 3.04M tokens, 2.9 concurrent 1M-token requests. ## Low-latency decode: a fused DSA decode path For Kimi K3, vLLM ships an opt-in decode path that replaces almost every operator with CuTe DSL kernels tuned for small batches. It fuses communication into compute, reworks the MoE schedule and prefetches weights into L2 (see [Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel)). For K3.1 Pro, this path now covers the DSA layers. A DSA layer runs as: - one packed input projection for the query, KV latent, output gate and the indexer's key and head weights; - a fused indexer front: the query norm, the indexer's query projection, its FP8 or MXFP4 quantization with the head weights folded in, and the new token's index key, in one kernel; - the MLA query (the up-projection and absorbed key projection, writing the new token's latent into the KV cache), overlapped with the indexer instead of running before it; - a fused indexer: a key-balanced scorer and an exact top-k select in two kernels that emit the physical KV rows the attention reads; - sparse attention: FlashInfer sparse MLA (trtllm-gen or PrimsTS, picked per batch size) or FlashMLA sparse; under DCP at batch 1–8, a CuTe DSL kernel built for the shape (11.9 µs vs 21.4 µs per layer at batch 1); - the value projection and sigmoid gate in one kernel, followed by K3's output projection with its fused all-reduce. Under DCP, the query is published to every GPU, each GPU's top-k candidates are exchanged and merged exactly, and the partial outputs are combined by LSE, all through NVLink mailboxes inside the kernels, with no NCCL collective on the path. *Figure 6: Time per output token on 8× GB300 with TP8 and a 1K-token input. The fused decode path is 1.63× faster at batch 1 and still 1.18× at batch 64. Hover a bar for its value.* With DSpark speculative decoding (7 draft tokens), the fused path lowers time per token at concurrency 1 from 2.86 ms to 2.14 ms. GSM8K accuracy is unchanged. Under DCP8, the fused path cuts TPOT at concurrency 1 from 11.48 ms to 5.96 ms at 32K context and from 11.58 ms to 6.04 ms at 128K. ## Speculative decoding with DSpark We trained a DSpark speculator for K3.1 Pro and released a preview checkpoint: [Inferact/Kimi-K3.1-Pro-DSpark-preview](https://huggingface.co/Inferact/Kimi-K3.1-Pro-DSpark-preview). At batch size 1 with TP8 on 8× GB300, that is a 3.0× decode speedup. The speculator also keeps its accuracy across K3.1 Pro's full context window of up to 1M tokens, measured on the long-context BEAM benchmark. This checkpoint is only a preview. We are training a more accurate and more efficient speculator right now and will release it soon. ## Agentic serving: AgentX vLLM delivers strong performance on agentic serving workloads.
