Hover a point for its configuration and metrics.* ## Zero-mismatch RL on day 0 For the first time, vLLM's day-0 support ships RL with zero mismatch: LoRA RL with [verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl), vLLM as the rollout engine and Megatron as the trainer, where the trainer's log-probs equal the rollout's bit for bit. Instead of bounding the gap with importance sampling or routing replay, vLLM eliminates it at the kernel level: the trainer's forward pass reproduces the rollout bit for bit, which takes RL training stability to a new level: - **LoRA RL on the whole model.** Rank-32 LoRA covers every attention projection and all 896 experts, and both the base model and the adapter are bit-identical between vLLM and Megatron. - **Batch-invariant kernels, natively.** With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` a token's log-prob does not depend on its batch, and more and more of vLLM's high-performance kernels are batch-invariant by design, such as the DeepSelect top-k. *Figure 9: Same tokens, same kernels, same log-probs. Switch to the default rollout to compare.* Over 100 steps on the full model, the rollout/trainer KL is exactly 0.0 at every step while AIME mean@8 rises from 0.451 to 0.664 (Figure 10). *Figure 10: A 100-step LoRA RL run on the full model.* Performance optimization of the batch-invariant path is ongoing. The source code is in [Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl](https://github.com/Inferact/zero-mismatch-rl). ## AMD On AMD Instinct MI355X, vLLM combines MXFP4 indexing with sparse attention and decode context parallelism. The optimizations reduce memory requirements for long contexts and improve prefill and decode efficiency. ### Quantization: Native MXFP4 indexer The indexer scans the context before selecting 2,048 tokens for attention. MXFP4 reduces each index key from 132 bytes in FP8 to 68 bytes, including scales, cutting index-cache storage by **48.5%.** Scoring uses native FP4 matrix instructions with FP32 accumulation and weighted reduction across heads. Keys are reused across query rows during speculative verification to reduce repeated reads. The smaller index cache leaves more GPU memory available for cached context, benefiting long-context serving at high concurrency. In AgentX sweeps, the MXFP4-indexer configuration delivered **5.3%** higher total workload throughput at concurrency 48. ### Prefill: Context-parallel sparse attention During prefill, GPUs gather index keys and divide query rows among themselves. Each GPU scores its assigned rows against the full context and selects the global top-k directly, avoiding a merge of per-rank candidates. Main attention can separately gather KV when this reduces communication and fits the workspace budget, then process all query rows for local heads. The combined DCP prefill optimizations improved throughput and latency in development benchmarks. | **Input / output tokens** | **Total throughput (tokens/s)** | **Output throughput (tokens/s)** | **Median TTFT (s)** | **Median TPOT (ms)** | |---|---|---|---|---| | 8K / 1K | 5,357.8 → **6,015.4 (+12%)** | 595.3 → **668.4** | 2.462 → **1.875** | 24.571 → **22.063** | | 128K / 100 | 6,950 → **17,678 (+154%)** | 5.30 → **13.48** | 268.7 → **105.5** | 331.5 → **129.6** | *Setup: MI355X, TP8/DCP8, concurrency 16, 64 prompts, prefix caching disabled.* FlyDSL sparse MLA reads the selected tokens directly from the FP8 KV cache. Each workgroup processes one query row across its local attention heads, providing parallelism across the many query rows in a prefill step. Smaller batches retain the Triton path, which exposes additional parallelism within each row. | **Implementation** | **Benchmark duration (s)** | **Median TTFT (s)** | **Output throughput (tokens/s)** | |---|---|---|---| | Triton | 432.8 | 96.2 | 14.79 | | FlyDSL | **404.4** | **89.8** | **15.83** | | Improvement | **6.6% lower** | **6.6% lower** | **7.0% higher** | *Setup: MI355X, TP8/DCP8, concurrency 16, 64 prompts, ISL/OSL 128K/100* ### Decode: Fused Low-latency decode For small speculative verification batches, DSA indexing and sparse attention run separately, followed by a persistent monokernel that fuses attention output projection, AttnRes and the full latent MoE computation, including tensor-parallel all-reduces, into a single launch. This reduces kernel-launch overhead and overlaps MoE weight loading with preceding reduction and residual processing. The specialized path supports up to eight verification tokens per step, including a single request with seven draft tokens. | Metrics | Normal Path | Specialized decode | Improvement | |---|---|---|---| | mean TPOT | 6.02 ms | 4.40 ms | 27.0% | *Setup: TP8/DCP1, FP8 indexer, 8K/1K, c1, draft tokens 7, synthetic AL 3.84* ### Communication: Efficient cross-GPU communication During decode, each GPU exchanges candidate scores while keeping token IDs local. A shared threshold and consistent tie handling determine which local candidates are selected. For 2,048 candidates, exchanging scores alone halves the candidate payload from 16 to 8 KiB per query per GPU. AITER accelerates DCP all-gather with a dedicated GPU kernel that reads peer buffers through HIP IPC and writes directly into the required output layout. This combines data gathering and layout conversion, avoiding a separate reordering copy. In standalone microbenchmarks on eight MI355X GPUs, the AITER path reduced all-gather latency by **53–61%** versus RCCL for the tested query and candidate tensor shapes ## TPU vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0 on TPU through vllm-torchtpu, validated on a 16-chip slice of TPU v7x. The layout is TP32 with EP32 for the MoE, with DCP that shards the MLA latent and index keys by token for long contexts. DSA's work is split between the TPU's two kinds of compute units: TensorCore scores the FP8 index keys, then SparseCore selects the top 2,048 tokens and gathers their latents into a dense buffer for TensorCore's MXU to run attention. As on GPU, the DSA and KDA state share one block-indexed KV pool, which keeps prefix caching working across the hybrid cache. ## Alibaba T-HEAD The Alibaba T-HEAD team added support for running Kimi K3.1 Pro on the Alibaba T-HEAD Zhenwu PPU (both M890 and 810E) through the [vllm-sail](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-sail) plugin. We also thank Inferact, AMD, and Alibaba T-Head for delivering day-0 support for the model in vLLM, and NVIDIA for their help. --- # Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4 Published: 2026-10-29 Authors: Mistral and the vLLM Team Tags: model-support, speculative-decoding, disaggregated-serving Summary: Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell. We're excited to announce day-0 support for **Mistral Large 4** in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new `vllm/models/mistral/` package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. ## Highlights - **Architecture:** 72-layer MoE with 128 routed experts (top-4) plus 1 shared expert and a hidden size of 6144. Attention is MLA (KV LoRA rank 512, RoPE dim 64) with a DSA sparse indexer that selects the top 2048 keys per query. 1 trillion parameters in total, 49 billion active per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers). - **Checkpoints:** FP8 (block-scaled weights) and NVFP4 (NVFP4 experts, FP8 attention/shared experts). Both use an FP8 latent KV cache (`fp8_ds_mla`) by default. - **Multimodal:** a Pixtral vision encoder for image inputs, including multiple images per prompt. - **Speculative decoding:** a built-in DSpark drafter (3 sliding-window MLA layers, depth 3) accepts ~2.9 tokens per step and gives about 2x output throughput on TP8. - **Long context:** DCP gives ~7.9x more KV capacity on TP8. PCP+DCP prefill cuts time to first token (TTFT) by up to 1.6x. DSpark works under both. - **Disaggregated serving:** NIXL prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregation with DP/EP, TP and PCP×DCP prefill nodes, with DSpark on both sides. - **HiSparse:** host-memory sparse KV offload, now with support for cross-layer KV sharing. - **AMD:** day-0 on AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs with ROCm, including DSpark, image inputs and expert parallelism with MXFP4 experts. ## Usage Mistral Large 4 support ships in the `vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4` Docker image, which also includes `mistral-common` 1.13. The commands below run `vllm serve` inside it: ```bash docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 ``` **FP8 on 8 GPUs:** ```bash vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}' \ --tool-call-parser mistral --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser mistral ``` **NVFP4 on 4 GPUs** (Blackwell; use `--tensor-parallel-size 8` on 8 GPUs): ```bash vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}' \ --tool-call-parser mistral --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser mistral ``` NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. *Comparison of FP8 versus NVFP4 scores and token consumption on core evaluations. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals estimated by bootstrapping. Across all domains, including multimodal reasoning (GDP.pdf, MathVision), long-context (Graphwalks 512k), coding agents (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 4), business automation (AutomationBench) and cyber (CyberGym), the NVFP4 checkpoint matches FP8 behaviour. **Long context (DCP).** Add `--decode-context-parallel-size 8` to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. **Multimodal.** Pass `--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}'` to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the [Mistral Large 4 recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B). ## Implementation details ### Model architecture | component | Mistral Large 4 | |---|---| | layers / hidden size / heads | 72 / 6144 / 64 | | attention | MLA, no query LoRA, KV LoRA rank 512, RoPE dim 64 | | sparse attention | DSA indexer, top-k 2048, 32 index heads; 44 layers own an indexer, 28 reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer | | positional encoding | YaRN + LeRoPE (learned per-frequency scaling); every 4th layer is NoPE | | query scaling | SSMax (length-dependent query scale) on every attention layer and indexer | | KV sharing | 9 layers (39, 43, …, 71) read layer 35's latent cache (1 every 4) | | MoE | layer 0 dense; layers 1–71: 128 experts, top-4, 1 shared expert | | output | logit soft cap 30 | | vision | Pixtral encoder (30 layers, hidden 2048, patch 14) | *The 72 decoder layers: every 4th layer is NoPE, 28 layers reuse the top-k of the closest preceding indexer layer, the NoPE layers 39–71 read layer 35's latent KV, and only layer 0 is dense.* What it took to support each piece in vLLM: **Sparse MLA + DSA indexer.** ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the `fp8_ds_mla` latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. **Cross-layer KV sharing.** Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added `kv_sharing_target_layer_name` to `MLAAttention` and `AttentionLayerBase`. Consumer layers skip the cache write, and the V2 runner resolves them to the target layer's KV cache spec. Consumers take no KV memory: 63 of the 72 layers own a cache. This is model-agnostic and is being upstreamed in [vllm#64095](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64095). **NoPE, SSMax and LeRoPE.** NoPE layers are expressed as MLA with zero RoPE dims, so they use the same kernels and cache layout. LeRoPE is folded into the YaRN frequencies. SSMax is fused into the MLA RoPE kernel (see fusions below). **A Mistral model package.** Rather than adding flags to `deepseek_v2.py`, the port builds on reusable Mistral components under `vllm/models/mistral/`: attention, indexer, SSMax, MLP, MoE, fused ops and a per-layer spec (`common/layer_spec.py`). The ML4 model itself is `vllm/models/mistral_large4/nvidia/model.py`, and the DSpark drafter sits next to it (`dspark.py`). Per-layer features (RoPE/NoPE, indexer owner/sharer, KV owner/consumer) come from a layer spec built from `params.json`, not from model-specific branches in shared code. **Model runner V2.** ML4 runs only on MRV2. The V2 attention utilities discover KV-sharing layers and look up their target specs. DSpark plugs into the V2 DFlash/DSpark speculator. **Breakable CUDA graphs and fusions.** ML4 runs without `torch.compile`. It uses breakable CUDA graphs, enabled automatically for the architecture (also when the text model sits inside the multimodal wrapper). They gave about a 6x speedup over eager mode. Hand-written fusions replace what the compiler would otherwise do, while enabling further optimizations: - First round: SSMax, MLA RoPE + SSMax, the indexer Q path and the indexer K path. These cut decode TPOT by 8–10%. - Decode round: FP32 router GEMM, a one-launch Triton LayerNorm for the indexer query, all-reduce + residual + RMSNorm in one FlashInfer kernel, and indexer K written straight into the FP8 cache. On TP8 FP8, c1 TPOT dropped from 10.22 to 9.00 ms (-12%) and c8 from 16.01 to 15.08 ms. ### Long context: decode and prefill context parallelism **DCP.** MLA keeps one latent KV head, so under TP the cache is replicated on every rank. DCP shards it by token instead. On TP8, DCP8 raises KV capacity from 2.38M to 18.88M tokens (FP8) and from 3.60M to 28.76M tokens (NVFP4). ![Long-context capacity on 8x GB300: TP8 vs TP8 DCP8](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4/long_context_capacity.png) *Concurrent 128k / 256k / 1M-token requests whose KV cache fits on 8× GB300 with ML4 NVFP4, TP8 vs TP8 DCP8: floor(KV pool / input length) - 3.60M and 28.76M tokens, gpu-memory-utilization 0.85.* Out of the box, DCP with sparse MLA paid a large fixed cost per decode step. A profile at 60k context showed about 7 ms per step of DCP-only work: - NCCL all-gathers of the LSE and of the indexer top-k candidates (44 indexer layers); - reduce-scatters; - a stable top-k merge; - query gathers; - small mask kernels and launch gaps. We replaced these with: - **a2a combine** for FlashMLA sparse (merged as [vllm#61285](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61285)): a symmetric-memory all-to-all LSE combine instead of all-gather + reduce-scatter. ML4 uses it by default. - **Direct top-k exchange:** each rank pushes its packed (score, id) candidates into its peers' symmetric-memory inboxes, and a selector reads them in place. This replaces an NCCL all-gather and a 6-pass radix select per indexer layer. - **Top-k compaction:** for batches of 32+ tokens, each rank compacts its valid top-k slots and bounds the kernel with `topk_length`, instead of scanning 2048 slots full of `-1`. In a 5k-token prefill profile, attention went from 165 ms to 38 ms. - A fused kernel neutralizes empty rows (a rank that owns none of a query's top-k slots). The DCP-specific overhead fell to 3.2 ms per step. Together with the decode fusions, on TP8 DCP8 FP8 (60k input / 1k output): | | before | after | |---|---:|---:| | c1 TTFT p50 | 6.89 s | 4.73 s | | c1 TPOT p50 | 17.82 ms | 12.50 ms | | c64 output tok/s | 139.1 | 204.0 (+47%) | ![DCP8 before and after the collectives port](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4/dcp_before_after.png) *TTFT and TPOT p50 vs concurrency on TP8 DCP8 (60k input / 1k output, no spec), before (a2db3f0b9d) and after (bbe5926511) the DCP collectives port and decode fusions.* These DCP optimizations ship with Mistral Large 4 support on day 0. **When to use DCP.** DCP trades per-step latency for KV capacity. On the same 8x GB300 NVFP4 deployment and workload (no spec decoding), DCP8 decodes about 16–28% slower per token than TP8: c1 TPOT is 11.1 vs 8.7 ms at 8k input and 11.4 vs 9.1 ms at 60k. With up to 128 concurrent requests of 8k–60k tokens, TP8's 3.6M-token pool is never the bottleneck, so TP8 delivers more throughput there. DCP8 pays off once KV is the limit: very long contexts, or many concurrent long-lived sessions. In our agentic P/D runs (~100k-token sessions), a TP4 DCP4 decode node kept TTFT at 0.7 s at 32 sessions, where a plain TP4 decode node ran out of KV and climbed to 15 s. **PCP + DCP prefill.** For long prompts, PCP splits one prompt's tokens across ranks. PCP+DCP now works on ML4 with CUDA graphs, including DCP > PCP and DSpark. Two fixes made this work: - Under PCP the MLA KV-cache write first all-gathers its inputs across PCP ranks, and that gather depends on the batch's prefill/decode split. Captured in a piecewise graph, the split was frozen at capture time. Now only the gather runs as an eager break, into fixed-size buffers, and the cache write itself stays in the graph. - The DCP group's ranks are ordered to match the order collectives return data in. With graphs on TP1×PCP4×DCP4, GSM8K-200 went from 0.315 to 0.975. With DSpark it reaches 0.980. As a P/D prefill node, PCP4×DCP4 gives the lowest TTFT we measured (see the P/D section). ### DSpark speculative decoding ML4 ships a DSpark drafter inside the checkpoint (`mtp_dspark.*` tensors and an `mtp` block in `params.json`). DSpark is a parallel drafter: a small non-causal transformer proposes all draft positions of a block in one forward pass. It conditions on hidden states tapped from target layers 1, 18, 36, 54 and 71. ML4's drafter adds: - **an RNN Markov head:** a gated recurrent state (rank 512) runs across the draft positions, so each position's logits depend on the tokens drafted before it; - **position-specific mask inputs:** each draft slot gets its own learned input embedding instead of one shared mask token; - **sliding-window MLA draft layers:** 3 MLA layers with a 2048-token window and a BF16 KV cache, in their own KV cache group. The Triton MLA backend gained sliding-window decode for them. *One DSpark step: target taps feed the draft's context K/V, the [anchor, mask_1, mask_2] block runs through 3 sliding-window MLA layers in one pass, the RNN head emits 3 draft tokens in sequence, and the target verifies them.* Enable it with `--speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}'`. **Results.** TP8, 200 real prompts, greedy (temperature 0), up to 512 output tokens: | | FP8 base TPOT | FP8 DSpark TPOT (AL) | NVFP4 base TPOT | NVFP4 DSpark TPOT (AL) | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | c1 | 8.84 ms | 3.50 ms (2.90) | 8.21 ms | 2.95 ms (2.93) | | c8 | 15.28 ms | 7.08 ms (2.85) | 12.85 ms | 5.80 ms (2.86) | | c32 | 29.92 ms | 11.57 ms (2.85) | 25.38 ms | 9.80 ms (2.86) | The table uses greedy decoding. At higher temperatures, set `"draft_sample_method": "probabilistic"` in the speculative config: at T=1.5 it raises AL from 2.04 to 2.36–2.53 (+12–22% throughput). Both modes are lossless thanks to standard rejection sampling. At the same concurrency, DSpark raises output throughput 1.9–2.1x on FP8 and 1.9–2.2x on NVFP4. It doesn't change what the model generates: every drafted token is verified against the target model, and we checked this empirically. When the base model re-scores DSpark's outputs, they match its own greedy choices as often as the base model's own outputs do. The sparse MLA runs on AITER's MLA decode kernels and the DSA indexer on AITER's gfx950 indexer. **MXFP4 experts.** On ROCm the routed experts run as OCP MXFP4 on AITER's fused MoE. There are two ways to get them: - **AMD Quark MXFP4 checkpoint** ([Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-Quark-MXFP4](https://huggingface.co/amd/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-Quark-MXFP4)). Quark re-quantizes only the routed experts, with static weight and dynamic activation scales. Attention, the shared experts, the dense feed-forward layers, the router, the output head, the vision encoder and the DSpark drafter keep their original precision. The checkpoint shrinks from about 1,061 GB to 578 GB, so it serves on four MI350 Series GPUs (288 GB each). The serving commands, evaluation results and the reproduction recipe are on the model card. - **Re-quantize the FP8 checkpoint at load** (`VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT=mxfp4`). The experts are converted layer by layer while loading, so peak memory stays low enough for TP4 as well. Expert weights drop from about 125 to 69 GiB per GPU at TP8, and output throughput rises 22–71% over serving the FP8 experts at 1–64 concurrent requests. `VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT_ACT` sets the activation format the MXFP4 experts compute with: `a8w4` (FP8 activations, the default) or `a4w4` (MXFP4 activations). Either way, one 8-GPU node serves two TP4 replicas, each with about 6× the HBM left for KV cache and activations that the FP8 experts would leave on the same four GPUs. **Features.** TP8 and TP4, expert parallelism, image inputs through the Pixtral encoder, and DSpark speculative decoding with the checkpoint's built-in drafter are supported on ROCm. On MI350X at TP4 with the FP8 KV cache, DSpark accepts 3.1 tokens per step on real prompts and lowers per-token decode latency 2.7× at one request, 1.9× at 8 and 1.8× at 32 (output throughput 2.1×, 1.6× and 1.4×). On ROCm the latent KV cache is FP8 (E4M3) by default, which gives 1.86× the KV capacity of bf16; `--kv-cache-dtype bfloat16` opts out. **AITER.** `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1` runs vLLM's hot paths on AITER, AMD's kernel library: the fused MoE (the MXFP4 experts on two-stage FlyDSL kernels), the block-FP8 and bf16 GEMMs, the MLA decode kernels, RMSNorm and the tensor-parallel custom all-reduce. The ROCm image ships AITER tuning tables for this model's MoE and GEMM shapes, which AITER merges with its own at startup; at TP4 they raise output throughput 9–16% at 1–8 concurrent requests. Two more settings help on top: `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1` runs the sparse MLA on AITER's Triton kernel, and `AITER_CUSTOM_AR_MAX_SIZE=134217728` keeps the all-reduces of large prefill steps (up to 128 MiB) on AITER's custom all-reduce. Together they raise output throughput a further 2–5% at TP4 and lower time to first token 5–7%. Both commands below set all three. **Specialized decode.** For latency-bound serving, `--additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}'` runs every MoE layer of a 1-, 2- or 4-request decode step as one persistent FlyDSL kernel launch. The launch fuses attention, the indexer, the router, the MXFP4 experts and both tensor-parallel all-reduces. On MI350X at TP4 it lowers per-token decode latency 1.5× at one request and 1.1× at four compared with vLLM's standard decode on the same GPUs. It composes with DSpark: a single request's verify block runs on the fused kernels, for 2.9× lower per-token latency than the standard decode without speculation. Larger batches and prefill run the standard path. It runs on the default FP8 KV cache, requires TP4 and `VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT_ACT=a4w4`, and refuses to start otherwise, giving the reason. The kernel is adapted from ROCm ATOM's GLM-5.2 fused decode. **Serving on MI350 Series.** Both commands enable AITER and re-quantize the FP8 experts to MXFP4 at load: ```bash # TP8, one replica per node VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT=mxfp4 VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT_ACT=a8w4 \ VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1 AITER_CUSTOM_AR_MAX_SIZE=134217728 \ vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}' \ --tool-call-parser mistral --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser mistral # TP4 with the specialized decode, for few concurrent users; two replicas per node (second on GPUs 4-7) VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT=mxfp4 VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT_ACT=a4w4 \ VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1 AITER_CUSTOM_AR_MAX_SIZE=134217728 \ vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --additional-config '{"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}' --max-num-seqs 64 \ --speculative-config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}' \ --tool-call-parser mistral --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser mistral ``` ### ROCm implementation details **Sparse MLA on AITER.** On ROCm, ML4's sparse MLA runs on the `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE` backend. The indexer's top-2048 positions are converted to global cache slots, and each query token becomes its own entry in the slot stream. AITER's MLA decode kernel then reads that stream in persistent mode, with work-split metadata built ahead of time to balance the load across CUs. AITER's MLA kernels take a multiple of 16 heads: TP4 gives exactly 16 of ML4's 64 heads per GPU, while TP8's 8 are padded to 16. `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_TRITON_SPARSE_MLA=1` switches to AITER's Triton sparse-MLA kernel instead, which needs no head padding and no separate FP8 copy of the query. NoPE layers on the bf16 cache have no RoPE part for AITER's kernel to read, so they run on vLLM's ragged Triton sparse-attention kernels. **DSA indexer on AITER.** A fused Triton kernel quantizes each indexer key to FP8 with one scale and writes it into the indexer cache, 132 bytes per token per indexer layer. Within a cache block, keys are stored in 16×16 tiles, the layout AITER's paged reader expects. A single layout rule is shared by the writer and every reader (insert, prefill gather and paged logits), so they cannot disagree. Prefill scores run on AITER's `fp8_mqa_logits` and decode scores on AITER's paged MQA-logits kernel, both reading FP8 keys. The top-2048 comes from AITER's indexer top-k where it supports the shape, and from vLLM's `top_k_per_row` otherwise. Shared-indexer layers reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, as on other platforms. **FP8 latent cache.** ROCm has no `fp8_ds_mla` layout, so when the checkpoint asks for an FP8 KV cache, ROCm uses a plain E4M3 cache instead. All 576 latent dimensions (512 NoPE and 64 RoPE) are stored as FP8 with one per-tensor scale, 576 bytes per token per layer, against 656 for `fp8_ds_mla` and 1,152 for bf16. The query is quantized to FP8 too, so AITER's kernel runs FP8 × FP8. With 63 cache-owning layers plus the indexer, a token takes 42,096 bytes, against 78,384 in bf16: the 1.86× KV capacity in the AMD section. **MXFP4 experts at load, one layer at a time.** With `VLLM_FP8_MOE_REQUANT=mxfp4`, the checkpoint loader is unchanged: it still loads block-FP8 expert weights with their block scales. Their parameters start on the meta device, and the layerwise loader materializes one layer at a time. As soon as a layer's experts are loaded, each expert is dequantized to bf16 and re-quantized to MXFP4 (E2M1 values, one E8M0 scale per 32 values), and that layer's FP8 copy is freed. Peak memory is the MXFP4 model plus one layer of FP8 experts, which is what lets the 1T model load on four GPUs. The weight error is about the same as quantizing the bf16 weights to MXFP4 directly. The experts then run on AITER's fused MoE: two-stage FlyDSL kernels with FP8 activations for `a8w4`, or MXFP4 × MXFP4 for `a4w4`. **Specialized decode: one persistent kernel per layer.** With `decode_backend=latency_specialized`, a pure decode step of 1, 2 or 4 requests (or a single request's DSpark verify block) runs each of the 71 MoE layers as one FlyDSL kernel launch. The launch uses 256 CTAs, all resident at once on the GPU's 256 CUs. Inside it run: - the input norm, the query and latent-KV projections with SSMax and LeRoPE; - the whole DSA indexer: projections, key-cache write, scoring and an exact top-2048; - sparse MLA over the latent cache, read in place in bf16 or FP8; - the output projection, the softmax top-4 router, and the shared and routed MXFP4 experts. The embedding, the dense layer 0 and the final norm stay on vLLM's modules. Both tensor-parallel all-reduces run inside the kernel, over peer memory between the four GPUs, so a layer is one launch with no host round-trip. The kernels are built for 1, 2 and 4 rows, which are vLLM's full CUDA-graph capture sizes, and are replayed inside those graphs. Any other step runs vLLM's layers: prefill, mixed batches, wider batches. The kernel is adapted from ROCm ATOM's GLM-5.2 fused decode, extended for ML4's layer types: - no query LoRA; - SSMax on the query and the index query; - softmax routing; - NoPE layers; - KV-sharing layers that read layer 35's latent cache; - index-sharing layers. **Fail-stop.** A persistent kernel that waits on peer GPUs must never hang the server. Every in-kernel wait gives up after 10 seconds, and giving up sets a sticky fault word on every rank, which ends the other ranks' waits at once. After every forward, a device-side assert checks the word before logits are computed. If the word is set, the step's remaining work never runs, the worker aborts and the engine stops, so no token from a failed step reaches a client. The check costs about 1 µs per launch. The path is also default-deny. If a deployment uses anything the kernels don't serve, startup fails with one error listing every reason, and all TP ranks agree on each check before anything collective runs. Unsupported features include other TP sizes, expert or context parallelism, LoRA, KV connectors, other speculative methods, and experts not stored as `a4w4`. ## TPU Mistral Large 4 runs on **TPU v7x from day 0** with `vllm-torchtpu`, including support for the Pixtral vision encoder. Our validated configuration combines intra-host tensor parallelism with cross-host data parallelism with expert parallelism across 16 TPU v7x chips. **Serving on TPU v7x:** The following command starts a single data parallel worker on one host: ```bash vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 --data-parallel-size 4 --data-parallel-size-local 1 \ --data-parallel-start-rank "$TPU_WORKER_ID" \ --data-parallel-address "$HEAD_IP" --data-parallel-rpc-port 29696 \ --enable-expert-parallel --enable-ep-weight-filter \ --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 ``` The TPU implementation relies on `vllm-torchtpu`'s sparse MLA and DSA indexer Pallas kernels, extending MLA with cross-layer KV cache sharing. We store the MLA latent KV cache in FP8 and support FP8 weight and activation quantization for dense linear projections. Routed experts use weight-only FP4 quantization (W4A16). ## HiSparse: host-memory sparse KV offload Sparse attention reads only 2048 keys per query, so most of a long request's KV doesn't need to live in GPU memory. HiSparse keeps the full latent KV in pinned host memory. It keeps a resident GPU working set plus a per-request hot buffer, and copies the selected rows from host on a miss. Enable it with the `HiSparseConnector`: ```bash --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector": "HiSparseConnector", "kv_role": "kv_both", "kv_connector_extra_config": {"host_pool_gib": 440}}' ``` **Known issue.** When the tensor-parallel group is on a single node, also set `VLLM_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_BACKEND=trtllm`. The default single-node FlashInfer all-reduce (MNNVL) can crash the engine with `CUDA error: unspecified launch failure` once HiSparse spills KV to host ([vllm#64327](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64327)). The fix is in [flashinfer#7782](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/7782). For ML4 we made HiSparse work with **cross-layer KV sharing**. The nine consumer layers bind to layer 35's resident view and host copy and keep only their own hot buffer and LRU (each has its own indexer). Nothing is duplicated, and no environment variable is needed. Compared with materializing the shared layers, this holds 14.3% more tokens for the same host pool. We also fixed: - reading `index_topk` from the text config of multimodal models; - a double host mirror during CUDA graph capture. **Capacity.** On a single GB300 node (TP4, NVFP4), the four TP ranks share one deduplicated host pool, so `host_pool_gib` is the total. With a 440 GiB pool, HiSparse admits 8.77M KV tokens at startup and holds up to 11.25M in steady state, vs 1.97M on the GPU alone (4.5x to 5.7x). GSM8K-200 is unchanged (0.975 both), and needle-in-a-haystack passes at ~98k (10/10) and ~248k (5/5) tokens. ![HiSparse KV capacity](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4/hisparse_capacity.png) *KV token capacity of one TP4 server on a single GB300 node (NVFP4, max_model_len 262k, prefix caching off): 1.97M tokens on the GPU alone; with HiSparse and a 440 GiB host pool shared by the four TP ranks, 8.77M admitted at startup (4.5x) and up to 11.25M in steady state (5.7x). Layers that reuse layer 35's KV are stored on the host only once.* ## Day 0 Support for RL with SkyRL We also enabled Day 0 RL for Mistral Large 4 in [SkyRL](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL), with vLLM for rollout and either FSDP2 or Megatron for training, on 8 GB200 nodes. On AMD side, we would also like to thank Hongxia Yang, Felix Marty, Andy Luo, Indira Vats for Day 0 enablement and optimization on AMD Instinct GPUs, and Bowen Bao, Chuan Li, Peng Sun for general support. --- # Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at Scale: vLLM Matches DeepInfer and Scales to GB300 NVL72 Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep Published: 2026-10-23 Authors: Inferact and the vLLM Team Tags: deepseek, performance, large-scale-serving, disaggregation Summary: With P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP on a GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9x our aggregated single-node result. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep/hero.png) **TL;DR:** On one NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at **954K tokens/s per GPU** at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, **7.9×** our single-node result from the [first post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-07-deepseek-v41-flash) and **$38.96 per GPU-hour** at DeepSeek's off-peak prices. A specialized decode path reaches **826 tokens/s** for a single user. Against DeepInfer, DeepSeek's own engine, vLLM's decode throughput is within **6%** across batch sizes 8–256, and its prefill tracks DeepInfer's published curve. The efficiency comes from deliberate engineering on components that vLLM already has, built on the kernels DeepSeek open-sourced. This post walks through our performance study, breaks down each optimization, and shares the lessons we learned: - **A general-purpose engine can match a model-specific one** - **Understand the model before optimizing** - **Small DEP instances work best for prefill**[^terms] - **Wide-EP decode scales well with EPLB** - **CPU overhead becomes critical at NVL72 scale** - **A specialized decode path unlocks low latency** ## Performance overview *Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72: vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP (gold) achieves a further 7.9× throughput increase over our aggregated single-node result from the [first post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-07-deepseek-v41-flash). Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ([source](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/inference/deepseek-v41-flash?i_xmode=interactivity&i_seq=agentic-traces&g_model=DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash&i_best=0&i_active=gb300_dynamo-vllm)).* ### Compared to DeepInfer [DeepInfer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer) is DeepSeek's own inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, released this week as an offline engine with published prefill and decode curves. It is the most relevant reference for this model, so before going into our optimizations we show where vLLM stands against it. **Decode.** Under DeepSeek's decode configuration (131K context, nextn=3), vLLM on GB200 achieves throughput within 6% of DeepInfer's published results across batch sizes 8 to 256 (Figure 2). *Figure 2: Decode output throughput per GPU vs. batch size at 131K context, nextn=3. vLLM on GB200 vs. DeepInfer's published results, read from the charts in its README ([source](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer)).* **Prefill.** DeepInfer's published prefill curve uses EP4DP4 with 32 redundant experts and a 140-token bounded replay, on hardware the chart does not state, and we read its values off the chart. Our run uses DEP2 on GB300 with no redundant experts, a 128-token replay and our own prompts. Because the setups differ, we do not read the gap between the two curves as an engine-to-engine speedup. What Figure 3 shows is that vLLM's DEP2 prefill tracks DeepSeek's own engine across the range they published. *Figure 3: Prefill throughput vs. new tokens. vLLM DEP2 on GB300 vs. DeepInfer's published curve (EP4DP4, 32 redundant experts, 140-token replay, hardware not stated), read from the chart in its README ([source](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer)).* The two engines land close because they share a lineage in both directions. DeepInfer was originally built on vLLM, and vLLM in turn has continuously integrated kernels from DeepSeek's libraries, including MegaAttn, MegaMoE and Mega-mHC, and has extensively optimized the rest of the stack around them. DeepInfer targets a single model in offline mode; the same vLLM build also serves this model online with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP across a full NVL72 rack, which is what the rest of this post measures. The sections that follow describe that work. ## Under the hood: where the speed comes from ### Measure the model first Before tuning, we started by quantifying DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's efficient architectural designs: - **Small KV cache footprint.** Only 890 bytes per token for global KV cache, thanks to cross-layer KV sharing and FP4 compression (see the [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19969)). - **Lightweight attention.** Layers 2, 8 and 14 use 2× compression for full-context indexing. With bounded replay, layer 20 writes global KV for all tokens but runs indexing and attention only on the last 128; layers 21–39 process only those tokens. - **Decode is MoE-bound even in a long context.** See Figure 5 below. With DEP4 decoding at 128K context and 64 requests per rank, MoE takes 62% of the target step, while attention and the indexer together take only 13%. [^terms]: DEP*n* is data-parallel attention plus expert parallelism over *n* GPUs. Target forward is the main model's full forward pass at each decode step, which verifies the draft tokens and produces the output; draft forward is the DSpark draft model's full forward pass, which proposes the tokens for the next step. The table below shows the target model's forward time at DEP32, with 16 requests per rank, 6 tokens per request (one token plus five DSpark draft tokens), and every request at the same context length, on GB300. Going from 128K to 855K, 6.7× the context only adds 0.6 ms (+7%) to the target model decode latency. | Context per request | 64K | 128K | 256K | 512K | 855K | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Target forward (ms) | 8.86 | 8.93 | 9.03 | 9.25 | 9.53 | | vs. 128K | −0.8% | – | +1.1% | +3.6% | +6.7% | These characteristics shape the rest of our optimization strategy: - **Prefill should run at a small DEP size.** Even a DEP2 instance on B300 or GB300 can hold both the model weights and the KV cache for many concurrent sessions. A smaller world size greatly simplifies DP/EP load balancing. - **KV capacity rarely limits batch size.** The KV cache fits comfortably in HBM, allowing us to push each operation toward its compute or memory bandwidth limits instead of working around KV capacity. This also keeps our sweep consistent and low-noise with no preemption or KV cache pressure. - **Wide-EP is effective for decode.** MegaMoE decode is bound by weight reads, and Wide-EP directly cuts this dominating MoE cost. - **Decode DP load balancing is simpler.** This model's decode step time varies little with context length, so DP load balancing can be simplified to least-load by request count per rank. - **Synthetic workloads remain representative for decode.** Using average input and output lengths gives us a good estimate of the performance without replaying the full agentic trace. #### How we measured Measuring performance accurately without overcomplicating the methodology is not trivial. We break it into two questions: what should a prefill or decode step cost, and how much additional overhead comes from DP and EP imbalance? - **Prefill and decode step time.** `vllm bench forward` ([#61339](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61339)) measures the model-forward time for an exact prefill or decode batch through the actual `execute_model` path across DP and EP ranks. This measures GPU time only and gives a clean trace. Further, vLLM's `DecodeBenchConnector` measures engine-level end-to-end decode performance at a given concurrency. The gap between GPU-only and serving step times reveals unexpected overhead. - **Prefill DP imbalance: mirror vs. lag replays.** Agentic traces vary from run to run, so DP imbalance is hard to isolate. We therefore replay identical requests on every DP rank. In a *mirror* run, all ranks receive their requests at the same time. In a *lag* run, rank *r* receives the same requests *r* × 5 s later, so the ranks are out of step but do the same total work. The difference between the two runs is the cost of DP imbalance. - **Decode EP imbalance: real vs. uniform routing.** For each MoE layer, we define balancedness as the mean rank load divided by the max rank load, per step and over EPLB's window. As the balanced reference, we run the same decode batch with tokens routed uniformly at random. This reference still has sampling noise: at DEP32 with 72 requests per GPU, uniform routing reaches about 0.96 balancedness for the target (top-6 routing) and 0.94 for the draft (top-3). The gap between real and uniform routing is the most that expert balancing can recover, and the EPLB run shows how much of that gap it actually recovers. ### Prefill: DEP2 works best As discussed above, a small DEP size is appealing for prefill. In an AgentX prefill-only run at concurrency 256, DEP4 gave only 83% of DEP2's per-GPU throughput (53.3K vs. 64.4K tokens/s). Mirror and lag replays with prefix caching off point to DP imbalance: when the ranks fall out of step, DEP4 loses 13.6% of its throughput.[^earlier-build] This makes DEP2 a simple default for us. | Prefill throughput per instance (tokens/s) | mirror (balanced) | lag (imbalanced) | loss | |---|---:|---:|---:| | DEP2 | 138.7K | 130.5K | 5.9% | | DEP4 | 267.6K | 231.1K | 13.6% | [^earlier-build]: Measured on an earlier build; the imbalance cost is a property of DEP size, not of the kernels. #### Optimizations hidden behind the trace Our [first post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-07-deepseek-v41-flash) covered a broad set of prefill optimizations. Cleaner traces helped us identify the remaining bottlenecks, particularly those that grow with context length. For example, on two GB300 GPUs, an 8K-token prefill takes **87.9 ms without prior context**, but **189.4 ms with 512K cached context**. We addressed three additional bottlenecks:
Extend SWA bounded replay to layer 20 (#59894): +19.9% at 32K new tokens SWA bounded replay already limits layers 21–39 to the last 128 tokens. Previously, layer 20 still performed indexer computation across all new tokens. Now it writes KV for all new tokens but runs its remaining computation only on the 128-token replay batch. This improves prefill throughput by **19.9% at 32K new tokens**, with gains increasing from 10.1% at 4K to 23.1% at 64K.
Use 2 MB pages for shared Engram host tables (#62359): another +2.8% at 32K Engram performs random reads from host tables shared across DP ranks. The previous `/dev/shm` mapping used 64 KB GPU pages, causing frequent GPU TLB misses. Moving the tables to host-NUMA cuMem allocations enables 2 MB GPU pages, improving prefill throughput by another **2.8% at 32K new tokens**.
Use DeepSelect top-k in the prefill indexer (#62240): another +15.6% at 32K The prefill indexer now uses DeepSelect to rank candidate blocks, matching the decode path. Its benefit grows with the number of keys being ranked, improving prefill throughput by another **15.6% at 32K new tokens** and 15.2% at 64K.
Together, these changes improve **new-token prefill throughput by 35.6–43.9%** across 4K–64K new tokens on top of a 128K cached prefix. At 32K, the combined gain is **42.5%**; at 64K, throughput increases from **71.2K to 102.5K tokens/s/GPU (+43.9%)**. *Figure 4: New-token prefill throughput per GPU on DEP2 after a 128K cache hit, adding layer 20 replay, Engram 2 MB pages and DeepSelect top-k one at a time.* ### Decode: scaling Wide-EP and balancing experts with EPLB On the decode side, Wide-EP with EPLB is an established practice, described in [DeepSeek's inference system overview](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/open-infra-index/blob/main/202502OpenSourceWeek/day_6_one_more_thing_deepseekV3R1_inference_system_overview.md). vLLM has supported both for a while (see our [large-scale serving post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-12-17-large-scale-serving#wide-ep)), and we found that they still work well. This section focuses on our new findings and empirical lessons. #### The scaling of Wide-EP We measured decode scaling from DEP4 to DEP32 with 64 requests per GPU at 128K context (with EPLB enabled; see the next section). Target MegaMoE time drops from 13.4 to 6.0 ms as each rank holds fewer experts, while the remaining work stays around 10 ms. As a result, per-GPU throughput gains gradually diminish. At DEP32, the draft's communication overhead also starts to offset the benefits of wider parallelism. *Figure 5: Decode step time per rank from DEP4 to DEP32 on NVIDIA GB200 with 64 requests per GPU at 128K context, and output throughput per GPU.* #### EPLB We let EPLB rearrange the experts every 3,000 steps, based on the load of the previous 1,000 steps. EPLB raises balancedness from 0.35 to 0.94 for the target and from 0.21 to 0.89 for the draft, recovering about 97% and 93% of the gap to uniform routing. *Figure 6: Decode on GB300 NVL72 with EPLB off, EPLB for the target model only, and EPLB for both the target and the DSpark draft. The tabs show per-step balance, the per-step time breakdown at DEP32, and throughput (mean of three runs; bars show the range).* Two changes make this work. [#62009](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62009) introduces an NVLink-based `symm_mem` backend that rebalances all of DEP32 in under a second without stopping decode, fuses EPLB's replica mapping and load recording into the MegaMoE kernels (saving about 0.2 ms per step), and removes host synchronization from the decode loop. [#61395](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61395) supports EPLB with heterogeneous target and draft models. The DSpark draft has 128 routed experts with top-3 routing, against the target's 384 with top-6, so EPLB tracks expert placement and load separately for each model and rebalances both. ### Overcome CPU overhead in fast large-scale decode Wide-EP decode synchronizes all ranks at every layer, so one slow rank stalls the instance. Async scheduling hides CPU overhead well at a small scale, but more ranks make this harder in two ways: GPU steps get shorter, which leaves less slack for CPU work, and it becomes more likely that one rank falls behind. In practice, we observed that an unoptimized DEP32 ran slower than DEP16 (17.57 vs. 13.84 ms per step), although its GPU execution was 1.1 ms faster. The table below lists every cause we found, ordered by effect. The effects come from different setups, so each row gives its own.

This work was led by **Inferact**. --- # GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse Published: 2026-10-23 Authors: vLLM Team Tags: glm, parallelism, kv-cache, disaggregation, performance Summary: vLLM serves GLM-5.3 on 16 H200s with PCP and DCP prefill and Hybrid HiSparse decode, reaching 1M-token contexts and 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of data-parallel P/D on the AgentX agentic benchmark. **TL;DR:** Long agentic contexts push GLM-5.3 against two limits on H200s: KV cache memory and prefill speed. We address both on 16 H200s, split into one prefill node and one decode node: * **Prefill Context Parallelism (PCP)** splits each prompt across GPUs by token instead of by head, which suits GLM-5.3's sparse attention far better than tensor parallelism. * **Decode Context Parallelism (DCP)** shards the prefill engine's KV cache by token, so a 1M context fits on the prefill node. * **Hybrid HiSparse** lets decode keep KV in host memory, so a 1M-token request fits. * On AgentX, PCP8 × DCP8 prefill with Hybrid HiSparse decode gives 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of a data-parallel deployment at the same throughput, and it is the only configuration we tested that serves 1M-token contexts. ## Serving long contexts in memory-constrained deployments Agentic workloads have long contexts that grow with every turn, which puts pressure on both GPU memory and prefill. On H200s, GLM-5.3's weights take up most of each GPU's memory, leaving little room for the KV cache of those long contexts. And because every turn adds more tool output and file contents to prefill, under load the prefill engines can become the bottleneck for the whole deployment. [Part 1](/blog/2026-09-08-glm53-part1-hybrid-sparse-offloading) showed how Hybrid HiSparse lets long contexts fit in an aggregated deployment on a single 8× H200 node. Prefill/decode disaggregation takes more than that. On the prefill node, we use PCP to speed up long prompts by parallelizing across the prompt's tokens. With MLA, however, this leaves every PCP rank holding a full copy of the KV cache, so we combine it with DCP to remove that replication. On the decode node, Hybrid HiSparse allows higher concurrency at long contexts. vLLM's new modular core ([Model Runner V2](/blog/2026-03-24-mrv2)) makes composing all of this much easier. ### Why not TP or DP? Two standard ways to run GLM-5.3 prefill on an 8× H200 node are DP8 and TP8: * **DP8** assigns each prompt to a single GPU, so its attention cannot use the other seven. This limits time to first token (TTFT) for long prompts, and the prompt's KV cache must fit in that GPU's memory. * **TP8** partitions the attention heads across GPUs. Because MLA's latent KV is shared by all 64 heads, every GPU stores the full cache and reads it to serve only 8 heads. The indexer, which scores every earlier token to select the 2,048 that sparse MLA attends to, is not partitioned at all, so its quadratic cost is repeated on every GPU. Neither scheme spreads one long prompt's attention work across the eight GPUs without also keeping its whole KV on each GPU that serves it. The next two sections address each half. PCP splits a prompt's queries across GPUs, and DCP splits its KV. ## PCP: split the tokens, not the heads In our 8× H200 prefill engine, PCP splits each prompt across the eight GPUs by token: every GPU computes the queries for one eighth of the prompt, with all 64 heads. A naive split would be unbalanced. Under causal attention a token attends to every token before it, so the GPU holding the end of the prompt would do far more work than the one holding the start. PCP instead cuts the prompt into 16 chunks and pairs them up: GPU $r$ takes chunk $r$ from the front and chunk $15 − r$ from the back, so every GPU gets the same mix of cheap and expensive tokens (Figure 3 shows this as a V-shaped pattern across the eight GPUs). This is the load-balanced sharding from [Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783). Finally, each GPU's new KV is all-gathered, so every query can still attend to the full context. ![Figure 1. One prefill on 8 GPUs under TP8 and PCP8, shaded by the GPU that owns each piece. The bars show sparse MLA's arithmetic intensity; the line marks where the H200 becomes compute-bound in BF16.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse/tp-vs-pcp-prefill.svg) Figure 1 compares the two splits. PCP fixes both problems. Each GPU indexes only its own tokens, so the indexer is no longer replicated on every GPU and each GPU does an eighth of it. And each KV row read from memory now serves all 64 heads instead of 8, raising sparse MLA from about 26 to about 191 FLOPs per byte moved,[^intensity] close to where the H200 becomes compute-bound in BF16.[^ridge] Not replicating the indexer matters most for long prefills. The indexer's cost grows quadratically with prompt length, while sparse MLA's grows only linearly, because each query attends to a fixed 2,048 tokens. Counting FLOPs for a prefill from scratch, the indexer overtakes sparse MLA under TP8 once the prompt reaches about 32K tokens; under PCP8, where no GPU replicates it, the crossover moves out to about 256K. Together, these make PCP a great fit to prefill long prompts. But PCP still has two costs. Each GPU holds all the attention weights, while the MoE experts stay split across the eight GPUs with EP8. And because the new KV is all-gathered every layer, every GPU still ends up storing the full KV cache. That replicated cache, not compute, is what limits context length, and it is what DCP addresses. ## DCP: shard the KV cache too A 1M-token GLM-5.3 request needs 53.4 GiB of FP8 KV,[^kvsize] but each GPU has room for only about 15 GiB. [Decode Context Parallelism](/blog/2026-08-07-decode-context-parallelism) (DCP) fixes this by splitting the cache itself: tokens are dealt round-robin across the eight GPUs, so each GPU stores every eighth token, and the same request needs only 6.7 GiB (=53.4/8) per GPU. Figure 2 compares this with DP8 and TP8. ![Figure 2. TP replicates MLA's latent KV, so eight GPUs buy no room. DCP divides it by eight.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse/pcp-dcp-kv-sharding.svg) > **Note:** **PCP splits queries; DCP splits KV.** The names are historical. DCP was built for decode, where each request has a single query token, so the KV cache is the only thing worth splitting. PCP was built for prefill, where the prompt’s many query tokens are the work. Our setup runs both in the prefill engine. As a result of this sharding, most of the KV that each GPU’s queries need now lives on other GPUs. In decode, DCP sends the queries to the KV: each GPU attends over its own shard, and the partial results are merged with their log-sum-exp. In this prefill engine it does the reverse: every layer, each GPU all-gathers the shards into a temporary full-context copy, attends for its own queries, and frees the copy. Only the persistent cache is divided by eight. Figure 3 puts it all together. Step through one layer of PCP8 × DCP8 to see which KV each GPU stores, which queries it computes, and what crosses the interconnect. Switch to DP8, TP8 or PCP8 to compare. Note that the two layouts do not line up: GPU $g$ stores every eighth token but computes the queries of chunks $g$ and $15 − g$, which is why every layer needs the all-gather.
That all-gather is not free: every layer, it re-sends the whole cached context, so its cost grows with context length. Figure 4 isolates it by running the same 2K-token prefill chunk on one PCP8 node with and without DCP8, at equal cached context. DCP8 adds about 6% per step up to 64K tokens of context, rising to 15% at 248K. That is the price of an 8× larger KV pool. This overhead could be reduced by overlapping each layer's all-gather with the previous layer's compute, an optimization we are currently working on. ![Figure 4. DCP8's per-step overhead for a 2K-token chunk on one 8× H200 PCP8 engine. The band spans 1K, 4K, and 8K chunks.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse/dcp-overhead.svg) Beyond roughly 250K tokens, PCP8 alone cannot hold the KV cache; there, DCP is not an overhead but what makes long prompts possible. Together, PCP8 × DCP8 gives the prefill engine both speed and room. ## The deployment We serve it as a prefill/decode (P/D) disaggregated deployment on two 8× H200 nodes. Both engines use an FP8 KV cache and MTP speculative decoding with three draft tokens (MTP3): * **Prefill:** one PCP8 × DCP8 × EP8 engine, with 512 GiB of CPU KV offload so later turns reuse their prefix. * **Decode:** eight DP ranks with EP8 and Hybrid HiSparse from [Part 1](/blog/2026-09-08-glm53-part1-hybrid-sparse-offloading) (48 GiB host pool + 16 GiB offload per rank), so decode concurrency is bounded by host memory rather than HBM. A prefix-aware [llm-d](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d) router sends each request to the prefill engine, the NIXL connector moves its KV cache to a decode rank, and the decode rank streams the tokens back. We compare PCP8 × DCP8 prefill against DP8 prefill (eight DP ranks with EP8 and 64 GiB of CPU KV offload each, the same 512 GiB in total), and Hybrid HiSparse against plain CPU KV offloading on the decode node, with the same 512 GiB of host memory either way (8 × 48 GiB of HiSparse pool + 8 × 16 GiB of offload for HiSparse). Every configuration uses the same 16 GPUs, host memory, and vLLM build. ## Results We ran the SemiAnalysis [AgentX](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx) benchmark: Claude Code traces replayed with prefix reuse, a fresh server per concurrency, one-hour runs, and MTP3 with a synthetic acceptance length fixed at 2.99, so every configuration gets the same speculative speedup. Throughput is logical tok/s per GPU (including cached): input plus output tokens, counting prefix-cached input, over all 16 GPUs. Interactivity is AgentX's P90 E2E-normalized output tokens/s per user, the x-axis of Figure 5. ![Figure 5. One point per concurrency, each on a fresh deployment, at two context limits: c8–c64 at 142K and c8–c32 at 1M. Labels give the concurrency for PCP8 × DCP8 prefill with HiSparse decode; the other configurations run the same concurrencies, right to left. Hollow points are off their own configuration's Pareto frontier.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-23-glm53-part2-pcp-dcp-hisparse/agentx-pareto.svg) Up to c32, the deployment is mostly prefill-bound, so the prefiller makes the bigger difference. With HiSparse decode in both setups, PCP8 × DCP8 prefill gives 1.7–3.2× the interactivity of DP8 at the same throughput and cuts median TTFT from 1.5–5.2 s to 0.8–0.9 s. The decoder makes little difference at this load: at c8 and c16 the two PCP8 × DCP8 configurations are within a few percent of each other, and offload-only decode is slightly ahead at c8. From c32 the deployment becomes more decode-bound, and HiSparse decode pulls ahead. At c64 it nearly doubles throughput, to 8,340 logical tok/s/GPU at 29.6 tok/s/user, while every other configuration drops to 1–2 tok/s/user. At 1M context, the deployment needs both. A DP8 prefill rank cannot hold one 1M-token request, and neither can an offload-only decode rank. ## Making it all compose Much of the challenging work in vLLM is making features like these compose. Each changes how the KV cache is laid out, scheduled, or moved, and every combination has to stay correct and fast. For P/D, the KV has to change layout between the two engines. The prefill engine shards each request's KV by token across eight GPUs. Each decode rank needs the whole KV, including the MTP layer's, in its own paged layout. The NIXL connector does this reassembly between the two nodes, and prefix reuse from CPU offload has to keep working alongside it. Every configuration here runs on [Model Runner V2](/blog/2026-03-24-mrv2). It keeps model-specific state out of the common execution path and runs speculative decoding without CPU–GPU syncs. Hybrid HiSparse is built on it. ## Try it Everything runs on vLLM v0.32.0 or later (the `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0` image). The results above were measured on vLLM main at `9e38b4111a`. The [reproduction gist](https://gist.github.com/LucasWilkinson/b39792adeea1cc2b1505fb6b7a2a2654) pins `2537629eb2`. The prefill engine's key flags: ```bash --prefill-context-parallel-size 8 \ --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \ --dcp-comm-backend ag_rs \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --attention-config '{"sparse_mla_force_mqa":true}' ``` Without `sparse_mla_force_mqa`, prefill batches whose prompts fit within the 2,048-token top-k take the dense MHA path. The flag keeps them on the sparse-MLA (MQA) kernel too, so every KV row serves all heads. ## Acknowledgements This work was done by Roberto L. We thank Maroon Ayoub (Red Hat) and Robert Shaw (Red Hat) for stress testing the deployment, reporting errors, and fixing bugs, as well as Wentao Ye (Red Hat) for other GLM-5.3 performance optimizations (see [#57406](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/57406)). ## Notes [^intensity]: Per query, sparse MLA reads 2,048 selected KV rows of 660 bytes each (656 of FP8 KV in FlashMLA's `fp8_ds_mla` format, plus a 4-byte index), about 1.35 MB. So 8 heads do 35.7 MFLOPs over 1.37 MB, about 26 FLOPs per byte, and 64 heads do 285 MFLOPs over 1.49 MB, about 191.
