For $2^{20}$ = 1,048,576 tokens, that is 54,728 MiB $\approx$ 53.4 GiB. --- # vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-minimax-m31-flash Published: 2026-10-23 Authors: Inferact and the vLLM Team Tags: minimax, day-0-support, performance, kernels, hardware Summary: Day-0 vLLM support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Blackwell, NVIDIA Rubin, and AMD MI350-series GPUs, with NVFP4 MSA kernels, NVFP4 MegaMoE, DSpark speculative decoding, AgentX results, and day-0 RL. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-23-minimax-m31-flash/hero.png) MiniMax-M3.1-Flash is the latest model in the MiniMax-M3 family, with improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic, and visual tasks. It is also built for inference efficiency, with a native NVFP4 KV cache, NVFP4-quantized MoE weights, and a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding. vLLM supports MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs with dedicated Rubin kernels, and on AMD MI350-series GPUs, with strong performance on agentic workloads. ## TL;DR - **MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA)** with an **NVFP4 KV cache** for both the indexer and the attention path, plus **NVFP4 MoE weights** and a **DSpark** drafter. - **Blackwell MSA kernels** use the new CUDA 13.4 `QMUL4` instruction to dequantize NVFP4 into FP8 inside the kernel: up to **1.7× faster** indexer QK decode and **1.3× faster** sparse attention decode. - **NVFP4 MegaMoE** with MXFP8 shared-expert fusion and early TMEM release: **20% lower kernel latency** in prefill and **7% higher prefill throughput**. - **Indexer decode context parallelism (DCP)**: up to **3.3× faster** indexer per sparse layer at 512K context on 4× GB300. - **QKV GEMM + norm + RoPE + KV-insert fusion**: **1.1–1.6× faster** prefill at 512+ tokens and about **19% lower P50 TTFT** at TP4. - **FlashInfer PrimiTS** backend for the DSpark drafter attention: **1.3–2× faster** than FlashAttention 4, **5% lower** total forward time. - **Rubin (SM107) MSA kernels** are also integrated into vLLM with state-of-the-art performance. - **AMD MI350 series**: the NVFP4-native MSA kernel, indexer decode context parallelism, dual-batch overlap, and the mono kernel deliver a **2–3×** performance boost across the board. - **Agentic Serving**: on NVIDIA GB300, up to **418.9 tok/s per user** at the latency-sensitive end; on NVIDIA Rubin, up to **724.9 tok/s per user** and **191.5K total tok/s per GPU**; on AMD MI355X, up to **133.3M total tokens per dollar** of TCO on the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark. - **Day-0 RL support**: end-to-end RL with veRL, FSDP2, and LoRA on the NVFP4 checkpoint. ## Quick start Prebuilt images are available for both vendors: - NVIDIA: `vllm/vllm-openai:minimax-m31-flash` - AMD: `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:minimax-m31-flash` Note that the model will only be available in the nightly PyPI wheel after the code is reviewed and merged upstream, which usually takes about a week. Full recipes are at [vLLM Recipes](https://recipes.vllm.ai/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash), and the checkpoint is at [MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash). ### TP4 on NVIDIA We recommend the CUDA 13.4 toolkit for the best performance. ```bash vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash \ -tp 4 \ --reasoning-parser minimax_m3 \ --block-size 128 \ --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 \ --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype": "nvfp4"}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"attention_backend":"FLASHINFER_TS","kv_cache_dtype":"fp8","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' \ --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager ``` ### TP4 on AMD ```bash vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash \ -tp 4 \ --reasoning-parser minimax_m3 \ --block-size 128 \ --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 \ --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype": "nvfp4", "indexer_decode_cp": true}' \ --quantization-config.moe mxfp8 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":3,"attention_backend":"TRITON_ATTN","kv_cache_dtype":"fp8","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' \ --disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager ``` ## MSA primer The MiniMax-M3 model family replaces full attention with a variant of block-sparse attention ([arXiv 2606.13392](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13392v1)) to make inference more efficient. The KV cache is split into blocks of 128 tokens. A lightweight indexer scores every key in the context with one index query per GQA group against a single shared index-key head, then max-pools those scores into one score per block. Main attention then runs exactly, but only over the top 16 blocks, and the most recent block is always kept. That caps each query at 2,048 keys, however long the context is. The payoff is largest in decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth. Each step still scans the index keys for the whole context, but that is only 128 bytes per token per layer, an eighth of the 1,024 bytes of K/V that dense attention would read (FP8, 4 KV heads × 128 dims). The full K/V is then read for just the 2,048 selected tokens. At long-context decode, per-step HBM traffic drops to about 12.5% of what dense attention reads. *Figure 1: MiniMax Sparse Attention. Each GQA group's indexer picks its top KV blocks, and every query head in that group attends exactly over only those blocks. Step through it.* ### What is new in the MiniMax-M3.1 architecture MiniMax-M3.1 greatly improves inference efficiency over the previous generation: it was natively quantization-aware trained for an NVFP4 KV cache, and its routed MoE weights are stored in NVFP4. The NVFP4 experts shrink the checkpoint from 451.5 GB (MiniMax-M3-MXFP8) to 250.1 GB, which is 44.6% smaller. The NVFP4 KV cache needs 34,560 bytes per token instead of 61,440 bytes in FP8, a saving of 43.75% per token. Together, on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs with DEP4 deployment and 256K-token sequences, M3.1 fits 76 concurrent sequences where M3 with an FP8 KV cache fits 28, about 2.7× as many on the same hardware, which directly raises serving throughput. *Figure 2: MiniMax-M3.1 is quantization-aware trained to use an NVFP4 KV cache for both the indexer and sparse attention. Change the KV cache dtype, parallelism, GPU, or context length to see how many sequences fit.* ## Performance optimizations vLLM delivers strong MiniMax-M3.1 performance across multiple hardware platforms. On NVIDIA GPUs, we ship kernels optimized for the NVFP4 KV cache. Our MSA repository ([vllm-project/MSA](https://github.com/vllm-project/MSA)) contains kernels tuned for different workloads and operations. These include MSA indexer prefill and decode, sparse attention prefill and decode, and an MSA-specific top-k kernel. *Figure 3: One MiniMax-M3.1 sparse decoder layer on Blackwell at decode (M ≤ 32), kernel by kernel. Numbered badges mark the optimizations in this post; click one to highlight its kernels.* ### NVIDIA Blackwell optimized MSA kernels The KV cache is stored in NVFP4 while the query stays in FP8, so we cannot use the native NVFP4 tensor core instructions for the matrix multiply. Instead, the kernel dequantizes the NVFP4 KV cache to FP8 and runs an FP8 MMA. To keep the dequantization cost low, we use a new Blackwell-specific PTX instruction introduced in CUDA 13.4, `mul.e4m3x4.e2m1x4.e4m3x4` (SASS `QMUL4`). It scales four NVFP4 values by their scale factor and produces four FP8 values in a single instruction. This takes far fewer CUDA core instructions than the previous FP16 round-trip path. The result is up to a 1.7× speedup on the indexer QK decode kernel and 1.3× on the sparse attention decode kernel. ### NVFP4 MegaMoE MegaMoE is a key building block for modern expert-parallel (EP) deployments. We extended DeepGEMM's MegaMoE to NVFP4 precision with fused MXFP8 shared experts, open-sourced in our fork ([vllm-project/DeepGEMM](https://github.com/vllm-project/DeepGEMM)). Adding NVFP4 support to MegaMoE is more than a dtype swap. NVFP4 halves the bytes per element and doubles tensor core throughput compared with the previous FP8×FP4 path. The rest of the kernel has to change too, or the pipeline falls out of balance. One such change is releasing the TMEM stage early in the FC1 epilogue. Previously, the TMEM stage was released only after the epilogue finished. That wait is unnecessary because the epilogue runs entirely in registers. TMEM can be released as soon as the accumulator has been loaded into registers, before any arithmetic happens. This cuts total kernel latency by 20% in prefill, where the faster NVFP4 compute matters most. It also raises overall prefill throughput by 7%. ### NVFP4 indexer DCP (decode context parallelism) In low-latency serving, each GPU scores its own index head over the full context. Across the four GPUs, that means every indexer layer reads the full index cache four times. Indexer DCP splits the work by context instead. Each GPU scores all four heads over a quarter of the pages. It then sends its local top-16 for each head over NVLink to the GPU that owns that head, which merges the candidates into the final top-16. The selection remains exact, and the indexer runs up to 3.3× faster per sparse layer at 512K context on 4× NVIDIA GB300 GPUs. ### QKV GEMM + norm + RoPE + KV insert fusion MiniMax-M3.1's QKV and indexer projections used to write the full QKV tensor to HBM. A second kernel then read it back for norm, RoPE, and KV cache insertion. We fused the whole chain into a single GEMM kernel whose epilogue processes the FP32 accumulator head by head. It applies norm and RoPE to the query and index query. It also quantizes K, V, and the index key to NVFP4 and writes them directly into their caches. The QKV tensor never touches HBM. On GB300, prefill batches of 512 or more tokens run 1.1–1.6× faster, and P50 time-to-first-token (TTFT) drops by about 19% at TP4. ### FlashInfer PrimiTS for the DSpark drafter MiniMax-M3.1 uses DSpark as its speculative decoding drafter, which runs non-causal GQA with a 4096-token sliding window. Previously, vLLM ran the drafter on FlashAttention 4, which is not optimized for decode shapes. We switched it to FlashInfer's PrimiTS backend. PrimiTS is 1.3–2× faster than FlashAttention 4 and cuts overall forward time by 5%. ### Agentic workload benchmark on NVIDIA GB300 vLLM delivers strong performance on agentic serving workloads. We benchmark our day-0 image on NVIDIA GB300 with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark (detailed in our [previous post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx)). At the latency-sensitive end of the frontier, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash holds 418.9 tokens per second per user. Further along the frontier, it keeps each user above 200 tokens per second while serving 38.6K total tokens per second per GPU. At the throughput end, it reaches 153.8K tokens per second per GPU, about 24× the most interactive point, while each user still sees about 127 tokens per second. *Figure 4: AgentX Pareto frontier for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA GB300, with 7 speculative tokens and synthetic acceptance lengths of 3.16–3.26 tokens (including the first token). Hover a point for its metrics.* ### NVIDIA Rubin optimized MSA We also optimized this model on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs. To mitigate the NVFP4 to FP8 conversion overhead, we convert NVFP4 directly to FP16 and run the score MMA in FP16 for the indexer. This cuts dequant instructions by about a third, and the scores become exact rather than carrying the E4M3 re-rounding to run FP8 MMA. With ≤4 queries, the one-head indexer decode kernel goes further: it applies each block scale once per MMA result with SM107's packed `fma.rn.f32x2.f16x2`, instead of once per K value. This also enables more latency hiding by running three CTAs per SM. Rubin's larger shared memory (328 KB vs 228 KB on Blackwell) and extra Tensor Memory columns (576 vs. 512 on Blackwell) make that possible. Finally, because Rubin has more SMs than Blackwell, the work planners size their tiles from the SM count, so the work is spread evenly across all 212 of Rubin's SMs. Prefill sparse attention also benefits from locality domain optimizations. We allocate the partial buffers through the CUDA virtual memory API so that 2 MB pages alternate between the two domains, and the combined kernel hands each tile to a CTA whose SM sits in the domain that holds that tile's data. On Rubin the prefill & decode attention kernels use dense FP8 MMA with K=64 per instruction, which halves the MMA instruction count and runs at twice Blackwell's FP8 rate. ### Agentic workload benchmark on NVIDIA Rubin On NVIDIA Rubin, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash pushes the frontier further on the same benchmark. At the latency-sensitive end, it holds 724.9 tokens per second per user. Further along the frontier, it keeps each user above 200 tokens per second while serving 157.3K total tokens per second per GPU. At the throughput end, it reaches 191.5K tokens per second per GPU while each user still sees about 134 tokens per second, about 1.5× GB300 at the same per-user rate. *Figure 5: AgentX Pareto frontier for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Rubin. Hover a point for its configuration and metrics.* ## AMD GPU support On AMD GPUs, we bring NVFP4 KV cache support, so AMD deployments can also use the low-precision format to cut KV cache memory. For decode, we add indexer DCP to speed up long-context decode, and a mono kernel that speeds up low-latency inference. For prefill, sequence parallelism and dual-batch overlap cut communication inside the engine, and a new KV cache layout lets each KV block move to the decode node in a single transfer. The MSA and mono kernels are built in [FlyDSL](https://github.com/rocm/flydsl), AMD's Python DSL for GPU kernels, with help from the FlyDSL team. ### NVFP4 MSA kernel MiniMax-M3.1 is trained with an NVFP4 KV cache (QAT) for both the main attention and the indexer, but CDNA4 has no native instruction to dequantize NVFP4. To keep the MSA kernels fast, we turn dequantization into a table lookup. There are only 256 possible E4M3 scales and eight E2M1 magnitudes, so we precompute every scaled value, already rounded to FP8, into a 2 KB table in LDS. One `v_perm_b32` byte permute plus one XOR for the sign bits then converts four FP4 values to FP8. The kernel also dequantizes a shared-prefix page only once for up to 64 requests that share it. Together, these make sparse decode attention up to 2.5× faster than converting the selected blocks to FP8 and running the FP8 attention kernel. ### NVFP4 indexer DCP We use the same indexer decode context parallelism on AMD as on NVIDIA, and on CDNA4 it brings an extra win. Without DCP, each GPU at TP4 scores its own index head over the full context, so the index cache is read four times. It also leaves the matrix cores underused. A DSpark-3 decode step has only 4 query rows per request, which fills just 4 of the 16 columns of the 16×16×128 FP8 MFMA. With DCP, each GPU scores all four heads over a quarter of the context, so 4 heads × 4 rows fill all 16 columns. A single kernel exchanges the index queries, scores its blocks, and writes each head's scores directly into the owning GPU's memory over Infinity Fabric. A device-side handshake keeps this working inside HIP graphs. The owner then picks the top 16 as before, and because the scores are bit-for-bit identical to the single-GPU version, the selection is exact. On 4× MI355X, the indexer runs up to 2.8× faster per sparse layer on 45 requests of 30K–210K tokens. ### SP + DBO prefill and one-read KV transfer At TP4, long-prompt prefill on MI355X is bound by communication, both between GPUs inside a node and between the prefill and decode nodes. Inside the engine, dual-batch overlap (DBO) hides the tensor-parallel collectives behind the other microbatch's compute. Sequence parallelism (SP) cuts the traffic itself. Each GPU keeps a quarter of the tokens, the attention output is exchanged all-to-all in MXFP8 so each GPU runs the full `o_proj` on its own tokens, and the MoE output is reduce-scattered. This drops traffic per GPU from about 36 KB to 20 KB per token per layer, and norms, quantization, and the router run on only a quarter of the tokens. A faster prefill engine only helps if the KV cache can also reach the decode node quickly. vLLM's layer-by-layer KV cache layout splits each KV block across 125 small pages, and each page needs its own NIXL RDMA read. We switch to a block-outer layout that stores each block in one contiguous 1.82 MB row, so NIXL moves it in a single read. Combined, the engine and KV transfer changes make prefill batches of 16K+ tokens 1.8–2.1× faster on 4× MI355X. ### Low-latency mono kernel At low concurrency, decode on AMD GPUs is launch-bound: kernel launch overhead takes more time than the math. Mono decode fixes this by running each sparse MoE decoder layer as a single FlyDSL kernel launch. That one launch covers everything from the QKV projection and sparse attention to the tensor-parallel all-reduces and the MXFP4 MoE, replacing roughly 1,170 kernel launches. On MI350X at TP4, this makes the decode step up to 2.3× faster and doubles 8K-in/1K-out throughput at low concurrency. On an agentic-coding trace, it raises interactivity by 50–65%. ### Agentic workload benchmark on AMD MI355X Our AMD implementation also delivers strong performance per cost. On the InferenceX AgentX benchmark, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash holds 331.0 tokens per second per user at the latency-sensitive end of the frontier. Further along the frontier, it keeps each user above 170 tokens per second while delivering 34.6M total tokens per dollar of TCO. At the cost-efficient end, it reaches 133.3M tokens per dollar, nearly 10× the most interactive point, while each user still sees about 79 tokens per second. *Figure 6: AgentX Pareto frontier for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on AMD MI355X, in total tokens per dollar of TCO. c1 and c4 use a synthetic acceptance length of 3.2 tokens with 7 speculative tokens; the other points use 2.45 tokens with 3 speculative tokens. Hover a point for its metrics.* ## Day-0 RL support We run RL on MiniMax-M3.1 starting from its NVFP4 checkpoint and train only rank-32 LoRA adapters. The veRL trainer quantizes the base model the same way the engine serves it, with NVFP4 on the routed experts and MXFP8 on the other projections, and syncs only the adapters to the engine after each step. On the engine side, expert LoRA runs inside FlashInfer's TRTLLM NVFP4 MoE kernel, so the base experts still run on the normal serving kernel. Before training, we checked that the trainer and the engine agree in three ways. The engine receives exactly the weights the trainer sends, both route each token to the same experts (routing replay), and both assign close logprobs to the same tokens. The remaining gap is corrected with token-level importance sampling (TIS), with the importance ratio capped at 2. Because each batch gets a single optimizer step, the trainer uses the rollout logprobs as the old logprobs and skips the extra forward pass that would recompute them. On DAPO-Math-17K with 16 GB300 GPUs, 200 GRPO steps raise AIME-2024 accuracy from 36.3% to 67.5%. Over the same run, training reward rises from −0.06 to 0.67, and train/rollout KL stays low, falling from 0.040 to 0.024. *Figure 7: Day-0 RL on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash with veRL on DAPO-Math-17K (16× GB300, 200 GRPO steps): AIME-2024 accuracy, training reward, and train/rollout KL. Use the tabs to switch between them.* ## Acknowledgments We extend our sincere gratitude to the MiniMax team for open-sourcing MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. Both its NVFP4 and BF16 checkpoints run on a single GPU, and a single request decodes at **about 500 tokens/s** on one GB200, even with 100K tokens of context. Flint is a 40B-parameter MoE that activates only about 2.5B parameters per token, with sliding-window attention in most layers and a 262K-token context. It ships as two separate checkpoints: NVFP4 (quantization-aware trained) and BF16. ## Quick start The day-0 Docker image `vllm/vllm-openai:flint` (x86_64 and arm64, CUDA 13.0) has Flint support built in: ```bash # NVFP4 checkpoint (GGUF): config and tokenizer come from the BF16 repo docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:flint \ RecursiveSI/flint-nvfp4-gguf \ --hf-config-path RecursiveSI/flint --tokenizer RecursiveSI/flint \ --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 \ --reasoning-parser glm47 --exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none # BF16 checkpoint docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:flint \ RecursiveSI/flint \ --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 \ --reasoning-parser glm47 --exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none ``` Flint support is being merged into vLLM ([#62938](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62938)). With a vLLM build that includes it, serve the same way: ```bash # NVFP4 checkpoint (GGUF): config and tokenizer come from the BF16 repo vllm serve RecursiveSI/flint-nvfp4-gguf \ --hf-config-path RecursiveSI/flint --tokenizer RecursiveSI/flint \ --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 \ --reasoning-parser glm47 --exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none # BF16 checkpoint vllm serve RecursiveSI/flint \ --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 \ --reasoning-parser glm47 --exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none ``` ## Model architecture Flint is a 49-layer pre-norm MoE with hidden size 2048. What sets it apart is how little of it looks at the whole context. *Figure 1: Flint's layer stack and its two sublayers. Gold marks what differs from a standard pre-norm MoE. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/flint-arch.html).* - **Mostly local attention.** 35 layers attend to a 513-token sliding window with RoPE; the other 14 attend to the full context with no positional encoding. Only those 14 keep KV for the whole sequence, so the cache costs 28 KiB per token. - **Learned attention sinks**, GQA with 32 query and 4 KV heads, and per-head Q/K RMSNorm. - **256 experts, sigmoid top-6, plus a shared expert.** Layers 0 and 1 use a dense MLP instead. The NVFP4 checkpoint is a GGUF file whose blocks are NVIDIA's NVFP4 format in a different byte order. vLLM repacks it losslessly at load time and runs it weight-only (W4A16), with BF16 activations and KV cache, as Recursive's reference implementation does. Every Flint kernel follows the reference's rounding points, and accuracy matches it on GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond, long-context MRCR and a tool-calling suite. ## Optimizations Our first implementation, built from vLLM's stock layers, was slow at small batch sizes: a decode step ran 1,096 kernels, many of them tuned for much larger batches. We replaced them with Flint-specific kernels one change at a time, checking each against the reference. *Figure 2: Model-forward latency on one GB200 after each change, for batch-1 decode at 100K context and an 8,192-token prefill. Toggle the checkpoint, or show the table for every shape. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/flint-opt-chart.html).* - **Fused Q/K norm, RoPE and KV-cache write** (−8%): one kernel instead of three. - **Small-batch MoE kernels** (−27%): router and expert GEMVs that read only the selected experts' weights. Also the largest prefill gain. - **Small-batch dense GEMV** (−25%) on the same packed NVFP4 weights as the large-batch kernel. - **Norm and SiLU kernels** (−10%) that follow the reference's rounding. - **Decode attention** (−5%) with sinks and sliding windows, in CuTe DSL. - **Low-latency decode path** (−14%), shown below. For up to 8 requests, the low-latency path runs each MoE layer as seven kernels: Q/K norm, RoPE, routing and the expert combine are fused into the neighboring GEMV kernels. Each kernel is launched with programmatic dependent launch, so it loads its weights while the previous one is still running. *Figure 3: The seven kernels of one MoE layer on the low-latency decode path.* In total, NVFP4 decode went from 4.81 to 1.78 ms (2.7×), BF16 decode from 3.53 to 2.34 ms (1.5×), and an 8K-token prefill from 207 to 145 ms (1.4×). A forward now runs 346 kernels instead of 1,096. Served end to end, batch-1 decode at 100K context takes 2.06 ms per token (about 485 tokens/s), which is the forward plus the LM head and sampling. ## Usage notes - Flint emits GLM-4.7-style tool calls and thinking blocks, hence the `glm47` parsers. `--exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none` drops tool definitions from the prompt when `tool_choice` is `"none"`, matching the reference. - The default sampling settings are temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20. Reasoning counts toward `max_tokens`, so allow at least 32K for hard problems. - The Flint kernels target a single Blackwell GPU (TP=1, BF16 KV cache); other configurations fall back to vLLM's standard layers. --- # Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-21-humming Published: 2026-10-21 Authors: Ant Group and the vLLM Community Tags: quantization, performance, kernels, moe Summary: Introducing Humming, a quantized inference kernel library from Ant Group and the vLLM community, with broad GPU and quantization support, dense and MoE performance results, and vLLM integration. Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features: - **Broad device support**: Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E. - **Extensive quantization support**: A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes. - **Strong execution performance**: Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads. Repository: [github.com/vllm-project/humming](https://github.com/vllm-project/humming) ## Background As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency. Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space. These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low. Developing and integrating a dedicated kernel for every combination creates a growing maintenance burden. Each addition can require its own weight preprocessing, kernel selection, framework adapters, and tests. Optimizations must then be carried across multiple implementations. Humming addresses this problem by separating quantization descriptions from execution choices and composing kernels from shared components. ## General-Purpose Architecture Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components. ### A Unified Quantization Representation Models exported by different quantization tools vary in numeric format, parameter organization, and weight layout. Humming converts supported export formats into the Humming standard format: a common quantization description with consistently organized weights, scales, zero points, and other tensors. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-quantization-format-en.svg) This representation preserves each scheme's quantization semantics while describing weight format, scaling granularity, scale data type, zero points, and secondary scales as separate parameters. Activations have their own numeric format and quantization settings. These parameters can be combined subject to format and hardware constraints. For example, groupwise INT4 weights can be paired with BF16 activations. Low-precision floating-point weights with different scaling schemes use the same parameter system. This gives inference frameworks a common interface for models from different sources. ### Tuning and JIT Compilation for Each Workload The standard format provides a common representation across export formats. Preprocessing then validates parameters, pads dimensions, and repacks these tensors into layouts suited to the target kernel. Humming combines the quantization description with the weight shape, GEMM type, target GPU, and compute options to configure execution. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-jit-inference-en.svg) Three configurations describe the kernel: - **Layer Config** describes tensor shapes, data types, quantization parameters, and the target architecture. - **Compute Config** specifies the GEMM type and computation options, such as batch invariance and input scale layout. - **Tuning Config** selects tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, memory access, and MMA instructions. It also controls concurrency and scheduling; TMA can be configured per tensor. By default, Humming selects tuning configurations using device-specific heuristics. It can prepare different configurations for ranges of input sizes and dispatch to the appropriate kernel at runtime. Humming’s unified architecture makes it straightforward to tune execution parameters and select pipelines for different workloads. At small batch sizes, a multistage pipeline using asynchronous copies (`cp.async`) and MMA can outperform a pipeline built around TMA and UMMA. At larger batch sizes, TMA and UMMA can offer better throughput. Humming accommodates both execution paths within the same configuration and component framework, allowing it to select the more effective strategy for each workload. Together, the three configurations specialize kernels compiled with NVRTC or NVCC. Compiled kernels are cached for reuse. Inference combines the selected kernel with the preprocessed weights and runtime activations. ### Shared CUDA Components Across Formats and Architectures At the CUDA level, Humming organizes task scheduling, data movement, dequantization and scaling, Tensor Core computation, and output processing into reusable components. It provides standard, warp-specialized, and dedicated UMMA pipelines. These pipelines share compatible components while using the dataflow and synchronization required by each execution strategy. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-cuda-architecture-en.svg) Each group of components handles a different source of variation: - **Numeric processing handles quantization formats.** Decoding and arithmetic components account for bit width, integer or floating-point representation, scales, and zero points. Dequantization and scaling are integrated into the kernel's computation. - **Memory and compute backends handle GPU architectures.** Humming selects data movement and Tensor Core implementations for the target architecture, using asynchronous copies, TMA, and multicast where supported. - **Task mapping and scheduling handle dense and MoE workloads.** Each GEMM type uses the appropriate scheduling logic. Scaling and bias addition can also be fused into the output stage. JIT compilation combines these components according to the three configurations and eliminates unused implementation branches. A new format or architecture can therefore be supported by extending the relevant components. Improvements to a shared component benefit compatible configurations, reducing the duplicated development and maintenance of separate specialized kernels. This CUDA implementation is lightweight and avoids heavyweight kernel framework dependencies, keeping JIT compilation fast as well. In our single W4A16 kernel compilation test on an H200 server with CUDA 13.4, compilation time dropped from **23.35 seconds for CUTLASS with NVCC** to **1.82 seconds for Humming with NVCC** or **1.88 seconds with NVRTC**, with compilation caches disabled. This reduces the cost of preparing kernels for new workloads and makes iterative tuning more practical. Humming also compiles kernels in parallel during model warmup. In our tests, compiling and loading the kernels covering all supported M sizes for a single layer's GEMM takes only **about 2–4 seconds**, making it practical to prepare multiple specialized kernels before inference. ### Performance Tuning Based on Device Parameters Humming deeply optimizes kernels using both the GEMM configuration and device parameters. Quantization formats, matrix shapes, GPU instruction support, SM count, shared memory, and register resources all inform execution choices, turning the benefits of low-bit storage into practical inference performance. **Efficient W4A8-MXFP4 inference on existing GPUs.** Architectures before Blackwell lack native MXFP4 Tensor Core support, and conventional W4A8-MXFP4 kernels can be limited by dequantization and scaling overhead at larger M. Humming addresses this with a fast MXFP4-to-INT8/FP8 dequantization path that converts MXFP4 weights into a supported compute format within the kernel. In this setting, the path substantially outperforms conventional W4A8 implementations at small M and approaches W8A8 performance at large M. GPUs such as H200 can therefore run high-performance W4A8-MXFP4 kernels while retaining the storage benefits of 4-bit weights. **Dequantization paths matched to each device.** The same quantization format can benefit from different implementations across GPUs. Humming selects decoding, numeric conversion, and scaling paths for the device, pairing them with suitable memory access and compute pipelines to reduce instruction and data movement overhead. Shared components make these optimizations reusable across compatible dense and MoE kernels. **Extensive tuning controls with device-specific heuristics.** Humming exposes tile shapes, pipeline stage counts, warp specialization, TMA, MMA instructions, CTA concurrency, and Stream-K scheduling. Device-specific heuristics combine GEMM shapes with resource constraints to balance parallelism, data reuse, and pipeline overhead, selecting different execution strategies as input sizes change. Developers can use the default configurations directly or refine them for particular models and deployment scenarios. ## Results ### Broad Device Support Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware. The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms. The figure below shows the high-performance activation types supported by Humming on each device: types that can take full advantage of the device's peak compute capabilities. Some types omitted from the figure can still run through other instruction paths. For example, UMMA instructions on the B300 (SM103) no longer support INT8 computation, but earlier MMA instructions can still execute INT8 GEMM, with substantially lower performance. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-device-support-en.svg) ### Quantization Support Humming's support for quantization types depends primarily on compatibility between activation and weight types. Its unified quantization representation and kernel architecture allow a wide range of integer and floating-point weight formats to work with activations at different precisions, providing flexible choices for model precision and deployment performance. The figure below shows the weight and activation type combinations supported by Humming. Rows represent weight types, columns represent activation types, and checks indicate supported combinations. Together with the device support matrix above, it outlines the high-performance quantized computation paths available on each hardware architecture. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-quantization-support-en.svg) Humming also supports a special floating-point format with zero exponent bits, whose representable values match those of symmetric integers at the same bit width. For example, INT8 excluding `-128` and `float8e0m7` both represent integers from `-127` to `127`. Weights in this format have the same activation type compatibility as INT weights of the same bit width. Humming automatically converts eligible symmetric integer weights to this format for faster dequantization. The community has also uncovered [two hidden capabilities in Blackwell Tensor Cores](https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2059376150565089368): native support for `float4e0m3` and `float8e3m4`, two special floating-point formats that are not exposed in the PTX type system. Humming supports these features across all Blackwell architectures, including datacenter SM100/SM103 and SM120/SM121 devices for workstations and personal computing. Both formats are integrated into its unified quantization and compute framework, providing more native compute options for low-precision inference. Rubin does not support these two hidden Tensor Core formats, so support for these native compute paths does not extend to Rubin. ### Performance The kernel microbenchmarks below, run by the vLLM community, measure GEMM performance with M covering every power of two from 1 to 8192. Kernels are fully warmed up and timed independently with a cold L2 cache, with a brief pause between samples. MoE speedups use the sum of Gateup and Down GEMM latencies. Each figure identifies its baseline, quantization formats, matrix dimensions, and software versions. #### WnA16 WnA16 is one of the most versatile and widely used approaches to quantized inference. It combines low-bit weights with FP16/BF16 activations, reducing weight storage and memory traffic while making use of widely available 16-bit compute capabilities. This makes it suitable for many GPU generations and model deployment scenarios. The W4A16 family has attracted particular interest from the community and is a major focus of Humming's optimization work. For dense W4A16, Humming matches or outperforms vLLM Marlin in most tested configurations, with substantial gains on several Hopper and Blackwell workloads. The figure below uses cuBLAS as a common baseline. At small batch sizes, Humming delivers roughly 3–4× speedups on several devices. As batch size grows, it continues to use the hardware efficiently, reaching approximately twice Marlin's performance on large-batch H200 workloads and more than three times its performance in some B300 cases. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-w4a16-performance-en.svg) These gains extend to MoE. Its shared dequantization and compute paths deliver strong performance for integer and floating-point weights at different bit widths, including INT1, INT2, INT3, and FP4 through FP8. The following figure shows broad gains across these formats at small and medium batch sizes, with the lowest-bit configurations on SM120 exceeding 5× the performance of BF16 cuBLAS. The right column above keeps DeepGEMM W8A8 as the baseline. At small and medium batch sizes, Humming's W4A8 reaches approximately 4.2× baseline performance on H20 and 4.5× on H200, also substantially outperforming Humming's W8A8 results in the same figure. Reduced weight traffic translates into lower GEMM latency. FlashInfer CUTLASS W4A8 is also an implementation based on Humming's approach, while Humming's current implementation achieves better performance in the benchmarks shown here. Blackwell adds native Tensor Core support for microscaling formats such as MXFP8 and MXFP4. From datacenter SM100/SM103 devices to SM120/SM121 devices for workstations and personal computing, Humming uses each architecture's low-precision compute capabilities to support W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4 within one kernel and tuning framework. On B300 (SM103), Humming demonstrates substantial performance gains across all three MX format combinations. Each panel below uses DeepGEMM Contiguous at the corresponding precision as its baseline. The unified architecture brings these low-precision inference optimizations to more devices, extending efficient quantized computation beyond the datacenter. ![](/blog-assets/figures/humming/humming-w4a8-w4a4-sm12x-performance-en.svg) #### End-to-End Inference Performance Humming's W4A8 gains extend to model serving. The throughput advantage grows with concurrency: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises from 442.37 to 633.94 tokens/s, while mean time per output token (TPOT) falls by approximately **31%**. | Concurrency | MoE backend | Input throughput (tokens/s) ↑ | Output throughput (tokens/s) ↑ | TTFT (ms) ↓ | TPOT (ms) ↓ | |---:|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 2827.15 | 88.30 | 543.13 | 9.24 | | 1 | **Humming W4A8** | 3226.23 (+14.1%) | 100.77 (+14.1%) | 383.80 (-29.3%) | 8.46 (-8.5%) | | 2 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 4781.06 | 149.33 | 794.31 | 10.33 | | 2 | **Humming W4A8** | 5646.98 (+18.1%) | 176.38 (+18.1%) | 555.66 (-30.0%) | 9.20 (-10.9%) | | 4 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 7427.64 | 231.99 | 1422.32 | 11.72 | | 4 | **Humming W4A8** | 9160.81 (+23.3%) | 286.12 (+23.3%) | 971.74 (-31.7%) | 10.22 (-12.9%) | | 8 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 9190.03 | 287.04 | 2049.81 | 19.90 | | 8 | **Humming W4A8** | 12263.89 (+33.4%) | 383.04 (+33.4%) | 1386.91 (-32.3%) | 15.49 (-22.2%) | | 16 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 11124.67 | 348.96 | 2463.69 | 36.28 | | 16 | **Humming W4A8** | 15171.00 (+36.4%) | 475.89 (+36.4%) | 1844.71 (-25.1%) | 26.44 (-27.1%) | | 32 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 12669.43 | 398.83 | 3546.74 | 66.44 | | 32 | **Humming W4A8** | 17804.79 (+40.5%) | 560.49 (+40.5%) | 2465.47 (-30.5%) | 47.48 (-28.5%) | | 64 | vLLM Marlin W4A16 | 13937.42 | 442.37 | 5467.35 | 123.25 | | 64 | **Humming W4A8** | 19973.00 (+43.3%) | 633.94 (+43.3%) | 3882.94 (-29.0%) | 85.70 (-30.5%) | ## Usage ### Installation Install Humming with pip: ```bash pip install humming-kernels ``` Humming uses a CUDA compiler to generate kernels on demand. If no CUDA compiler is available on the system, choose one of the following installation options to include the compilation dependencies for your environment's CUDA major version: ```bash pip install "humming-kernels[cu12]" # CUDA 12 pip install "humming-kernels[cu13]" # CUDA 13 ``` Humming itself is extremely lightweight, with simple dependencies and a wheel package of only about 500 KB. On-demand compilation avoids bundling a large collection of precompiled kernels. In principle, any environment capable of running PyTorch 2.7 can also run Humming, making it easy to integrate into existing inference environments. ### Using Humming in vLLM Humming is deeply integrated into vLLM. Starting with vLLM 0.22.0, CUDA installations include Humming as a dependency, so no separate Humming installation is needed. Humming supports NVIDIA GPUs across all architectures from Turing onward (SM75 and above). The `--linear-backend` and `--moe-backend` options select Humming as the compute backend for dense GEMM and MoE GEMM, respectively. For example, enable Humming for both with tensor parallel size 8: ```bash vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --linear-backend humming --moe-backend humming ``` The `--quantization humming` option is intended only as a compatibility path for formats that Humming supports but vLLM no longer supports or does not yet support natively, such as GPTQ INT3. For example, load a GPTQ INT3 checkpoint through this compatibility path: ```bash vllm serve hfl/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct-GPTQ-Int3 --quantization humming ``` ### Selecting Activation Types By default, Humming uses the activation type specified in the checkpoint and adapts execution to the device. If the GPU does not support that compute type, Humming falls back to a supported higher-precision type. For example, devices without native MXFP4 support can automatically use FP8, BF16, or FP16 compute paths, allowing the same quantized checkpoint to run across GPU generations. Users can override the default through vLLM's quantization configuration interface to select an activation type for their deployment. The following example sets the activation type for MoE layers to MXFP8: ```bash vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-20b --moe-backend humming --quantization-config.moe.activation mxfp8 ``` ## Future Plans ### Broader and Deeper Device Support Humming will continue expanding hardware coverage while adapting to the compute and memory capabilities of new devices, helping more platforms realize the performance potential of quantized inference. Priorities include: - Supporting more Rubin architecture features, including Locality Domains, to further optimize task mapping and data access. - Extending support to more T-Head PPU devices, including the Zhenwu M890. - Supporting more devices compatible with CUDA programming, bringing existing quantization formats, kernel components, and tuning capabilities to additional hardware platforms. ### Adding Autotune With targeted tuning, Humming can already achieve state-of-the-art performance in most scenarios. However, the wide range of model shapes, quantization configurations, and device resources makes it difficult for heuristics to select the optimal configuration in every case. Humming therefore plans to introduce autotune, benchmarking candidate configurations on the target device to find better execution parameters for each workload. Autotune will complement existing heuristics, reducing manual configuration search and helping more workloads approach the kernels' best achievable performance. ### Deeper Integration with Inference Frameworks Humming will continue deepening its integration with inference frameworks such as vLLM, expanding support across quantized model loading, backend selection, parallel inference, runtime scheduling, and device adaptation. We aim to make more quantization methods work with the full range of framework capabilities, including optimizations such as quantized All-to-All (A2A) communication for expert parallelism (EP). These efforts will make high-performance quantized kernels easier to use across diverse deployment scenarios and help translate kernel performance gains into end-to-end inference benefits. ## Acknowledgments We thank Jinzhen Lin, Zekai Gu, and Zhilin Huang from Ant Group, as well as Michael Goin, Roberto L. Castro, Chauncey Jiang, and other members of the vLLM community, for their contributions and support throughout Humming's development. We also thank the vLLM community for providing development, testing, and CI resources that made it possible to validate and improve Humming across a wide range of hardware and workloads. Humming's design and optimization draw inspiration from Marlin, vLLM Marlin, LMDeploy, DeepGEMM, FlashInfer, CUTLASS, and other open-source projects. We are grateful to their authors and contributors for sharing their ideas and implementations, helping advance high-performance quantized inference for the entire community. --- # Introducing vLLM TorchTPU Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-20-vllm-torchtpu Published: 2026-10-20 Authors: Inferact and Google Teams Tags: hardware Summary: vllm-torchtpu is a new vLLM backend for Google Cloud TPUs built on TorchTPU, with Pallas kernels, multi-host parallelism, KV cache offloading, and disaggregated serving.


Today we're releasing [vLLM TorchTPU](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu) (`vllm-torchtpu`), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's [TorchTPU](https://developers.googleblog.com/torchtpu-running-pytorch-natively-on-tpus-at-google-scale/) stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code. This work comes out of the [engineering partnership between Inferact and Google](https://inferact.ai/news/google-tpu-partnership) we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to: 1. Make it easy to bring new models to TPU by reusing vLLM's existing model code. 2. Push TPU inference performance in open source, with Pallas kernels for attention, Mixture-of-Experts, and quantized matmul. 3. Keep the vLLM experience the same: the same CLI, OpenAI-compatible server, scheduler, and KV cache manager you use on other hardware. ### How It Works `vllm-torchtpu` is an out-of-tree vLLM platform plugin. Once installed, vLLM picks it up automatically through the `vllm.platform_plugins` entry point. Models run through vLLM's standard model runner and are compiled with `torch.compile(backend="tpu")`, which lowers to XLA. Each TPU device gets its own worker process, the same way vLLM runs on GPUs, and communication between devices goes through `torch.distributed`. This means the scheduler, workers, KV cache manager, and API server are all unmodified upstream vLLM. The TPU-specific work sits underneath them, mostly in a set of JAX/Pallas kernels that are registered as custom ops and called from inside the compiled graph. #### Getting Started 1. Install ```shell pip install vllm-torchtpu ``` This requires Python 3.12 on a Cloud TPU VM, and installs a matching vLLM, `torch`, `torch_tpu`, and `libtpu` alongside the plugin. The [installation guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/getting_started/installation.md) also covers `uv`, source builds, and [Docker](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/getting_started/docker.md). 2. Serve a model ```shell vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --max-model-len 16384 \ --async-scheduling ``` The first startup compiles TPU graphs for the configured shapes, which can take a few minutes. Set `VLLM_XLA_CACHE_PATH` to reuse compiled artifacts across restarts (see [Compilation & Warmup Cache](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/user_guide/compilation_cache.md)). Speculative decoding, prefix caching, multi-LoRA, structured outputs, and multimodal inputs are all enabled with the usual vLLM flags. See the [quickstart](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/getting_started/quickstart.md) for more examples, including offline batch inference, multimodal models, and multi-LoRA. ### Kernels `vllm-torchtpu` uses custom Pallas kernels for complex operations that benefit from hand-tuning on TPU. Some examples: * Ragged Paged Attention v3 for MHA/GQA models * Dense and sparse Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM * Gated DeltaNet and Kimi Delta Attention for hybrid linear-attention models * Fused Mixture-of-Experts with expert parallelism * FP8, INT8, MXFP4, and NVFP4 quantized matmuls ### Scaling Out We've focused heavily on the workloads that put the most pressure on serving systems today, especially multi-turn agentic and multimodal traffic, where contexts keep growing and tool outputs can be long. #### Parallelism All six of vLLM's parallelism dimensions are supported, on both single-host and multi-host TPU slices, and they can be combined: | Dimension | Flag | | :--- | :--- | | Tensor Parallelism (TP) | `--tensor-parallel-size` | | Data Parallelism (DP) | `--data-parallel-size` | | Pipeline Parallelism (PP) | `--pipeline-parallel-size` | | Expert Parallelism (EP) | `--enable-expert-parallel` | | Prefill Context Parallelism (PCP) | `--prefill-context-parallel-size` | | Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) | `--decode-context-parallel-size` | For large MoE models, we usually get the best throughput from data-parallel attention with expert parallelism (for example, `DP=8, TP=1` with EP on a single v7x host). This keeps attention local to each device and spreads the experts across the whole slice. For long contexts, PCP and DCP split prefill and the KV cache across devices. The [parallelism guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/user_guide/parallelism.md) has more detail and example configurations. #### KV Cache Offloading and Disaggregated Serving `vllm-torchtpu` uses [TPU Sync](https://github.com/google/tpu-sync), an open-source C++ library that can read TPU device buffers directly, outside the Python runtime. Through vLLM's KV connector interface, this gives us: * Zero-copy KV cache offloading to host DRAM, so the prefix cache for long multi-turn sessions isn't limited by HBM. * Disaggregated prefill/decode serving across TPU hosts with low KV transfer overhead. Prefill and decode can use different layouts, for example prefill on `PCP=4, TP=2` and decode on `DP=8, TP=1`, and the KV cache is resharded during transfer. See the [disaggregated serving guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/user_guide/disaggregated_serving.md) to set it up. #### Speculative Decoding and Prefix Caching Speculative decoding supports MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark, n-gram, and suffix decoding ([guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/user_guide/speculative_decoding.md)). Automatic prefix caching also works for hybrid models like Qwen3.5 and Kimi K3, where linear-attention state is cached along with the KV cache. ### Models, Features, and What's Next `vllm-torchtpu` can serve most models supported by vLLM, with TPU-specific kernel, quantization, and parallelism work for the Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, GPT-OSS, and Gemma families. TPU v7x (Ironwood) is the recommended hardware and is tested in CI on every pull request; v6e, v5e, and v5p are experimental. The [Supported Models & Features](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/user_guide/supported_models.md) page has the full list of validated checkpoints and features, with how to enable each one. The [nightly support matrices](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/tree/main/support_matrices/nightly) track TPU v7x correctness and benchmark results from CI. #### What's Next? We want new open models from the major families (Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Gemma, GPT-OSS) to run on TPU on the day they're released. Some of what's coming, from the [public roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md): * An automated CI pipeline that onboards, benchmarks, and publishes support matrices for new open-weight models within 24 hours of release. * Prefix-, cache-, and session-aware routing, and llm-d TPU memory-tier routing. * PyTorch interfaces for [Tokamax](https://github.com/openxla/tokamax) kernels, shared with other projects in the TorchTPU ecosystem. * Diffusion model serving through `vllm-omni`. [Contributions are welcome!](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) ### TPU Capacity for Contributors We're also opening a Community Contribution TPU Capacity Pool. If you're building on `vllm-torchtpu`, you can apply for free TPU time, and core vLLM maintainers at Inferact will help with design and PR reviews. [Apply for contributor TPU access here.](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1Jm0uUXvcwYJRrvRojfS2RzMLjaqlt2a7lNyALFZs-nQ/viewform) ### Try It Out * [Quickstart](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/getting_started/quickstart.md) * [Cloud TPU Setup](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/getting_started/tpu_setup.md) * [TPU v7x (Ironwood) Serving Recipes](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/deployment/v7x_recipes.md) * [vLLM TorchTPU Recipes on Ironwood](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-recipes/tree/main/inference/ironwood/vLLM/vLLM-TorchTPU) * [Kubernetes Deployment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/docs/deployment/kubernetes.md) * [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) If you have questions or want to get involved, find us in `#sig-tpu` on the [vLLM Developer Slack](https://slack.vllm.ai). --- # Achieving near-zero-downtime scaling in Elastic Expert Parallelism Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-19-elastic-ep-near-zero-downtime Published: 2026-10-19 Authors: Itay Alroy (NVIDIA) Tags: large-scale-serving, elastic-ep, expert-parallelism, moe, nixl, cuda-graphs Summary: How asynchronous preparation and NIXL EP enabled near-zero-downtime Elastic EP scaling in vLLM. Traditionally, changing the number of GPUs in a vLLM service required adding or removing entire model replicas or restarting the engine with a different GPU count. As models grow larger, each replica needs more GPUs, so scaling by replica adds or removes GPUs in increasingly large increments. Restarting vLLM to scale DeepSeek V4 Pro from 16 to 20 GB200 GPUs stopped serving for **197 seconds** (see the [performance section](#performance-on-deepseek-v4-pro) for details), leaving those expensive GPUs allocated without generating tokens. In our [first Elastic EP post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-14-elastic-expert-parallelism), we showed how vLLM could add or remove GPUs from a running DEP deployment (data-parallel attention with expert-parallel MoE) without restarting it. While we avoided a restart, serving still stopped throughout reconfiguration as we initialized new workers, prepared the expanded communication groups, loaded model weights, and repeated kernel warmup and CUDA graph capture. In our DeepSeek V4 Pro benchmark, this pause lasted **100 seconds when scaling from 16 to 20 GPUs** and **56 seconds when scaling back to 16 GPUs** (full details in the [performance section](#performance-on-deepseek-v4-pro)). In this post, we describe how asynchronous preparation and [NIXL EP](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/blob/main/examples/device/ep/README.md) enabled Elastic EP reconfiguration with near-zero downtime. In the same benchmark, we reduced downtime to **0.82 seconds when scaling from 16 to 20 GPUs** and **1.96 seconds when scaling back to 16 GPUs**, allowing us to scale up and down with almost no impact on serving performance. ## Overlapping topology preparation with serving We reorganized vLLM's reconfiguration flow into two phases: background preparation and a short commit. Existing workers use separate background threads to prepare and warm up target communication, transfer model weights, and synchronize execution-related information (such as autotuning results) with joining workers, while continuing to serve requests with their current communication groups and CUDA graphs. In parallel, joining workers initialize, receive model weights, and prepare their communication and GPU execution. During the commit phase, vLLM briefly pauses its schedulers, activates the prepared topology, and resumes serving. These changes were introduced in [asynchronous preparation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47288) and [prepare/commit optimizations](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51885). Preparation covers four main tasks: 1. **Initialize joining workers.** Start their processes and allocate storage for the model and execution. 2. **Prepare communication.** Set up the target communication groups and expand the EP communicator. 3. **Transfer model weights.** Transfer the required weights from existing workers to joining workers over NVLink or RDMA. 4. **Prepare execution.** Complete the required compilation, kernel warmup, tuning setup, and CUDA graph construction on joining workers. After the commit phase, asynchronous Expert Parallel Load Balancing (EPLB) allows new workers to begin handling attention while existing workers handle expert computation. EPLB then redistributes experts across the expanded group in the background. The main challenge is preparing communication and GPU execution without involving or disrupting the workers that are serving requests. ## Expand EP communication in place Before NIXL EP, the EP communication backends available in vLLM used fixed membership: each instance was created for a specific set of ranks. Adding or removing ranks requires a new instance. Even when that instance can be created in the background, two problems remain. First, the old and new instances need separate communication buffers and other resources, including memory registrations, IPC handles, and RDMA Queue Pairs (QPs). Keeping both instances alive increases communication memory usage and requires repeating setup rather than reusing existing resources. Second, switching EP communicators changes the buffers and communication state used by the EP communication kernels. This invalidates previously captured CUDA graphs, which must be recaptured before serving can resume. That requires repeating warmup and graph construction for many batch shapes across all retained workers. In our DeepSeek V4 Pro benchmark, even with asynchronous preparation, performing warmup and graph recapture during the commit phase resulted in serving pauses of **58 seconds during scale-up** and **44 seconds during scale-down**. To solve these problems, we designed **NIXL EP**, an EP communication library tailor-made for Elastic EP. It adds or removes ranks in place, reusing the same NIXL agent, buffers, and connections. New peers can be connected while existing workers continue serving, and only joining peers need new connections and registrations. NIXL EP also keeps captured EP dispatch and combine entries valid across reconfiguration, allowing retained workers to reuse their existing CUDA graphs. During preparation, vLLM's background thread connects joining peers without activating them. The commit phase then activates the prepared peers without replacing the communicator. ![The same NIXL EP communicator progresses from the current active group to connected inactive joining peers, then activates the target group at commit.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-05-elastic-ep-near-zero-downtime/figure02-nixl-ep-lifecycle.png) *Figure 1. Connecting and activating new EP peers. Green ranks are active; gray ranks are connected but masked. During the commit phase, new peers are activated without replacing the agent or buffers.* vLLM still creates new DP coordination groups and EPLB groups for the target topology, **but their communication runs outside the captured model forward pass**, so switching to them does not invalidate CUDA graphs. ## Preserve CUDA graphs on existing workers A CUDA graph records GPU operations so that vLLM can replay a forward pass without repeatedly launching each operation from the CPU. A captured kernel node includes its launch configuration and argument values, including pointers to input and output tensors. Memory contents can change between replays, but the recorded pointers must remain valid. These requirements are part of the [CUDA graph execution contract](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/cuda.html#cuda-graphs). vLLM [captures separate graphs for different batch shapes and execution modes](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/cuda_graphs/) and runs warmup forward passes before each capture. Preserving captured CUDA graphs requires more than keeping the communicator object alive. NIXL EP also keeps kernel launch configurations, graph-visible communication arguments, and input and output tensor addresses stable across reconfiguration. Its kernels read active group membership from device state that can be updated in place. We also changed vLLM to keep the captured arguments, launch configurations, and input and output tensor addresses of the surrounding compute kernels stable across reconfiguration: - We reuse retained workers' fused-MoE execution objects instead of rebuilding them for a different active EP size. - We keep the addresses and layouts of graph-visible workspaces and dispatch outputs stable across reconfiguration so that captured expert kernels can continue using them. Dispatch outputs also serve as inputs to expert computation. If their addresses or layouts changed with EP size, captured expert kernels would still use the old pointers and offsets. - We preserve the backing storage of expert-routing tensors and update mappings in place. This allows EPLB to change the mapping contents without moving the tensors used by captured kernels. Together, these changes allow retained workers to [reuse their existing CUDA graphs](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54985) after both scale-up and scale-down. ## Prepare joining workers independently Existing workers have graphs to preserve. Joining workers have none. Joining workers normally prepare by running model forward passes with EP dispatch and combine, as well as exchanging batch information with other workers. These steps require other workers to participate, but existing workers are already serving real requests on the current topology. NIXL EP lets each joining worker temporarily mask every remote EP peer during warmup and graph preparation. Only that worker's local rank is active for EP communication. We also modified vLLM so that these preparation passes do not wait for DP batch information from other workers. This lets joining workers run their dummy batches and capture CUDA graphs without requiring existing workers to participate. ![Existing workers serve with their current peers active and joining peers masked. Each joining worker keeps only itself active for local warmup and graph capture, masking all remote peers, including other joining workers.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-05-elastic-ep-near-zero-downtime/figure04-independent-capture.png) *Figure 2. Green ranks are active for EP communication; gray ranks are masked. Existing workers serve together while each joining worker masks all remote EP peers for preparation.* After capture, NIXL EP can reactivate peers without invalidating the graphs. Joining workers reuse their locally captured graphs when they begin serving as part of the expanded group. ## Performance on DeepSeek V4 Pro All experiments in this section used [DeepSeek V4 Pro](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro/tree/b5968e9190ef611bbf34a7229255be88a0e937c1) on GB200 GPUs, with TP=1 and DP/EP sizes of 16 and 20. Model weights were pre-downloaded in safetensors format on shared Lustre storage and loaded using the default `--load-format auto`. Measurements used warm kernel-compilation caches (Triton, TileLang, and FlashInfer). ### Scale-up and scale-down timings The table shows which stages run while serving is paused and which run in the background while existing workers continue serving. | Stage | A: Blocking | B: Async preparation | C: Async preparation + graph reuse | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Initialize joining workers | Serving paused | Background | Background | | Prepare target communication | Serving paused | Background | Background | | Transfer model weights | Serving paused | Background | Background | | Warmup and graph capture on joining workers | Serving paused | Serving paused | Background | | Warmup and graph capture on existing workers | Serving paused | Serving paused | Not needed (existing graphs stay valid) | | Activate the target topology | Serving paused | Serving paused | Serving paused | Configuration C is supported **only by NIXL EP**. - **Downtime:** the observed serving interruption, when in-flight requests stop progressing and new requests are not admitted. - **Total time:** the duration of the full scaling operation, including preparation. The next challenge is getting new capacity ready sooner. We plan to integrate [Dynamo Snapshot](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-dynamo-snapshot-fast-startup-for-inference-workloads-on-kubernetes/) so joining workers can restore initialized process and CUDA state instead of repeating compilation, kernel warmup, graph construction, and other startup work. Communication for the target topology must be prepared separately because it is not restored from the snapshot. Work toward this integration is already underway across the vLLM, Dynamo, and llm-d communities.
