For Kimi K3, we used agent-assisted development to build a unified CuTe DSL decode path on the NVIDIA GB300, covering attention, MoE, and communication across 8 or 16 GPUs. The optimizations deliver over **840 tokens/s** at batch 1 on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with DSpark (synthetic AL=6), **1.5–2×** higher decode throughput in several tested configurations, and up to **1.8×** higher P90 interactivity on the AgentX workload. Agent-optimized inference code is outpacing our review and maintenance workflow. The manual review process of understanding every line of every kernel, mapping out potential issues, and testing every supported configuration, is very time-consuming work. On the other hand, if we omit this work then we risk shipping buggy software that could fail in production. There is a clear line-of-sight on how to achieve both goals: we need to change how we organize performance work. Alongside agentic optimization, we need to design systems that allow automatic verification of reliability and performance, and we need to structure the software to enforce isolation and risk minimization by design. The proposed [fast-track model optimization RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59665) provides a foundation for this approach. Our guiding principle is to decrease review burden while managing *risk*. To accomplish this, we: 1. **Isolate changes.** Keep optimizations within the model’s code. 2. **Bound the scope, preserve the core features.** Define the supported hardware and workloads but preserve must-have features for production LLM use. 3. **Validate correctness systematically.** Run an established suite of performance and correctness benchmarks to ensure integrity and reliability, and strictly better performance on all supported configurations. 4. **Scale validation.** Let contributors run standard evaluations on their own GPUs and share reproducible results before requesting maintainer attention. Kimi K3 is our first contribution following this approach. This post covers how we optimized Kimi K3, how we build the confidence needed to ship and maintain those optimizations, and the performance results. ## Table of Contents - [Part 1: Optimizing Kimi K3](#part-1-optimizing-kimi-k3) - [Part 2: Moving Fast and Responsibly](#part-2-moving-fast-and-responsibly) - [Part 3: Performance Deep Dive](#part-3-performance-deep-dive) - [What's Next](#whats-next) - [Acknowledgements](#acknowledgements) ## Part 1: Optimizing Kimi K3 This contribution introduces a new decode path for Kimi K3 which fuses and replaces almost all operations with customized CuTe DSL kernels, tuned for certain subproblems. It targets NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with 8 or 16 GPUs, decode batches from 1 to 64, and optional decode context parallelism for long contexts. The GPUs share one NVLink domain with multicast support. [For more details, please refer to the PR](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61867#issue-5869895165). ![Kimi K3 kernel timeline: stock vLLM uses 130 microseconds and 23 kernels per layer; specialized decode uses 69 microseconds and 13 kernels.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel/kimi-k3-kernel-timeline.png?v=250506bea01d) ### 1. Tune shapes for the workload Different batch sizes need different kernel choices. For attention input projections, we use specialized small-matrix kernels at batch sizes 1–2 and split-K kernels at larger batches, which divide the matrix multiplication across more GPU workers. All such projections have been finely tuned to launch well-sized kernels that fully utilize GPU resources and overlap memory reads / communication and compute work as much as possible. [KDA](https://github.com/benchislett/vllm/blob/620c50482d15d092ad6086c106ce42916efc39cc/vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/specialized_decode/cutedsl/kda/prepared.py) also uses an optimized CuTe DSL decode kernel, with scheduling tuned for the batch size and number of attention heads on each GPU. For long contexts, decode context parallelism (DCP) splits the KV cache across GPUs. Each GPU computes attention over its local portion, and a tuned fused kernel combines the partial results with v-proj and gating. ### 2. Overlap computation and communication We fuse attention output projection directly to its all-reduce and the following attention-residual computation. GPU kernels publish partial results into NVLink-accessible buffers, and receiving kernels combine them and continue the computation. Some small-batch configurations fuse the producer and consumer into one kernel. Data exchange is done with a fence-less approach with minimal overhead. At larger batches, the implementation switches to a [two-stage reduction](https://github.com/benchislett/vllm/blob/620c50482d15d092ad6086c106ce42916efc39cc/vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/specialized_decode/cutedsl/oproj/prepared.py): GPUs first combine assigned portions of the output, then distribute the results. This reduces the data movement between GPUs. ### 3. Improve MoE scheduling and overlap Although the experts already use tensor parallelism, the baseline computes the full router scores and latent input projection on every GPU. We split these calculations across the TP ranks and combine each rank’s share into one matrix multiplication. The GPUs exchange the results over NVLink. This reduces repeated computation, weight reads, and kernel launches before expert execution begins. The shared expert runs on a separate stream. Its work overlaps with routing or routed-expert computation, depending on the configuration. The schedule controls how many GPU resources each operation uses, and is carefully tuned to ensure well-balanced parallelism without contention. Details are in [experts_runtime](https://github.com/benchislett/vllm/blob/620c50482d15d092ad6086c106ce42916efc39cc/vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/specialized_decode/cutedsl/moe/experts_runtime.py). ### 4. Prefetching upcoming weights into cache In small-batch inference, we are often memory-bound: limited by the speed with which we can load the weights from memory. Some phases cannot fully utilize the available memory bandwidth, such as communication: while this work happens we can run a dedicated kernel on a side stream to ensure that once the communication completes, the weights for the next operation will have a much higher cache hit rate. ## Part 2: Moving Fast and Responsibly Kimi K3 is just one of the first examples. We believe the community can build this together, to bring more models, GPUs, and workloads towards the speed of light. Different contributors/agents will find different opportunities: a better communication schedule, or a fusion that helps a particular deployment. But if every contribution arrives with different assumptions, incomplete tests, and a benchmark that is hard to reproduce, the validation and maintenance work quickly becomes the bottleneck, or we risk shipping broken code. We need a common way to turn those ideas into improvements that users can rely on for their long-term production use-cases. This changes what we ask agents to deliver. We should set clear expectations on testing, validations, and requirements for the code agents produce. Agents will construct tests, run comprehensive evaluations and benchmarks, investigate failures, and document the conditions under which the optimization works. Human reviewers still judge the design and the evidence, but they can start from a high-level abstraction, instead of a line-by-line code review. Building on the proposed [fast-track RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59665), we organize this work around four principles. ### 1. Isolate changes Keep model-specific optimizations within the model’s code. This makes the affected paths easier to identify and reduces the blast-radius a reviewer needs to consider. Isolation also needs to hold at runtime. Reviewers should be able to trace when the optimized path is selected, what state it changes, and how execution returns to the standard path. This constraint *does* exclude some optimizations: input preparation, sampling, and KV cache management can cause overhead that isolation excludes. This is a consequence of the design and is largely intentional: these components are all shared among most vLLM deployments, and changing them to optimize for a specific workload risks breaking dozens of other stable vLLM configurations. Work on these components is important, and should involve core maintainers much more closely than the fast-track would permit. ### 2. Bound the scope, but preserve the user’s features An optimization does not need to improve every deployment to be useful. It can target a particular GPU, parallelism setting, or range of batch sizes. Clear boundaries make the work easier to tune and give us a defined set of configurations to validate. For K3, the initial hardware validation covers GB300 with TP8 and TP16, decode batches up to 64, speculative decoding with various draft lengths, and decode context-parallel configurations within one NVLink domain. These boundaries describe where the optimization applies, but not cutting ‘feature coverage’. Production deployment needs fundamental features that make the endpoint useful. Features like full-context serving, temperature sampling, and structured output cannot be “optimized away” or “opt-out”, they are first-class serving features and belong to the validation plan alongside kernel shapes and numerical checks. ### 3. Validate correctness Kernel tests and model evaluations answer different questions. Kernel tests check numerical results across shapes and input values. Model evaluations check whether the complete execution path preserves the model’s answers. We need both. The tests must actually exercise the changed code. A small-batch optimization needs evaluation at small batches. An attention kernel change needs long-context coverage. Tests that silently use the standard path provide little evidence about the optimization and are a common trap. K3 development shows why this matters. Our audit discovered that the compiler moved activation reads ahead of a synchronization wait. The fix restricted that load type to static weights. Such errors can survive simple functional checks and require targeted investigation. Additionally, long-context and long-generation evaluations such as MRCR and AIME25 surfaced sensitive numerical issues in attention and communication kernels that were not reproducible in standalone kernel tests using mock inputs and/or consistent launch timings. ### 4. Check performance broadly A headline speedup is a starting point. We also need to know how the change behaves across the workloads it affects. That means sweeping batch sizes, context lengths, and supported parallelism configurations. MoE measurements should include real prompts because expert selection affects which weights are read and how much work can be reused. Pure decode results should also be distinguished from workloads that mix prefill and decode. Reliable validation also takes GPU time. The related [Bring-Your-Own-GPU evaluation RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/61698) proposes standard evaluation images that contributors can run on their own hardware. Reproducible result bundles and submissions linked to GitHub PRs would make the evidence much more accessible. Different evaluation tiers and shared community compute would help expand coverage while managing GPU demand and reducing pressure on project-funded CI. ## Part 3: Performance Deep Dive ### Decode performance with DSpark With DSpark, Kimi K3 reaches **842 tokens per second on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs** in the controlled AL=6 benchmark. That is **1.73× faster** than stock vLLM with the same speculative decoding setup. It preserves these workload patterns while replacing private content with synthetic text, testing the serving system under realistic agent traffic. [AgentX methodology](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/agentx). ![Kimi K3 AgentX results: P90 interactivity versus total throughput per GPU, comparing the earlier GB300 vLLM curve with specialized decode.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel/kimi-k3-agentx.png?v=bc3e36a7c869) ## What's Next For DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, [#61868](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61868) follows the K3 design patterns: behind the same opt-in `decode_backend: latency_specialized` switch, the implementation also supports up to 64 concurrent requests, seamless fallback for prefills and mixed batches, and speculative decoding. Instead of chasing a single hotspot, that executor cuts kernels and host work: it fuses all-reduce + mHC at every sublayer boundary, replaces the large-batch MoE and GEMMs with CuTe DSL kernels built for low-latency, deduplicates and shards the indexer’s work, and takes per-step work that stock vLLM runs eagerly on the CPU and replays it as a CUDA graph instead. ![DeepSeek AgentX results on four GB300 GPUs: P90 interactivity versus total throughput per GPU with and without optimized decode.](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel/deepseek-v41-flash-agentx.png?v=fb6493531579) Within two days of Meta’s [Muse Spark Open](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4) release, our early results already exceeded **950 tokens per second per user**, with seven draft tokens (K=7) and an acceptance length of six (AL=6). More optimizations are underway. We are also releasing a similar mechanism to optimize the decode latency for GLM5.3 under a low-concurrency scenario too. We’ll share its optimization details and performance results in a follow-up. For each contribution, we will continue to focus on concrete performance gains, production feature support, and reproducible correctness and performance checks. ## Acknowledgements We would like to thank Rohan Varma (NVIDIA) and Alex Steiner (NVIDIA) for their contributions to this work. On AgentX, an eight-GPU AMD Instinct MI355X system serving Kimi K3 with vLLM delivers **24.4% more total tokens per second per GPU** than NVIDIA HGX B300 at 50 tokens/s/user P90 interactivity. Under the benchmark’s ownership-cost model, it delivers **87.4% more tokens per dollar**. In this post, we’ll unpack the engineering behind Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X, connecting vLLM’s serving decisions to GPU kernels and the hardware underneath. We’ll explain why the optimizations worked and build the intuition to spot wasted work, identify bottlenecks and find the next optimization in your own inference stack. Published dense matrix peaks are 10.1 PFLOP/s MXFP4 for AMD Instinct MI355X and 13.5 PFLOP/s FP4 for NVIDIA B300. Both have 288 GB HBM3E and 8 TB/s peak memory bandwidth. Reaching this serving performance reflects sustained software engineering by AMD and collaborators across the vLLM community. ## AgentX: the workload and results The public [AgentX](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx) benchmark replays real coding-agent session traces with synthetic tokens, retaining request lengths, timing and prefix-sharing patterns. The workload offers over 96% theoretical prefix reuse with unlimited cache. Speculative runs use a fixed synthetic acceptance reference. At **50 tokens/s/user P90 interactivity**, AMD Instinct MI355X serves approximately **7,567 total tokens/s/GPU**, compared with **6,083 for NVIDIA HGX B300**, a **24.4% throughput advantage**. Using SemiAnalysis’s modeled TCO of **\$1.50 versus \$2.26 per GPU-hour**, respectively, that translates to **18.16 million versus 9.69 million total tokens per dollar of TCO: 87.4% more tokens per dollar**. The public curves compare complete serving stacks. The measurements beside each optimization come from separate tests and explain individual mechanisms under their stated configurations. ## Inside Kimi K3: experts, attention and recurrent state A returning agent turn can reuse most of its prefix, but processing a short continuation still touches three kinds of data. Kimi K3 uses two kinds of attention. Its **24 MLA layers** retain a compressed KV history that grows with the conversation. A new query still consults that history. Its **69 KDA layers** instead carry forward state matrices with fixed dimensions, updating them as new tokens arrive. [Model configuration](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3/blob/c5d1dd4c428bd1ce8b88c5044f3b6ccde9e3b721/config.json). In MoE layers, a router selects expert networks to transform each token. Their weights are shared across requests. **Across turns:** cache reuse and offload (Section 1).
**Within a model step:** expert projections, kernel handoffs, and MLA/KDA scheduling (Sections 2–5).
**Choosing draft depth:** committed output versus complete cycle cost (Section 6). ## 1. Cache: keep conversation state available for reuse DCP reduces duplicate history in GPU memory; CPU offload preserves reusable state outside it. ### DCP: share the history across GPUs Under TP8, each GPU handles 12 of Kimi K3’s 96 MLA query heads but stores the entire compressed KV history. Tensor parallelism divides the heads without dividing the cache. With [eight-way decode context parallelism (DCP8)](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-08-07-decode-context-parallelism), each GPU stores one eighth of the cached positions. During decode, the GPUs exchange queries, compute against their local history and merge their partial answers. Each partial answer carries normalization information so the merge can weight shards correctly. [#51705](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51705) extends the ROCm AITER DCP path to multi-token verification. For a 142,000-token conversation, the estimated MLA payload is 24 layers × 142,000 positions × 576 FP8 bytes ≈ 1.96 GB per GPU. DCP8 reduces this to about 245 MB, before allocation overhead. Each GPU processes eight times as many heads against one eighth of the history, leaving the leading attention arithmetic roughly unchanged. ### CPU offload: keep state that no longer fits in HBM When state no longer fits in GPU memory, the [AMD recipe](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/blob/8adb5c5589b84c0afdccc60bab521eb1114f52b5/inferencex-e2e/benchmarks/single_node/srt-slurm-recipes/kimik3/vllm/mi355x-fp4-mtp/agentic.yaml)’s native vLLM CPU offload preserves MLA history and KDA checkpoints in host DRAM. A cache hit needs matching resume points. If MLA history reaches token 3,072 but the latest compatible KDA checkpoint is at 2,048, the request must resume at 2,048 and recompute the remaining prefix. Saving the attention-block tail alongside the KDA checkpoint aligns their resume positions ([#54736](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54736)). Restoring that state trades a transfer back to the GPU for avoided prefix recomputation. Once a request resumes, its new tokens can still make several GPUs repeat the same calculation. ## 2. MoE: remove duplicate work across GPUs On one GPU, the routed-expert output projection returns the complete vector its consumer expects. In the original ROCm path, an earlier reduction and normalization gave all eight GPUs the same latent input, and each held the full weights. **The same projection therefore ran eight times.** The output coordinates can be divided among GPUs, but every rank still needs the complete result. Kimi K3 already has an all-reduce for its shared-expert partials. Each GPU adds only the routed outputs it owns to its shared-expert partial. The existing all-reduce assembles the complete result, with no new collective ([#51253](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51253)). The ROCm implementation builds on the corresponding CUDA strategy. Each output coordinate receives its routed contribution exactly once. The full projection weights remain replicated. Output throughput rose 3.05–4.91% in the PR’s test on eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs at TP8, across concurrency 8–128 with random 8K-input/1K-output requests and prefix caching disabled. ### Free up GPU memory to keep more cached state Each rank now computes only its assigned projection coordinates while retaining the full weights. Loading only the rows each rank uses frees about **3.85 GiB per GPU** across 92 MoE layers at TP8 ([#59591](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59591)). The fused path’s calculation stays the same; the extra space can hold MLA history and KDA checkpoints. This change landed after the image used for the headline public result. Its separate AgentX experiment found **less than 1% higher throughput at concurrency 32 and 48, but 28.9% at 70**, where the reported prefix-cache hit rate rose from 74.8% to 80.1%. The larger gain at high concurrency is consistent with cache pressure. Comparing both implementations at equal cache capacity would help isolate that effect. More on [expert routing and four-bit activations](#technical-note-expert-routing-and-precision). ## 3. Memory traffic: fuse operations and remove unnecessary copies Within each GPU, the next place to look is the data passed between kernels. Kimi K3’s single-token KDA path ran three compute kernels and two output copies. Convolution ran before a kernel that already fused Q/K normalization, decay and beta gates, and the recurrent update; output normalization ran afterward. The fused HIP path performs these operations in one launch and writes directly to the destination buffer ([#50654](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50654)). Intermediate handoffs stay on chip. Convolution history and recurrent state still go to GPU memory for the next token. AttnRes mixes earlier layer-block outputs with the running residual. Combining that mix with RMSNorm keeps the temporary mixture in registers ([#50593](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50593)). The running residual saved for later layers retains its BF16 rounding; the mixture stays in FP32 through normalization. Tests require exact persistent updates and allow numerical tolerances for normalized output. With AttnRes fusion, output throughput rose 14.2% on eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs at TP8, with 100K-input/1K-output requests and prefix caching disabled. Long-prefill latency was effectively unchanged. ### Copy inputs only for kernels that use them The ROCm matrix-multiplication dispatcher packed inputs before choosing a kernel. When it selected the fallback, that kernel read the original input and left the copy unused. Moving packing into the specialized branches removed these copies ([#58566](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58566)). The profile made the waste visible: **69 unnecessary copies per decode step**, one per KDA layer. Each moved only 1,792 bytes but took about 4.8 microseconds. Moving those bytes faster would barely help; launch overhead dominated. ## 4. MLA: faster long-context decoding with AMD AITER assembly Kimi K3 has twelve query heads per GPU at TP8. Padding to sixteen made AMD AITER’s assembly decode path available. In the reported long-context test, time per output token fell from 43.8 to 23.6 milliseconds. The comparison used TP8 without DCP, at concurrency one. The adapter in [#50578](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50578) copies four query heads, packs them into the sixteen-head layout and discards their outputs. DCP8 presents a different, 96-head shape. This preserves the model's operation because each query head attends independently over cached positions. Adding another head does not change the original head's softmax. Only the query is padded in this decode path; the stored compressed KV history stays the same size. A long conversation gives attention plenty of work, but that work needs to be spread across the GPU. In the historical code we inspected, a conservative [scheduling hint](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/7b9f2dad8920f115c1caea36e096e43c04c3da68/vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/rocm_aiter_mla.py#L1092) restricted the Gluon path to [one workgroup per request](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/blob/31350226161346314b3d8882c8085bd31dce6a34/aiter/ops/triton/gluon/mla_gluon.py#L937). That workgroup still processed the entire conversation. Padding made AMD AITER’s assembly path available, with a [different policy](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/blob/31350226161346314b3d8882c8085bd31dce6a34/aiter/mla.py#L149) for dividing the history into parallel pieces and combining the results. | **Input / output tokens** | **Original Gluon path** | **Padded assembly path** | | --- | --- | --- | | 1K / 1K | 22.9 ms/token | 22.8 ms/token | | 32K / 1K | 43.8 ms/token | 23.6 ms/token | PR-reported mean time per output token: eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, TP8, concurrency one, MXFP4 model weights, BF16 attention and ordinary single-token decode. The short-input case barely changes; the long-input case nearly halves time per output token. These serving measurements include query preparation and output handling. ## 5. KDA: parallelize prefill and speculative verification MLA can split a retained history among workgroups. KDA presents a harder scheduling problem: each token depends on the preceding state. Fused prefill in [#54038](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54038) prepares each token group’s combined transformation before its incoming state is known. For example, “halve the state and add two,” then “halve it and add one,” combine into “take a quarter of the starting state and add two.” This rule can be computed before the starting state arrives.
Step through the KDA dependency sequence
KDA does this with matrix transformations. An ordered scan of the group summaries determines each group’s starting state; the groups then replay their tokens in parallel. Token order stays intact, but each group no longer waits for the preceding group’s replay. Grouping adds a second walk and expands the fused chunk path from two launches to four. It helps when few sequences or heads expose too little parallel work; otherwise, the extra passes can cost more than they save. Within each group, the recurrent walk keeps state in matrix-accumulator registers between chunks, avoiding a global-memory write and reload. [State storage diagram.](#state-between-chunks) Fused KDA delivered 5.3–5.6% more input throughput than Triton at 4K and 16K input lengths in a separate three-backend comparison: eight AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, TP8, concurrency 32, prefix caching disabled and one-token outputs. This measures the complete backend. [Benchmark results](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56036#issuecomment-5667437134). ### Use smaller tiles for speculative verification Short verification batches need a different split. At TP8, each GPU has 12 KDA heads with 128 value columns. Splitting each head into four 32-column tiles launches only 48 workgroups on 256 compute units. [#58045](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58045) switches to four-column tiles, raising the count to 384. In a separate graph-replay kernel test on one AMD Instinct MI355X GPU (TP8 dimensions, one sequence, four verification positions), time fell from 16.20 to 5.61 microseconds per layer (2.89×). This includes narrower tiles, single-wave workgroups, uniform-length specialization and hoisted token-invariant work. Ragged batches retain a dynamic path; tests compare outputs and recurrent state. ## 6. Speculative decoding: choose how many tokens to draft Faster verification can change how many draft tokens are worth checking. The useful rate is committed output divided by the full draft–verify–commit cycle time. For example, AgentX’s fixed acceptance reference gives 3.00 expected committed tokens per cycle with three drafts, and 3.36 with four, including the recovery or bonus token. That is 12% more committed output per cycle. **Four drafts improve throughput only if the complete cycle takes less than 12% longer than three drafts.** The [public AMD recipe](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/blob/8adb5c5589b84c0afdccc60bab521eb1114f52b5/inferencex-e2e/benchmarks/single_node/srt-slurm-recipes/kimik3/vllm/mi355x-fp4-mtp/agentic.yaml) uses three to seven drafts with DCP1 and disables speculation at the larger DCP8 concurrency settings. ## What to optimize next Ongoing prefill/decode disaggregation work adds another place to look: worker balance and whether transfers finish before their data is needed. For another model or workload, start with the deployed request shapes and make three checks: **Compare ranks.** Are several GPUs computing the same result before a collective that could assemble it? **Follow buffers.** Does each temporary tensor have a consumer on the selected path? Can the data stay on chip? **Count independent work.** Do the actual heads, tokens and tiles produce enough workgroups to spread the load? Measure the complete request at the response speed you need, and check both outputs and saved state. A faster kernel matters when it shortens the work holding up the next token. ## Contributions and acknowledgments The Kimi K3 effort spans **more than 50 merged AMD/ROCm-related vLLM PRs** from AMD, Embedded LLM and the wider community, alongside AITER development, integration, review and benchmarking. Contributions cover attention, recurrence, MoE, quantization, graph execution, cache support and platform integration. ## Technical note: expert routing and precision Kimi K3 selects 16 of 896 experts per token, so a substantial server batch can still leave few rows per expert. The resulting expert tiles may contain padding. A4W4 reduces a different part of the traffic: the integration in [#53940](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53940) changes activations from eight bits to four, while weights remain four-bit. Total traffic also includes BF16 intermediate outputs and expert-tile padding.
## Technical note: KDA precision and on-chip memory Each chunk still needs to resolve dependencies between its tokens. The kernel combines them into a transformation that later matrix products can apply. That creates two practical questions: which precision preserves the answer, and how much temporary data fits on chip? A small example shows the idea. Substitute the earlier corrections into the later ones, and each answer can be expressed directly in terms of the known inputs. The resulting coefficient table has already accounted for the chain of dependencies: The real prologue computes the inverse of the 64×64 within-chunk dependency matrix. Later matrix products use this transformation to account for those dependencies. The inverse's intermediate values can grow and cancel. Rounding them too early loses information the final result needs. The implementation uses AMD's native [**FP32 matrix instructions**](https://www.amd.com/content/dam/amd/en/documents/instinct-tech-docs/instruction-set-architectures/amd-instinct-cdna4-instruction-set-architecture.pdf#page=295), retaining FP32 inputs and accumulation for the sensitive inverse. Only the completed inverse is rounded to BF16 for subsequent products. [Kernel implementation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/af1c01499b289be555c475669ba50a88e96d846e/csrc/libtorch_stable/kimi_k3/fused_kda_chunk_kernel_rocm.cu#L1639). ### Why FP32 accumulation cannot recover rounded inputs Consider subtracting 256 from 256.5. Both inputs are exact in FP32. At this magnitude, converting 256.5 to BF16 rounds it to 256: | **Input precision** | **Subtraction performed in FP32** | **Result** | | --- | --- | --- | | Keep the original FP32 inputs | 256.5 − 256 | 0.5 | | Round the inputs to BF16 first | 256 − 256 | 0 | FP32 subtraction cannot recover information lost before it starts. These toy values illustrate why the inverse uses native 16×16×4 FP32 matrix instructions, retaining both input and accumulation precision. An FP4 model also relies on operations at higher precision. Their performance depends on making those numerical paths efficient. The prologue also has a local-memory budget. AMD calls its on-chip shared scratch LDS. Q and K tiles reuse storage because they are needed at different times; the triangular input stores only its ten occupied 16×16 blocks. The workgroup requests **79.5 KiB**, which rounds to **80 KiB**, half of an AMD CDNA 4 compute unit’s [160 KiB LDS budget](https://www.amd.com/content/dam/amd/en/documents/instinct-tech-docs/instruction-set-architectures/amd-instinct-cdna4-instruction-set-architecture.pdf#page=14). Test this threshold by reserving enough unused LDS to cross it while keeping the kernel binary fixed. If runtime barely changes, the extra resident workgroup was contributing little for that shape. ### State between chunks [Return to the KDA serving result](#KDAResume).

--- # Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0 Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-reflection-beam Published: 2026-10-16 Authors: Inferact, Reflection, and Nvidia Tags: reflection, performance, kernels, speculative-decoding Summary: vLLM supports Reflection's Beam-1.0 (501B total, 23B active) from day 0, with agent-driven optimization that cut decode latency 2.71× and DFlash2 speculative decoding with adaptive verification. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-reflection-beam/hero.png) **TL;DR:** Reflection's Beam is a 501B-parameter MoE with 23B active parameters per token. vLLM supports it from day 0 and optimizes it on NVIDIA Blackwell: - **Full feature support.** Reasoning, tool calling, and structured outputs work out of the box, and you can run the model with tensor, data, or expert parallelism. - **Agent-driven optimization.** Coding agents optimized the model autonomously, making batch-1 decode 2.71× faster and prefill 1.87× faster than our first implementation. - **DFlash2 with adaptive verification.** With Beam's DFlash2 drafter, a single request reaches **708 tokens/s** on TP8, with an acceptance length of 3.7. Adaptive verification, which decides each step how many draft tokens are worth verifying, adds **10% more throughput** at high concurrency. To try it, use our Docker image `vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam`: ```bash docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ vllm/vllm-openai:reflection-beam \ reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ -tp 4 \ --max-num-seqs 128 \ --reasoning-parser beam \ --tool-call-parser beam --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER"}' \ --kernel-config '{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false}' \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2", "num_speculative_tokens": 7, "attention_backend": "FLASH_ATTN" }' ``` ## Model architecture Beam is a 52-layer MoE decoder with hidden size 5120. The MoE routing follows DeepSeek-V3. The main differences are in the attention layers and in how the residual stream is normalized. *Figure 1: Beam's layer stack and one sparse decoder layer. Gold marks the parts that differ from a standard pre-norm MoE. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/beam-arch.html).* ### Attention - **Hybrid sliding-window and NoPE layers.** 43 layers use sliding-window attention over the last 512 tokens, with RoPE. The other 9 (every sixth layer, plus the last) attend over the full context with **no positional encoding (NoPE)**. - **SSMax on NoPE layers.** Without RoPE, attention flattens as the number of keys grows. SSMax scales each query by `(1 + p/2048)^0.1`, where `p` is the 1-based position, so the softmax sharpens as the context grows. - **GQA with per-head Q/K norm.** 48 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128. Q and K are RMS-normalized per head before RoPE or SSMax. - **Sigmoid output gate.** Before `o_proj`, each head's output is multiplied by σ(gate + bias), where the gate comes from its own full-width projection with a learned per-head bias. A head can be turned down or off token by token. - **Small KV cache.** Only the 9 full-attention layers keep KV for the whole sequence: - 9 × 2 × 8 × 128 values per token, or 36 KiB in BF16 and 18 KiB in FP8. - About 18 GiB of FP8 KV for a full 1M-token context, before sharding. ### MoE and residual stream - **DeepSeek-V3-style MoE.** 256 routed experts (d_ff 2,560, NVFP4), routed the same way as DeepSeek-V3: sigmoid scores plus a correction bias pick the best 4 of 8 expert groups, then the top 8 experts, and the renormalized weights are scaled by 2.5. Unlike DeepSeek-V3, there is no shared expert. Layers 0–2 use a dense SwiGLU MLP (d_ff 20,480) instead. - **FP32 router.** The 5120 × 256 router weights, accumulation, and logits are all FP32. - **Sandwich norm.** Every sublayer has an RMSNorm before it and another after it. - **Depth-scaled residuals.** The *n*-th residual add computes `h ← √((n−1)/n)·h + x/√n` instead of `h + x`. With unit-variance sublayer outputs, the residual stream keeps unit variance at every depth instead of growing with it. ## Agent-driven optimization Our initial version of implementation was an unoptimized, almost pure PyTorch version of the model. We then optimized it autonomously with coding agents: they profiled the model, wrote the kernels, and benchmarked each change. On TP8, the seven changes below brought batch-1 decode from 8.95 ms to 3.30 ms per step, and an 8 × 2K prefill from 328 ms to 176 ms. *Figure 2: TP8 model-forward latency on GB200 after each change, for batch-1 decode and an 8 × 2,048-token prefill at ~100K context. The two panels use different scales. Show the table for exact values, or [open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/beam-opt-chart.html).* 1. **Fused norm → residual → norm** (−40% decode). The post-norm, scaled residual add, and next pre-norm at each of the 104 sublayer boundaries now run as one Triton kernel, with FP32 math and the reference's BF16 rounding points. 2. **Fused Q/K norm, RoPE/SSMax, and output gate.** Per-head Q/K RMSNorm and RoPE (or SSMax) run as one kernel, and the sigmoid gate as another. 3. **All-reduce fused into the norms.** Both TP all-reduces in each layer run inside the norm kernel, built on FlashInfer's multicast all-reduce. After the MoE, the same kernel also combines the top-8 expert outputs. 4. **Specialized GEMM kernel for the FP32 router.** The router used to fall back to a generic path. vLLM's small-batch FP32 router kernel now supports Beam's 5120 × 256 shape, keeping FP32 weights, accumulation, and logits. 5. **Merged QKV + gate projection with a low-latency GEMM.** The Q, K, V, and gate weights are packed into one matrix at load time, so the four projections run as one GEMM. For small batches it uses a low-latency CuTe DSL GEMM or FlashInfer's TinyGEMM. 6. **Fused KV-cache update.** The Q/K norm and RoPE kernel now also writes K and V into the KV cache, so there is no separate cache-write kernel. 7. **Dense-MLP activation in one kernel** for the three dense layers. ## The fused graph After these changes, one MoE layer runs as **13 kernels** in batch-1 decode on TP8. *Figure 3: Kernels in launch order for one MoE layer, from a rank-0 trace of batch-1 TP8 decode. Gold kernels were written, fused, or extended for Beam. Each kernel lists the operations it computes. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/beam-fused-graph.html).* - **6 kernels were written, fused, or extended for Beam.** Every small Beam-specific op is merged into a neighbor, and both all-reduces live inside norm kernels. - **7 kernels come from libraries:** TRTLLM-gen attention, the cuBLAS output projection, and the TRTLLM NVFP4 MoE path (quantization, two routing kernels, two grouped GEMMs). Most of the remaining time is here, so they are next. ## Attention DP + MegaMoE ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-reflection-beam/megamoe.png) *Figure 4: FlashInfer CuteDSL NVFP4 MegaMoE can fuse the communications with expert computation.* In the high concurrency region, Beam's performance can be further improved by combining Attention DP with MegaMoE, powered by FlashInfer's CuTe DSL NVFP4 MegaMoE kernel. The Finalize + norm boundary fusion remains applicable. | Configuration | Peak input token throughput | |:---|:---| | Attention DP + MegaMoE | 168.8K tokens / second | | TP (`flashinfer_trtllm`, `flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`) | 98.7K tokens / second | Attention DP with MegaMoE delivered 1.71× higher peak prefill throughput than TP4. Benchmark setup: 4×GB300, with an input sequence length of 32K tokens and an output sequence length of 1 token to isolate prefill performance. To enable Attention DP + MegaMoE, replace the MoE and parallel settings with: ```bash --moe-backend flashinfer_moe_ep_cutedsl \ --data-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel ``` ## DFlash2 speculative decoding Beam ships with a **DFlash2** draft head, which vLLM supports from day 0. Instead of drafting one token at a time, it predicts a whole block of tokens in a single forward pass from the target model's hidden states. - **Drafter.** 5 sliding-window layers that read hidden states from 5 target layers and share the target's embedding and LM head. A grouped convolution and a small candidate selector restore some of the left-to-right dependency a parallel drafter loses. - **Adaptive verification.** With `"enable_adaptive_verification": true`, vLLM predicts how likely each draft token is to be accepted and verifies only the ones worth their cost, instead of a fixed number per step. DFlash2 has no confidence head, so the acceptance estimate comes from the drafter's own logits (see our [recent post on adaptive verification](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-adaptive-verification-online-estimator)). - **Kernels.** The drafter's convolution, norms, and KV writes are fused, and the whole draft step runs in a CUDA graph. FP8 KV cache works for the drafter too, with no change in acceptance. Serving results on TP8, with and without adaptive verification, on the low-entropy category of [SPEED-Bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/SPEED-Bench)'s `throughput_1k` split: ~1K-token prompts, mostly code completion and text sorting, with greedy decoding and up to 4K output tokens. Low-entropy text is easier to predict, so expect lower acceptance on open-ended chat. | Concurrency | Fixed draft (tok/s) | Adaptive (tok/s) | Change | Acceptance length | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 708 | 707 | −0.1% | 3.71 → 3.61 | | 8 | 3,232 | 3,221 | −0.3% | 3.67 → 3.57 | | 32 | 7,744 | 8,275 | +6.9% | 3.68 → 3.29 | | 128 | 15,012 | 16,632 | +10.8% | 3.68 → 3.23 | Adaptive verification pays off under load. At concurrency 128 it raises output throughput by 10.8% and cuts p99 TPOT by 9%, while verifying fewer draft tokens per step, which lowers acceptance length slightly but saves more compute than it loses. At low concurrency, where extra draft tokens are nearly free, it is neutral. ## AgentX benchmark ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-reflection-beam/agentx.png) *Figure 5: Beam 1.0 NVFP4 AgentX benchmark showing up to 88K total tok/s per GPU and up to 350 tok/s per user on GB300.* We also tested Beam on AgentX, which replays multi-turn coding conversations to measure serving performance. With DFlash2, vLLM reached approximately 88K total tokens/s per GPU at 96 concurrent requests. Total throughput counts input and output tokens, including cached input. Input-token cache hit rates ranged from 91.4% to 95.6% across the sweep. AgentX benchmark configuration: Beam 1.0 NVFP4 on 4× GB300 with TP4/EP1 and FP8 KV cache for both target and drafter. DFlash2 uses real acceptance (average AL 3.6 across measured points), block size 8, and probabilistic sampling. AgentX uses trajectory ratios 0.55–0.75, maximum reasoning effort, temperature 1.0, and 20 minutes per point. Total throughput includes cached input tokens. Source commits: vLLM 8e0922. ## Getting started The command at the top of this post is a good default: TP4 on a single GB300 node, with DFlash2 and FP8 KV cache. To enable adaptive verification, add `"enable_adaptive_verification": true` to the `--speculative-config`. Other optimizations above are on by default. - **Choosing a parallel setup.** - For the lowest latency, use TP4 or TP8. - For higher throughput, use data-parallel attention with expert parallelism, e.g. `-dp 4 --enable-expert-parallel`. - **Reasoning and tool calling.** The `beam` parsers read the response template that ships with the checkpoint. By default, vLLM also constrains every response to that template, so tool calls always parse and match each tool's JSON schema. `response_format` and `thinking_token_budget` work as usual. To turn the default constraint off, set `VLLM_BEAM_ALWAYS_CONSTRAIN_OUTPUT=0`. ## Day 0 Support for RL with SkyRL We also collaborated with the SkyRL team to enable Day 0 support for RL on Beam. LoRA, BF16 full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL are supported out of the box, with an upgraded RL stack for the 500B scale. The SkyRL team post-trained the Beam model on the DAPO recipe with vLLM for inference and Megatron for training. LoRA, full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL achieve similar gains in performance in 50 training steps, or 100 optimizer updates (reasoning `minimal`), with an average accuracy (avg@8) jump from ~61% to ~79% on AIME25. Average absolute log-probability difference between Megatron and vLLM stays under 0.01 with Rollout Routing Replay (R3) enabled for LoRA and BF16 full fine-tuning, and under 0.03 for MXFP8 RL. ![](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-16-reflection-beam/skyrl-rl.png) Check out the SkyRL [blog](https://blog.skyrl.ai/day-0-beam) for more details! ## Acknowledgements This work was a close collaboration between the Inferact, Reflection, and Nvidia teams: - **Inferact:** Woosuk Kwon, Ziqi Zhao, Ao Shen, Tiezhen Wang - **Reflection:** Kaixing Wu, Yoni Gozlan, Neil Gollapudi, Thibaut Barroyer, Aymen Kallala, Matthias Reso, Florent Gbelidji - **Nvidia:** Siyuan Fu, Jinze Xue --- # Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-15-muse-spark-open Published: 2026-10-15 Authors: vLLM Team Tags: model-support, speculative-decoding, reinforcement-learning Summary: Day-0 vLLM support for Muse Spark Open: 816B MoE, 1M context, multimodal inputs, DSpark speculative decoding, NVIDIA and AMD serving, initial TPU support, and LoRA RL. ![Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-15-muse-spark-open/hero-vllm-muse-spark-open.png) We're excited to have worked with Meta Superintelligence Labs to bring Muse Spark Open to vLLM on day 0. Muse Spark Open is an open-weight sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, built for long-horizon agentic coding workflows. It is the most capable US open-weights model to date and it is the model Muse Glimmer 30B was distilled from. ## Highlights - Architecture: 816B total parameters, 42B active per token with a 1M context window. - Quantization: Meta released the model in both BF16 and NVFP4. MXFP4 weights were released by AMD. - Multimodal: Native image and video perception through the same Perception Encoder as Muse Glimmer, with additional audio support. - Parallelism: Tensor Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism on both Nvidia and AMD. EP, TEP, DEP and PD disaggregation on Nvidia. Initial support on TPU is also available. - Speculative decoding: We have trained a DSpark draft model, supported on both CUDA and ROCm that accelerates the model performance, tested on the SPEED bench. ## Usage Prebuilt images are available for both vendors: - Nvidia: vllm/vllm-openai:muse-spark-open - AMD: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:muse-spark-open Note that the model will only be available at nightly PyPI wheel after the code ([PR #61879](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61879)) is reviewed and merged, which usually takes about a week. ```bash # Rust frontend is recommended export VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 vllm serve meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 1048576 \ --reasoning-parser muse \ --tool-call-parser muse \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model": "Inferact/Muse-Spark-Open-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}' ``` To use this model with plain text: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this module."}], "reasoning_effort": "xhigh" }' ``` For multimodal perception: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/screenshot.png"}}, {"type": "video_url", "video_url": {"url": "https://example.com/demo.mp4"}}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": "https://example.com/clip.wav"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "What is happening here, and when?"} ]}] }' ``` ## Implementation details ### Model architecture *Figure 1: One of the 62 identical decoder layers. Every block is normalized before and after, `x + post_norm(F(norm(x)))`. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/muse-spark-open-decoder-layer.html).* Muse Spark Open is a mixture-of-experts model with 816B total parameters including the text decoder, plus a 2B vision encoder and a small audio encoder alongside it. The decoder has 62 layers, and every one of them is a mixture-of-experts layer. Here is where the weights sit: | part | size | |------------------------------|--------------------| | 256 experts per layer | 799 B | | attention | 13.5 B | | MoE latent projections | 4.2 B | | embedding and output layer | 3.3 B | | vision tower (separate) | 1.9 B | The model architecture is similar to Muse Glimmer. For folks who haven't used Muse Glimmer. There are a few things in this model architecture worth a closer look. *Figure 2: Inside the attention block. Queries and keys are normalized before they meet, and each head's output is normalized before a learned gate scales it. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/muse-spark-open-attention.html).* **Sandwich normalization.** Most decoders put one normalization layer before each block, giving x + F(norm(x)) Muse Spark Open, similar to Muse Glimmer, place one before and one after, like the two slices of a sandwich with the block sitting in between, giving x + post_norm(F(norm(x))) *Figure 3: The mixture-of-experts block. A shared squeeze halves each token from 8192 to 4096 before the experts and an expand restores 8192 after. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/muse-spark-open-moe.html).* **Latent MoE**. Every mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer carries two extra matrices, shared by all 256 experts in that layer. The code calls them the pooler and unpooler, though neither is pooling in the usual sense, instead both are learned projections to squeeze and expand the dimensions. The pooler is an 8192 × 4096 matrix that halves each token's width before it reaches the experts; while the unpooler restores the full width afterwards. The experts therefore work entirely at 4096 rather than 8192, which effectively halved the number of parameters required in the two expert projection layers. *Figure 4: Which layers attend to what. 46 of the 62 layers keep a 2048-token window of KV and 16 keep every token, so the KV cache at 1M tokens is about a quarter of all-full attention. [Open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/muse-spark-open-attention-pattern.html).* **Hybrid attention.** Layers alternate between full attention and Sliding Window Attention (SWA) on a repeating cycle of 4 with three attending to a 2048-token window and the fourth looking at the whole context. The cycle is anchored to the end of the stack so the final layer is always a full attention layer. Across 62 layers, that gives 46 narrow layers and 16 wide ones where the narrow layers only hold recent KV. At 1M tokens, this brings the cache to just over ¼ of what all-full attention would need. This is what makes 1M context length affordable. **Vision Encoder.** Muse Spark Open uses the same Perception Encoder as Muse Glimmer, a 2B parameter tower that reads images at their native resolution, rather than resizing them to a square. Videos run through the same encoder: frames are sampled at load time as a series of sampled video frames with timestamp tokenized in the prompt. **Audio Encoder.** Audio is read as raw waveform at 24 kHz and Every 1920 samples, i.e. 80ms become one token through a series of transformations. The whole audio encoder is just 118M parameters. Note that the video's audio track is not processed. To give the model both the pictures and the sound of a clip, send the video and the extracted audio as two separate content parts in the same request. ### DSpark To accelerate Muse Spark Open inference on vLLM, we trained a speculator using DSpark, a speculative decoding algorithm that uses block diffusion to propose up to seven draft tokens in a single pass. Confidence-based scheduling helps sustain significant speedups even at large batch sizes, where speculative decoding traditionally offers diminishing returns, as shown in the results below. *Figure 5: Aggregate output throughput against per-user decode speed on 4 × NVIDIA GB300 (TP4), one point per concurrency level from c1 to c256. Hover a point for every series' values, or [open it full-screen](/assets/interactive_pages/muse-spark-open-dspark-throughput.html).* Our speculator also uses the Muse Spark Open sliding-window attention to keep drafting lightweight, even with a 1M-token context. Together, these choices make it well suited to production workloads spanning a wide range of batch sizes and context lengths. To enable it, add this when the server starts: ```bash --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model": "Inferact/Muse-Spark-Open-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}' ``` ### Nvidia Nvidia team improved Muse Spark Open inference across FlashInfer and vLLM through fused normalization, gating, and residual kernels; fused MoE finalization with tensor-parallel communication and RMSNorm; a new low-latency BF16 GEMM implementation and reduced compilation overhead; TEP pooler/unpooler sharding with fused MNNVL collectives; TF32 router GEMM fed by the norm's FP32 output; and improvements to data movement, hardware support, and runtime reliability. ### AMD Thanks to the AMD team, we have also supported the model on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, in both FP8 and MXFP4 quantized formats, providing improved inference performance and deployment efficiency. Note that ROCm currently supports both Tensor-Parallel and Pipeline-Parallelism. ### TPU We have added support for Muse Spark Open on TPU on top of TorchTPU. Please contact us or Google for code access. We have also built [megakernels](https://github.com/Inferact/tpu-megakernels) for Muse Spark Open. With DSpark speculative decoding (acceptance length = 6), they reach over 650 tokens/sec on 4 TPU v7 chips and over 960 tokens/sec on 8 chips. Without speculative decoding, they still deliver over 270 and 350 tokens/sec, respectively. ## Reinforcement learning in vLLM vLLM also supports LoRA RL on Muse Spark Open from day 0, serving as the rollout engine with Verl FSDP2 as the trainer. vLLM serves the original NVFP4 checkpoint with the LoRA adapter applied on top. The trainer runs on a BF16 dequantization of the same weights and updates only the adapter (rank 32, alpha 64), which covers attention, the MoE latent projections and all routed experts. It also replays the rollout’s MoE routing (R3), and only the adapter is synced back to vLLM after each step. We trained with GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K for 150 steps on 16 GB300 GPUs, sampling 8 responses for each of 32 prompts per step with up to 4K tokens per response. The accuracy on AIME-2024 (mean@8) went from 0.56 before training to 0.85 by the end of the run. Throughout the run, the k3 KL between the trainer’s and vLLM’s log-probabilities held near 2×10⁻⁴. More details are available in https://github.com/verl-project/verl/pull/8257. In the vLLM ecosystem, Titan RL also uses vLLM as its rollout engine to provide day-0 RL support. ![Muse Spark Open LoRA RL results](/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-15-muse-spark-open/lora-rl-results.png) ## Acknowledgement We extend our sincere gratitude to the teams at Meta Superintelligence Labs and the vLLM community for their close collaboration in delivering Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM. We also thank Inferact for training the DSpark speculator and TPU integration, alongside NVIDIA and AMD for their vital hardware optimizations.
